en: Om. Salutations to the venerable gurus;
salutations to the illustrious Sundaragaṇapati.
The Thousandfold Tantra:
Oṃ,
the Eightfold Binding— Re 15540.
Notes: • Words or letters within brackets are my suggestions (to the extent of my understanding).
• Dots (... are used to indicate missing portions, damage to a leaf, or unidentified characters.
• Generally nine to eleven lines per side • i = "image" • (#) = line number
Hariḥ Om!

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the procedure for the eightfold binding (aṣṭabandha), which removes all sins, is meritorious, brings about all perfections, and is auspicious. (I.4b)

One should practice the eightfold restraint (*aṣṭabandhana*), which brings about the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, bestows auspiciousness upon all the world, and results in the cessation of all faults.
When the king suffers a defeat in battle characterized by eightfold bondage, it becomes difficult for him to overcome; moreover, affliction befalls the world through Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas.
In the case of one who is free from the eight bonds, however, there is worship and the offering of food;
likewise, the ritual oblation, the daily festival, prostration, and circumambulation.
Dancing, singing, and instrumental music— whether performed regularly or on special occasions— as well as all ritual services, are ordained to be fruitless [if performed otherwise].
One should know that in the east there is strife, while in the southeast there is burning by fire;
in the south there is illness and suffering, and in the southwest there is the destruction of the village.
In the northwest there will be the destruction of rain; in the north, the destruction of crops;
in the northeast, the destruction of trees; and in the north-northeast, the destruction of sons.
If it is devoid of binding on all sides, it will cause total destruction;
if the *nirmālya* is placed in locations other than those for the *śaktis*, the class of Śaivas will perish. (8)

If the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) are placed in the portion of Viṣṇu, the class of kings perishes; if the remains of offerings are placed in the portion of Brahmā, it is the destruction of the class of Brahmins. (9)

If the *nandyāvarta* is located on the stone surface, the *viṭ* and *śūdra* castes perish. However, if the *nirmālya* is placed in the position of the tortoise (*kūrma*), it brings about the destruction of everything.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the eightfold binding (*tvaṣṭabandhana*).

The first is the immediate binding (*sadyabandha*); the second is the sequential binding (*kramabandha*). The third method of binding is that which is devoid of binding on all sides. When [the stalk] is severed at eight *yava*s from the base, one should perform the immediate binding.
On the altar for the daily ablution, one should place a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva.
Having placed the water-pot upon that, the wise practitioner should perform the worship as prescribed for the ritual bathing.
Then, having performed the fire-offering rites before the pot according to the rules, the wise one [proceeds].
Having performed the joining with the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandha*), one should perform the consecration with products of the cow;
likewise, the consecration with jars and the consecration with a weight of milk.
One should cause the food offering (*naivedya*) to be given to Śambhu; this is declared as the "immediate binding" (*sadyobandhana*). (4–5)
The binding is said to be performed in sequence with twelve finger-breadths marked off.
Having fashioned the archway, the sacrificial pit, the altar, and the sacrificial hall, one should take the form of the Liṅga and join it to the water-pot in due order. (6–7)
And having completed the worship and the fire-oblation (homa) according to the method of sacrificial worship.
Having performed the binding as before and offered up the remainder of the night,
one should perform the consecration at dawn and carry out the binding in due order.
When the binding is severed on all sides and the *nandyāvarta* is absent;
when there is a displacement of the base of the *liṅga* and the *liṅga* itself is subject to movement. (9)
That is declared to be the destruction of the kingdom; otherwise, O King, there would be calamity.
Therefore, with every effort, one should again perform a reconciliation. (10)
Now, the entire procedure for binding and the purification in sequence is explained:
seven days is declared to be the best, while nine days would be the middling.
In the case of a *svāyambhuva* (self-manifested) *liṅga*, the lowest [period] is known to be seven days;

in a *devika* (divine) and a *divya* (celestial) *liṅga*, the best is seven days. In the case of *ārṣa* (sage-made) *liṅgas*, it is five days, and likewise nine days for a *gāṇapa* (Gana-related) *liṅga*.
The specific distinction regarding honey is stated for both Rākṣasas and humans.
(3) For human signs, however, the placement of the vessel is the performance of the mantra-rite; if it remains in the jar beyond that time, O Lord of Gods, it causes all defects. (4)
Therefore, with every effort, at the end of a month or even earlier,
one should join that which resides in the *kumbha* to the *liṅga*, and then perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Beginning from the day of the sprouting [of the seeds], on the third, fifth, ninth, seventh, or [other auspicious] day...
One should perform the sacrifice especially; its specific procedure is now declared:
for three days one should perform it twice daily, for five days six times daily; it is recommended that this be done in the sequence of morning and evening for one day. (6–7)
Alternatively, one may have it performed in another manner for a number of days:
for a three-day rite, four sessions are prescribed; for a five-day rite, eight are proclaimed.
For a seven-day rite, twelve are declared; for a nine-day rite, sixteen are remembered.
Twenty-eight *kālas*, however, are proclaimed as one *pakṣāha*.
The fifty divisions of time for the month have been proclaimed;
the number of days from the sprouting [of the seed] until the consecration has also been proclaimed.
Having performed the consecration immediately, one should offer oblations into the fire at night;
this should be done in all months, and one should practice the eightfold binding.
The wise man should avoid unfavorable days, muhūrtas, and so forth;
as well as the eight-fold binding, the three-fold binding, and the five-fold binding. (11)
One should likewise bind [the thread] within the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the image (*pratimā*) according to that procedure— eight, five, or three times.
The wise practitioner should then perform the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

The eight-fold binding is for prosperity, while the five-fold binding brings fortune. The three-fold binding leads to liberation; the five-fold binding brings fortune, and the three-fold binding leads to liberation, serving to join the bamboo joints and promote growth.
Saffron, sugar powder, an equal amount of red cotton,
lac powder, resin (madhūcchiṣṭa), vermilion, *kunduriṣka*,
and buffalo butter— these are said here to be the eight substances.

Three parts of powdered sugar, two parts of *kunduriṣka*, one part of powdered lac, and three-quarters of a part of decoction; likewise, three-quarters of a part of resin (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) and red cotton (*raktatūlaka*). (5–6)
Fresh butter is said to be three-quarters [of the measure], and cinnabar is said to be one-quarter;
however, if that cinnabar is deficient, the binding will be weak.
The preceptor, being most excellent, should divide this substance into portions in the proper sequence with his hands, and having rubbed it with both palms, he should then bind it.
Alternatively, the method of binding should be performed in another way:
the *kundariṣka* fruit, the *nāḍī*, and sugar in the proportion of five parts.
One *phala* of *kāṣāya* is called a *phala* for the purpose of lac;
half of that is *madhūcchiṣṭa*, and half of that is called *guḍa*. (9)
Half of that [weight] should be cotton, likewise mixed with butter;
one *pala* from the scale, mixed with *hastāhlā*, should be rubbed together.
The eightfold binding has thus been described; beyond that is the fivefold binding:
lac, sugar, stone, buffalo [fat], and *kundariṣka*. (I.6b)
Combined with beeswax (*madhu-cchiṣṭa*), it is released from the fivefold bond (*pañca-bandhana*).
Sugar, *kunduriṣka*, and fresh butter constitute the threefold bond (*tri-bandhaka*).
In the case of the *svāyambhuva*, *daivika*, *bāṇa*, and *bandhya* [types of semen], there is the threefold bond.
In the case of divine, celestial, and ṛṣi-made [images], the fivefold binding is prescribed;
for human, rākṣasa, and images on pedestals,
as well as for all attendants and the like, the eightfold binding should be performed.
One should bind it with gold, silver, or indeed lead;
thus, the method of binding is twofold: unrefined and refined.
That which is ripe is fit for the application of cauterization, while that which is unripe requires massage.
Having discerned whether this [condition] is ripe or unripe, the wise physician should apply the bandage very firmly.
The unripened [state] is said to be divine (*devika*), while the well-ripened is called honey (*madhuka*).
Then one should perform the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) with oil, cow's milk, and chalk (*gaurika*).
Guggulu, sand, *sistha*, water, *sajjalākṣaka*— (7) [these are] the sky, wings, fire, the *ṛc*s, arrows, tastes, the other, the three, and the movement of the Tāga.
The proportions of the oil have been declared in sequence; its cooking should be like that of *citkaṇa*.
[One should prepare it] with conch-shell powder, sesame seeds, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *kundarī*, and *iṣṭakā*. (8)
Having prepared plantain fruit combined with curd, cooked, and bound eight times,
and having pressed it while identifying it as Śiva himself, one should worship Śiva within.
One should perform the eight-fold binding with devotion according to one's wealth;
for the wise should arrange it so that the fruit is equal for both the rich and the poor.
He who performs it with a display of wealth, being wealthy, shall travel in a celestial chariot.

Those whose minds are overcome by greed do not attain this strength. Having divided one's own wealth into three parts, one should designate one part for the necessities of life; then, from the remaining two parts, one should always live for the sake of dharma. (2)
Having placed [the image] in a copper vessel made of the substance of Dharma for the sake of Śiva,
gold should be offered with affection as an offering dedicated to Śiva.
Even very wealthy kings, out of devotion, should do so with their own wealth.
Let the people there, free from deceit and pride, practice the Śivadharma.
Therefore, O King, greed for wealth is a source of fault;
one who possesses little wealth and is poor, having begged for much money, [suffers]. (4)
They were desired by him as objects to be grasped for their wicked deeds; yet they practiced the dharma of Śiva, having solicited and obtained great wealth under the pretext of the Śiva-dharma.
Let them perform the duties of Śiva; one should not cause them to be performed with excessive expenditure of wealth.
Even those who give wealth to beggars obtain the fruit, while the giver of much [wealth] obtains even more.
By whatever means possible, O men, accumulate wealth and practice the Śiva-dharma; for the Śiva-dharma is indeed difficult to attain.
Human birth is difficult to obtain, and indeed the Dharma of Śiva is difficult to attain;
through merit accumulated over many births, a living being may partake of both. (8)
Those people who practice the dharma of Śiva by any means whatsoever,
having attained supreme desired enjoyments, are honored by others.
Those people who accept [teachings] with reference to the Dharma of Śiva indeed dwell together with Śiva himself in the world of Śiva. (10)
Those people who give wealth shall obtain both of these states:
the accomplishment of desired goals and proximity [to the deity], through the investigation of the threefold activity. (I.7b)
Those who give wealth to supplicants with the Śivadharma in mind, as well as those who incite others, those who distribute sweetmeats, and likewise the makers and the instigators—
these shall quickly attain proximity to Śiva in the hereafter. (2)
Having designated it for the Śivadharma,
those whose wealth has been purified by sweeping [the temple grounds] should place a portion of the substance in a copper vessel and perform the purification of the substance.
Having recited the Astra-mantra one hundred times, one should perform the fire-oblation with the most excellent Śiva-mantras.
By that, there shall be the purification of the substance; and the purified substance may be offered to Śiva.
Afterward, having honored the Guru, one should practice the duties of Śiva.
One should divide the substance intended for Śiva into eleven portions:
three parts for the purpose of sacrifice, and likewise one part for the preceptor.
Indeed, the feeding of Brahmins shall constitute one part;
likewise, two parts are to be understood as being for the purpose of recitation and giving.
One should complete the remainder for the purpose of performing the sacrifice after three fortnights;
one should construct the sacrificial pavilion to the south, in front, or on either side.
In the northeastern direction, in a place free from fire or elsewhere,
having purified the ground for as far as the knees, made it level, and smeared it [with cow dung].
It should be one fist in height and resemble the surface of a mirror;
specifically, in the Śiva sacrifice, it should measure five cubits.
Having made it square and even with one cubit for the *vividhya* and four cubits for the *manuhasta*, one should perform the laying out of the lines (*padavinyāsa*).
The line for the sun (*ravisūtra*) should have its tip pointing eastward, and likewise, its tip pointing northward.
One hundred and twenty-one divisions of the site are prescribed.
(I.8a) In the center, within the single Brahma-pada, there is the principal Vardhanī; in the eight Deva-padas, there are the Kumbhas, and the Paiśāca-pada shall be the sixteenth. (2)
For the sake of worship, pillars are prescribed in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions.
The remaining [pillars] in the eight squares are said to be eight *aṅgulas* each.
(3) Then, outside at the fifty-sixth [square], there is the *ghaṭa-toraṇa* in the Rākṣasa [direction].
The movement of the teacher and the disciple should result in a position appropriate for the disciplined.
Thus established in the positions, with the pillar-position on the outer side,
it is joined with sixteen pillars or indeed twelve pillars.
One should construct either a pavilion, a quadrangular hall, or even a shed;
in the center of that pavilion, however, there should be a pedestal at the end of a square.
Then, it should be square and level, with its width and height equal;
the height should be twelve finger-breadths and the width six finger-breadths.
One should cause the interior of the *mukuroda* and the *upavedī* to be constructed;
one should fashion sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) all around, situated within the human portion (*mānuṣapada*).

One should fashion a quadrangular [mandala] in the east, a vulva-shaped one in the southeast, a lunar crescent in the south, a bow-shaped one in the southwest, a hexagon in the west, a lotus in the northwest, and an octagon in the north and other directions. (8)
Between the Rudra and Khaṇḍala [sections], the form of the primary seat (mūlapīṭha) is likewise declared to be the form of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa); this is called the principal pit.

In the Pañcāgniyatana rite, one should place the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the west of the altar. Indra’s nine-pit array, beginning with Tvaṣṭṛ-bhoga and so forth, bestows success. (11) The fruit of the five pits is declared to be the granting of desired accomplishments.
One should smear with cow dung a single sacrificial pit that brings prosperity.
One should have the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) proclaimed there and then feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Afterwards, having cleared away the remnants of the meal, one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite once more.
On the day before the [consecration of the] sprout, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests,
should perform the shaving of the head in due order for the sake of purifying the body.
On the day prior to the day of formal acceptance (*adhivāsa*), at the conclusion of the daily worship,
one should especially worship Vighneśa and the primary image (*mūlabera*).
Facing north, the wise and supreme instructor, having first meditated upon the Lord of the Gaṇas there, should perform the ritual visualization according to the rules.

Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and the like, and having offered betel-leaf and coconut for the sake of the image-bearers (*mūrtipa*), the Guru should obtain permission [from the deity], saying:
"O Leader of the Gaṇas, quickly dispel obstacles and be gracious toward this procession! (5)

Having thus made this request under an auspicious lunar mansion, on a favorable day, and during a movable ascendant, one should approach the primary *liṅga* while standing facing north; first performing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and thereafter making the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). (6–7)
Having worshipped with the eight flowers, one should offer betel leaves and other items, saying:
"O Śiva, Lord of the entire universe, Sadāśiva, salutations to you!
(8) O Lord, grant me permission for the performance of the eightfold binding."

"So be it," said Śiva; having received permission by the command of Śiva, [the practitioner] should go into the presence of the Goddess and others once their bonds have been severed. The wise one should cause them to grant permission and then begin the collection of clay. (9–10)

Having placed these deities at the forefront and having especially worshipped the Caṇḍa weapon, he should then proceed with them accompanied by all musical instruments. (11) The northern-eastern direction is considered the best, while the southern is said to be middling.
The lowest [place] is said to be the western one; the supreme teacher should reside in a secluded spot on a riverbank, at the root of a *bilva* tree, by a pond, in a grove of *tulasī*,
in a field, at the root of *darbha* grass, on an anthill, or in the Nandana forest.
Or, having gone to the base of an Aśvattha tree according to the prescribed rule, the Guru,
having reached a pure location, should cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed.
One should prepare the sacrificial mound with rice grains and likewise the mound with sesame seeds;
having placed a six-petaled lotus in its center, one should set down all the ritual jars.
One should worship the seven oceans— provided with *kūrca* grass and sprouts, and containing water along with blood (or gems)— in the jars at the tips of the petals starting from the middle.
Alternatively, one should place either a single pitcher or seven pitchers representing the oceans;
one should especially provide offerings such as food, incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having drawn nine squares upon a sacrificial mound in front of the water-pot,
one should worship Brahmā in the center, followed by Ananta and the others up to Jayantaka.
The wise one should worship Indra and the other deities in the center of the eastern and other compartments.
Having worshipped them according to the rule, he should offer the bali-oblation at the end of the word "svāhā."
One should worship the Goddess of the Earth in the eastern part of the *balimaṇḍala*;
there, facing either east or north, one should worship the spade.
O Goddess, one should first visualize her with her head facing upward and her face turned upwards, appearing in various forms.
(9) Pure earth in the region of the belly brings prosperity, while [earth] on the head causes the destruction of the kingdom.
O King, one who places it on the sides meets destruction; one who places it on the foot perishes.
If placed on the neck, there is ruin for the installer; if placed on the waist, the installer suffers and is destroyed.
One should collect earth from all around a village that has been destroyed;
having dug the earth in three places with a spade, the wise one should place it in a vessel and,
after carrying it away, cover it with a cloth as prescribed.

In order to eliminate the defects that cause harm within the womb of the Earth Goddess, and for the sake of pacifying the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should sprinkle the seven oceans. Having placed jars filled with clay, one should set them down and perform the sprinkling. (2–3)
Having summoned an attendant, he had him carry the clay on a palanquin or even on an elephant;
afterwards, accompanied by dance and song, [he proceeded].
Having performed the circumambulation of the village, the Guru should enter the palace;
this should be done within five nāḍīs after sunset, provided the auspicious moment (lagna) is favorable.
Alternatively, one should perform the offering of the sprouts within seven *nāḍīs*. However, whatever rite is performed without the sprouts, that rite shall be fruitless.
If there is no destruction of karma, then from sprout to sprout it does not cease;
[one should perform] the sacrifice of pairs in a single abode, sowing, and the rite for the pacification of the site.
One should perform [the rite] in one place alone; however, for festivals and the like, one may act elsewhere—in the northern part of the temple, or in the southern part, or in another location. (7)
In the northeast, or in the northwest of the sacrificial hall, the Guru should cause [the ground] to be sown;
he should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with *śāli* rice, arranged in the form of a lotus.
Having likewise laid five lines facing east and five facing north,
one should establish a four-square area in the center and worship the Soma-vessel.
Having offered the seat and meditation, one should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra and worship him.
Having presented the food offering, incense, lamps, and so forth, the Guru should then place the *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas* outside of that in sequence. (10)
Beginning with Īśāna and each [subsequent deity] according to the number of the Yugas—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the *pālikā* and the other vessels;
one should worship the twelve Ādityas in sequence within the *pālikā* and the other vessels. (1.10a–2)
One should collect these nine seeds: sesame, mustard, mung beans, black gram, peas, horse gram, lentils, barley, and wheat.
One should wash the substance with water and sprinkle it with milk.
And for the western direction, he should recite the mantra "yājātā" according to the sacred text.
Then, having consecrated the spear and worshipped it, one should sow the seeds of Śiva;
one should sprinkle the *pālikā* vessels and the others with water from the moon-pitcher.
Having worshipped the moving seat within the pitcher according to the previously mentioned procedure, the Guru should offer a piece of sugar,
betel leaf, milk pudding, and other such items.
Having prostrated with offerings of incense and lamps, the preceptor should make a request;
then, having offered the recitation according to the rules, the wearing of the thread follows.
Twenty-four are prescribed for the festival, and sixteen for the purificatory rite (*pavitra*).
Twelve *pālikās* are prescribed by means of the eightfold binding beginning with the sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
The wearing of a protective thread for the purpose of observing vows and other restraints;
(8) as well as betel leaf, ashes, rice grains, and coconut.
One should worship the eight nāgas within the thread made of gold and other materials;
this is declared to be the best *homa*, while that which is devoid of *homa* is the middling one.
Where the Sūtrakāra is the youngest [of the officiants] and there is no sacrificial fire-pot (*homakumbha*),
the tying of the *kautuka* (protective thread) shall take place at night before the designated day.
In the absence [of such conditions], the Guru should perform it on the very day [of the rite] or even earlier than that.
For the sake of accomplishing the mantra, that ritual action must necessarily involve the recitation of the thread (sūtra).
Having performed worship day after day according to the prescribed rule until the designated day arrives, the wise practitioner should dismiss the Moon on that appointed day. (I.10b–2)
Having cast the sprouts into water, one should dismiss the ritual curiosity (*kautuka*).
For the purification of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), one should worship the deities of the site (*vāstudeva*).
[One should do so] either in the center of the sacrificial pavilion or at the front of the offering altar (*balipīṭha*).

One should perform the Vāstu sacrifice at the site of Brahmā, or in a pavilion and so forth. Then, one should have a pavilion constructed measuring nine cubits, provided with an altar and a sacrificial pit, and equipped with four doors. (4–5)
In the center of the eighty-one squares, one should worship Brahmā and the other deities upon the altar.
To the eastern direction is the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and in the south-eastern direction is the Puṇyāha ceremony.

The station of the Guru, Dharmarāja, is in the southwest; there is the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), the two nooses, and the wind; this is the yoga of the subsidiary means (yogopasādhana).
The Brahma-pitcher should be in the north, and the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) in the northeast.
Having worshipped Brahmā facing eastward, one should worship him in the pitcher as well as in the mandala.
In front of that, one should perform the fire-rite with the fire facing forward;
at night, the wise man should offer the bali-oblation in the primary villages and dwellings.
Whether by night or by day, in temples of gods and goddesses and other such places,
one should worship Maṇḍūka, the deities, and the auspicious Vāstu.
The station of the goddesses and other Śaktis is the supreme abode,
the eternal destroyer of obstacles, which grants the accomplishment of desired and wished-for goals.
For the sake of accomplishing that rite and the mantras, one should perform the Vāstuyāga.
Specifically in the center of the altar, one should [draw lines] with rice grains and sesame seeds as well.
(2) One should lay down nine threads with their tips pointing eastward and likewise nine with their tips pointing northward, thereby forming sixty-four squares, complete with corner-threads. (3)
One should fashion the Maṇḍūka [altar], which has four spikes, four circles, is adorned with eight cords, and is provided with twelve vital points (*marmas*).
Having thus conceived it, one should perform the worship of the Lord of Obstacles (*Vighnarāja*) and the sprinkling of the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) water.
The Guru should sprinkle [the site] with water for the *arghya* offering consisting of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), according to the prescribed rule.
(5) In the center, upon four squares, is Brahmā; in the four directions, having joined six squares each, [he places] Saṃyama and the others in due order. (6)

One should worship the *dvandva* deities who cause misfortune in the locations previously mentioned, starting from Īśāna and proceeding clockwise through the half-squares (*ardhapada*) and full squares (*pada*) of the corners. (7) Outside, in the four corners according to the rule, one should worship those who occupy half-squares and single squares. (8)
The others are each one by one, and the trident is likewise circular.
Remaining there, one should perform the invocation of the fifty-three deities in sequence;
having worshipped them with perfumes and flowers, one should offer betel leaves and other items.
(9) The wise practitioner should place the sacrificial offering (*bali*) in thirteen squares in the middle of the thread. (10)
One should offer the bali-oblation in the middle of the site according to the number thirty-two, which corresponds to the [thirty-two] forms.
One should offer eight oblations at the word *vikārārtha*;
the Guru should give fifty-three oblations as prescribed for the *bali* offering.
The bali offering for Brahmā consists of rice mixed with curd, ghee, and sugar;
for the other four [deities], the bali is said to be milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with honey.
In the intermediate directions, the offering for the eight primary deities consists of *kṛsarā* rice;
for the deities presided over by Īśa, the offering is said to be mung bean porridge.
The food offering for the eight Brahma-devas is said to consist of rice cooked with black gram (*māsa*).
In its absence, the end of the offering is declared to be mixed with black gram.

Having thus performed the worship, the Guru should thereafter establish the ritual jars (kalaśas). To the north or the west, one should indeed prepare the mound of sand (maṇḍala) as previously described.
One should worship the Vāstu-pitchers according to the procedure prescribed for the ablution rite;
having worshipped Brahmā in the center, one should then worship the deities of the Vāstu.
Bhāratī, however, is on his left; one should then place the jars starting from the east:
Trayīmaya, Trimūrti, Padmākṣa, and Padmayonika.
Caturmukha, Dhātṛ, Pitāmaha, and likewise Aja—
having worshipped these eight forms, or else the guardians of the world (lokapālakas).
Having worshipped with incense and flowers, one should present the food offerings;
there, in the central position, the place for the fire sacrifice (homa) is prescribed.
One should perform the fire-ritual either in a sacrificial pit or upon a consecrated mound;
one should worship the deities, beginning with Vāstu and Brahmā, in the midst of the fire.
Having first offered twenty-eight hundred oblations of clarified butter,
one should then offer the sacrificial materials, such as fuel-sticks and parched grain, in ten parts in successive order.

Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of each substance, one should subsequently offer to the deities in sequence. Having offered to the deities beginning with Samayyaka, one should indeed perform the oblation ten times their respective portion.
For each of the eight [deities] beginning with Āpa, there is one oblation each;
for each of the deities beginning with Īśāna, there are five each.
One should perform a fire-oblation for the deities bitten by Carakī with three oblations;
having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) to those same deities, one should offer the raw flesh (*kravya*) to Carakī.
One should perform [the rite] with substitute substances such as kūṣmāṇḍa and the like;
likewise, in the absence of meat, one should act accordingly, but the local practitioner should avoid using seeds.
Having split the kūśmāṇḍa with the Khaḍga mantra and offered it with the sruva ladle,
one should then offer the pūrṇāhuti and perform the incense and lamp offerings.
One should join that which stands in the fire to the *pada*; likewise, one should join that which stands in the *pada* to the *kumbha*.
Having joined that which stands in the *kumbha* to the heart, this is considered the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire).
The purification by circumambulation with fire is declared to be the burner of all afflictions;
for the sake of purifying the jar, one should perform the oblation that increases according to the sequence. (8)
Having again firmly formed a handful of *palāśa*, dry *darbha* grass, and other materials,
he should sprinkle it with water while reciting the Heart Mantra, and then ignite it with that fire.
Perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) for the sake of purifying the sacrificial hall and other sites.
Having sprinkled the *pañcagavya* equally, join it with the water from the *vardhanī* vessel.
Having worshipped the weapon-mantra according to the rules and having offered it together with that water,
[one should perform the rite] accompanied by all musical instruments and joined with the deity of the weapon.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, the wise man should discard the torch outside. (3) The preceptor should cause all to proclaim an auspicious day and sprinkle water everywhere.
At the clear dawn, the wise man should perform his bath according to the rules;
having adorned himself with garments and ornaments, he should perform his daily rites.
O Śambhu, for the sake of the propitiatory worship, one should perform the ceremonial bathing after first performing the expiation;
then one should offer oblations according to the prescribed number of *homa* rites in due order.
Then, having entered the inner sanctum, one should worship according to the prescribed rite,
offering the food oblation, incense, lamps, and other ritual services.
Having performed the *prasannayajana* for the sake of prosperity and for the purpose of adornment,
the wise man, having completed the decoration and other preparations, should enter the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*).
It has four gates in the four directions and is adorned with four archways;
in the eight directions, one should hang eight banners in a clockwise direction.
In the east, blue cloth is prescribed; in the southeast, red cloth. In the south, there should be black cloth, and in the southwest, smoky-colored cloth.

In the western direction, there is a garment with the luster of a conch shell; likewise, in the north-western direction, it is variegated. In the northern direction, there is a golden-colored cloth; and in the north-eastern direction, it is yellow in color.
The base should be thirteen finger-breadths in width and twenty finger-breadths in length; its height should be equal to its width, and the pinnacle should be half of that.
The wise man should draw a four-fold, three-fold, or even a two-fold grid in the center of the banner, and especially depict the elephants of the directions.
On the side, however, it should be provided with a row of plantain trees and joined by two drivers;
its height should be nine cubits, eight cubits, or even seven cubits.
The remainder should be made like the banner, and one should have it fashioned with various cloths.
(5) The characteristics of the flagstaff have been declared; now hear the procedure for the small banner.
The width should be one arrow-length (five fingers) and the length twelve finger-breadths;
it should be joined with two cords, while the remainder is for the mouth, which is heavy at the front.
The procedure for the small banner has been declared as being joined with a crest and a tail;
it may measure eleven cubits, or even twelve cubits.
Or else, it may be joined with a handle at the opening, or provided with a sacrificial ladle and a cord;
it is adorned with various cloths and endowed with various forms. (8)
Thus the wave-pattern is described; now the "encircling at the junction" is being explained:
black and white in the eastern quarter, while white and red are in the south.
In the west it should be red and yellow, and in the northern direction yellow and black.
One should wrap [the image] with that cloth, which is of equal length for the limbs, seamless, and without holes.
One should make [the cloth] from red silk, fine cotton, or other such materials;
it should be twenty-six cubits in length and eight spans in width.
The preceptor should suspend a canopy between the two [pillars] at the center of the sacrificial ground;
it should be adorned with mangoes, coconuts, strings of pearls, and beautiful flowers.
One should adorn it with sugarcane, sprouts, betel, and creepers;
and one should suspend a "sky-hand" [a loop] made of *darbha* grass, measuring four cubits.
The space between [the pillars] should be four finger-breadths wide, adorned with mango sprouts;
it should have the circumference of a thumb and be encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass.
Then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should arrange colorful patterns and the like,
provided with various lamps and endowed with the eight auspicious symbols.
One should sprinkle [the image] endowed with the ten weapons with the water of the *puṇyāha* rite.
(6) One should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains in the center upon the altar.
(7) That which is honored with two hundred and twenty-five grains of rice—
It should be known as being merely a *śakti* [in measure]; one must certainly not cause it to exceed the *āna*. (8) A *śakti*, a *sthala*, a *prakūja*, a *prasṛti*, and likewise a *kuḍupa*;
likewise for that, a *dañjali*, a *prastha*, a *pādaka*, and an *āḍhaka*. (9)
A *droṇa* is said to be one *khārī*, while each subsequent measure is double the preceding;

three *khāris* constitute a *bhāra*, and beyond a *bhāra* is the measure called *anāmaka*. (10) [This is measured] by *śāli* rice according to the standard of thieves, using grains of rice resembling *ūḍu* beans.
When filled with ten bhāras, that is proclaimed as the best;
thirty-eight droṇas, however, is known as the middling;
and the inferior one should be made with thirty droṇas by the preceptor.
Half a *śāli* grain of rice, half a grain of rice of *taṇḍula*, and likewise half a grain of sesame;
half a grain of sesame of parched grain (*lāja*)—thus are the seven grains, the triad of Śiva.
One *āḍhaka* each of mung bean, black gram, wheat, and mustard seed.
One should worship with chickpeas, flat beans, and the seven types of grain.
(4) Having drawn a lotus there in the center with eight petals and a pericarp, one should assign one *droṇa* each for the retinues beginning with the Sun. (5)
One should likewise have two *droṇas*—one of rice and one of sesame—each measuring half of the other; and for Śambhu, one should have a water-pot (*ghaṭa*) fashioned from gold.
One should also have a very sturdy *vardhanī* vessel made of silver, filled with a *droṇa*.
One should have eight jars filled with Śiva made of copper alone.
(7) These pitchers are declared to be full with one āḍhaka each;
everything should be made of copper, or else of bell-metal, or even of clay. (8)
The maker should fashion [the image] according to his wealth as described by the characteristics:
the best [size] is the measure of a sesame seed, the middling is the measure of a barley grain, and the inferior is the measure of a finger-joint; or else, it may be like the eye of an elephant. (9)
A single thread is for disease; two threads are for malevolent rites.
(10) Three threads shall bring all success; one should wrap them clockwise.
One should wrap the jars with three threads, and the *vardhanī* vessel with two threads. (11)
Many threads [were placed] upon the jars and vessels;
having enveloped it like a window-lattice with the armor of Sadyojāta.
The washing is performed with the Vāmadeva [mantra], and the fumigation with the Ghora mantra.
Then, one should indeed place the mantras of Puruṣa and Īśāna upon the downward-facing and upward-facing [faces].
One should fill the water-jars with water using the mantra "āpo vā" [RV 10.9.1],
employing pure water from a river or from a well, covered with a cloth.
One should fill an earthen vessel with cool, fragrant water;
having gathered the bathing substances, one should fill it with water filtered through a cloth.
Sandalwood, musk, camphor, saffron, musk-deer musk, and gorocana— these six are celebrated as the "six fragrances."
One should worship it well within a water-pot filled with snow-water.
The best [image] should be worth ten *niṣkas*, the middling half of that, and the inferior should be known as half of that; thus the wise man should have the image fashioned. (5)
One should have an image of Manonmanī made, measuring half of that [of Śiva].
For the pitchers of the Vidyeśvaras, there should be a golden band measuring half of that;
for the pitchers of the retinue, there should be a golden band measuring half of that.
The wise one should always fashion the forms of Sadāśiva, Gaurī, and the Vidyeśvaras according to their respective images;
the best of teachers should place each of those [images] into the center of its corresponding pitcher.

The best [image] should weigh twelve niṣkas, the middling eight niṣkas, and the smallest five niṣkas; this is for the principal [deity] and yields great fruit. A wise person should place a blue lotus weighing half of that in the *vardhanī* vessel.
For the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas), half of that [measure] is prescribed for the golden trident.
Likewise, there are ruby, sapphire, diamond, and emerald;
(11) as well as lapis lazuli, crystal, ruby, and pearl.
One should place coral and the nine gems into the center of the pitcher.
One should sequentially place the five gems— diamond, lapis lazuli, sapphire, pearl, and coral— into the *vardhanī* vessel.
One should have the ruby, crystal, and diamond, as well as the golden sacred thread for the three-jeweled pitchers,
fashioned with five *niṣkas* of gold.
One should have the protective cord (*rakṣāsūtra*) fashioned from seven *niṣkas* of gold.

The *kautuka* (sacred thread), made of gold or silver, should be tied with a thread; it should be equal in length to the circumference of the *liṅga*, and it should be offered upon both the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the image (*bera*). It should be fashioned with its own measure increased by one-quarter, and adorned with the hoods of the king of serpents (*nāgarāja*).
Ask about that [thread] which is joined together, in the form of a band or even equal [in length];
and the most excellent *kūrca* (grass-bundle), fashioned from thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass.
One should make a knot two finger-widths long in the form of a clockwise turn.
The tip is said to be four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula), and the stalk eighteen finger-breadths long.
One should place a smooth, symmetrical, and dark-colored [stalk] into the Śiva-pitcher;
the stalk is fourteen finger-breadths long and consists of twenty-five blades of darbha grass.
The "top-knot" (*agra-granthi*) is as previously described, and the *kūrca* is said to be placed upon the *vardhanī*.
It consists of fifteen blades of *darbha* grass with a three-finger-width top-knot and a stalk thirteen fingers long, joined according to its proper measure. (9)

Having inserted the *kūrca* [bundle of grass] into the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*) in due order—(10)—that with the tips pointing upward is said to be for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), while that with the tips pointing downward is for pacification (*śāntika*).
One should fashion the *kūrca* according to this sequence, or alternatively, one may apply a knot or a mouth [to it]. (i.15b)
One should place twenty-five mango leaves upon the water-pot (kumbha),
and it is traditionally taught that fifteen mango leaves should be placed upon the vardhanī vessel.
Upon the jars, there should be eight-petaled lotuses sixteen finger-breadths in length;
alternatively, they are proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths long and with a stalk.
It should be made round like the neck of a water-pot and shaped like an arrow;
in its center, one should place it joined with a hole and provided with a lid.
The coconut is said to be the head of the jars;
the pomegranate fruit is the middle, and one should weigh the mango blossom.
And having thus proclaimed the command of the deity, one should arrange the offerings according to what is available.
(5) A coconut fruit is said to be the head of the pitcher, and its inner substance is the essence.
One should thus arrange the worship upon the face, which is indeed the mouth.
(6) Having fashioned a *kūrca* with thirty-one petals, the wise one should place it in the water-pot (*kumbha*).
A wise person should place twenty-one *darbha* grasses upon the *vardhanī*;
with eleven petals, one should form the lines of the knot, which shall measure one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).

Indeed, the knot of the cord is prescribed to measure four finger-breadths; the foremost knot is considered to have the same measurement as the base, while the first step is desired to begin from the head.
Thus, these characteristics of one with a long beard (*lambakūrca*) should be known by the wise:
the best is one with a long hand, while the middling is one with a ten-hand measure. (9)
The lowest [size] should be eight cubits long and five tālas wide;
having wrapped it with two pieces of cloth, one should likewise wrap it with fine silk (dukūla).
One should employ a yellow, very firm, and fine [cord] upon the Śiva-pitchers;
[the dimensions being] nine, eight, or seven cubits for the best, middling, and inferior [shrines], respectively. (I.16a)

In the same manner, the Guru should wrap the *vardhanī* vessel with red silk cloth (*dukūla*) and other materials. For the six *vidyeśa* jars, however, a circumference of six cubits is prescribed for each individually;
for all the jars, a circumference of four cubits is ordained.

The best [altar] should be thirty cubits, the middling twenty-five, and the lowest is said to be twenty; its width should be six *tālas*. One should wrap the altar with a borderless cloth as a protective cord (*pratisara*). (4–5)
The Rudrākṣa rosary, the sacred thread, the turban, the upper garment,
and the ash-mark— these are proclaimed as the five insignia of the Śaivas.
Wear the Vibhūti and the Phalavardha on the region of the neck in thirty-two [marks].
It is taught that a necklace of one hundred and eight [beads] is adorned with a central gem;
(7) a rosary should be fashioned with twenty-seven [beads] in sequence, or it may be six or seven [beads] in length, or one part wide in the hand. (8)
One should have it made well-knit, very firm, fine, white, free from hair and the like,
and devoid of a snout as well as ears. Indeed, one should cause the tail to encircle the left ear in a clockwise direction.

In this manner, one should wrap the remainder around the head as a single coil; thus the characteristic of the *uṣṇīṣa* has been declared. Now the characteristic of the cloth is being described for use in sacrifice, installation, fire-rituals, and likewise in Śaiva festivals. (I.16b)

The best [mandala] should be ten cubits, the middling nine cubits, and the lowest eight cubits; it should be five *tālas* in width. Thus, equipped with two garments, the preceptor should maintain [the proportions] in sequence.
The linen cloth should be yellow or red; in its absence, one may accept another.
(3) One should avoid five kinds of cloth: that burnt by fire, that with hair on it, that defiled by mice, that which is old, and that which is worn out. (4)
A garment that is burnt leads to the destruction of the kingdom; one with mouse-holes brings fear; one with loose threads leads to affliction; one that is worn out leads to the loss of wealth;
and an old garment brings about the ruin of the sacrificer.
Therefore, having abandoned any defects, one should indeed cause a cloth to be given.
(6) The characteristics of the cloth have thus been stated; now the upper garment (*uttarīya*) is described: it may be five *hasta* in length, or even as long as eight *hasta*. (7)
Having fastened it with two tails and a width of two cubits, one should distinguish the upper garment (*uttarīya*) as being like a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) in its length;
fine silk (*dukūla*) is said to be the best, while a cord made of tree-fiber is middling. (8)
Alternatively, the yogapaṭṭikā is of three kinds, whether made of thread or as a finished product. (9) That which serves as an upavītaka is three finger-breadths in width;
its length is ten finger-breadths and its width is five finger-breadths. (10)
One should cause it to be offered to the preceptor, fashioned in the shape of a ball joined with two pieces of *dukūla* cloth and smeared with white ashes.
A golden ring, a bracelet, a waist-band,
and an earring, along with a golden sacred thread— these are known as the five-fold ornaments.
The sacred thread (*pavitra*) should consist of five *niṣkas*, and the bracelet (*kaṭaka*) should be twelve;
the waist-string (*kaṭisūtra*) eight *niṣkas*, and the earring (*kuṇḍala*) ten *niṣkas*.
And a golden sacred thread is proclaimed to consist of five *niṣkas*.
Having thus worn [the ornaments] according to the rule, the preceptor should invoke Śiva.
One should invite the deity at night, except on a day when the planetary positions are stable.
Having taken [the deity] and joined it within the water-pot, one should perform the sacrifice and fire-oblation at night.
The most excellent preceptor should perform [the rites] in sequence, both evening and morning.
Then, having gone to the inner sanctum, [he should prepare] a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
In the center, there should be the Śiva-pitcher, and the Vardhanī vessel to its left;
having taken eight pitchers, one should place them around it in the proper sequence.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and then the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited there and strew darbha grass and flowers around the site. (270)
Having taken hold of the long beard, he should place it upon the liṅga.
(8) The Guru should arrange the seat, the enclosure, and so forth, as previously described.

One should cause coconut, betel-leaf, incense, and a lamp to be offered. (9) Having prepared a movable seat upon the pitcher, one should worship [the deity] in sequence up to the limit of one's capacity.
Having assigned the seat and the form, one should fashion the stalk of *darbha* grass;
then, after performing the assignment (*nyāsa*) of the food offering, incense, and lamps, one should further assign the six paths (*adhvan*) and the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*). (10)
Having invoked the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) into the jar, one should fashion the eyes [of the deity].

Following the path instructed by the Guru, one should slowly recite the mantra, together with all the protective coverings (*āvaraṇas*) and endowed with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the others. (I.17b–2)
Having invoked the deity residing in the *liṅga*, one should slowly unite it with the water-pot (*kumbha*).
One should then offer betel leaf, jaggery, pieces of sugar, and plantain fruit,
as well as water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), incense, and a lamp.
Having invoked the *pīṭha-śakti*, one should properly unite it with the *vardhanī* vessel.
(4) One should also properly unite Ananta and the others with their respective pitchers, starting from the east;
having worshipped them with perfumes and flowers, one should offer food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth. (5)

Then, before that [liṅga], the wise one should perform the sacrificial oblation (*homa*) either in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), according to the previously mentioned procedure.
(6) Having taken its form with a flower, he should place it into the Śiva-vessel (*śivakumbha*).
Thereafter, one should cause the gift for the journey to be given, as well as the gift of affection for the household.
(7) Having summoned the initiated attendant who is endowed with discipline, one should cover his head with a cloth and adorn him with perfumes and other ornaments. (8)
Then, having carried Śambhu’s jar, which is adorned with silk and other ornaments,
the initiated ones should carry it in sequence for the sake of the jar of the Vidyeśas.
Having recited the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should touch the jar together with *kuśa* grass.
Accompanied by the sound of auspicious chants and endowed with the flame of a lamp,
and provided with umbrellas, chowries, and all kinds of musical instruments—
then, O Lord of Gods, having gone to the hall, [he should place it] upon the central altar.
Having placed it facing west, the wise and attentive person should, with discernment,
place it upon the *vardhanī* on the left side of the deity.
He should then place the *vidyeśvaras*, starting from the east, facing toward the principal [deity].
For the rites of binding, consecration, festival, and sprinkling,
one should likewise arrange the western door in the hall;
however, whichever direction the entrance faces, one should designate that as the east.
He should sequentially place the face [of the deity] facing that door and facing upward,
and he should install Yāgeśa and Śivāgni facing westward. The most excellent preceptor should perform the daily worship of the door and offer oblations.
One should worship the heart in the region of Vāyu, and the head in the south-western direction (Nairṛta).
One should worship the crest-lock (śikhā) in the north-eastern quarter (Īśāna), and the armor (kavaca) in the southeast (Pāvaka).
One should worship the eye in the northeast (Īśāna), and the weapon (astra) in the east (Yakṣa).
In this very manner, having worshipped [the deities] together with incense and lamps,
one should arrange the second enclosure and the others in the directions beginning with the east.
One should also arrange the arches, the door-pitchers, and the pitchers for the world-protectors.
One should worship the eight auspicious *kuṇḍas* and the ten weapons in the east;
likewise, one should offer oblations (*homa*) into the *kuṇḍas* dedicated to the Vidyeśvaras, starting from the east.
When the sacrificial rite is performed during the day, one should worship the Sun in front.
When the night sacrifice has arrived, one should worship Soma in front;
thereafter, having worshipped the Sun, one should worship the door and so forth immediately after that. (2) It is recommended to begin the worship during the day for a sinful person, or at midnight.
At the commencement of the *homa*, if the night has passed into day, one should immediately perform the rite of seating (*divāsana*).
After praising that, one should then proceed with the commencement of the *homa* and other rites.
First, one should worship Śānti, Nandī, Mahākāla, and Kālarātri. (3–4)

Between Indra and Agni, one should worship Bhānu; and in the south-east, one should worship Agni, Vidyā, Bhṛṅgin, Gaṇeśa, and Yama. In the south-west, one should worship Vāstu, Brahmā, Rākṣasa, and Viṣṇu.
One should worship Nivṛti, Vṛṣabha, Skanda, and Vāruṇa in the western direction.
One should worship Kṣetreśa, Vāyu, and Vighneśa in the northwestern direction;
and one should worship Pratiṣṭhā, Gaurī, Caṇḍeśa, and Ghanada in the northern region.
In the northeast, one should worship the Guru, Īśāna, and Brahmā;
likewise, O Mistress of Weapons, one should worship the Weapon-mantra between Kubera and Īśāna. (300)
One should perform the worship of the pavilion by the very path previously described.
(9) One should pray to the Guru, the Lord, and proceed to the vicinity of the Śiva-pit.
One should perform the study of Śaiva mantras in the cardinal directions and in the intermediate directions. (10) One should study the Ṛgveda in the east and the Yajurveda in the south.
In the north, however, one should place the Sāmaveda, and likewise the Atharvaveda in the west.
The Prāsāda-mantra should be in the northeast corner, and the Aghora-mantra in the southeast corner.
One should place Mṛtyuñjaya in the southwest and the Astra-mantra in the northwest;
it should be performed in this very manner, though the specific details are now being stated.
The wise man should recite the Śivasaṅkalpa, then the Āmā Rudra-sūkta,
"kadrudrāya," and "tvamagne" in the eastern part.
[He should also recite] the Śrī-sūkta, the Pavamāna, the Puruṣa-sūkta, and the Tryambaka.
The wise man should especially recite the two *śāntis* on the south;
(4) the *Kālasūkta*, the *Śannavarga*, the *Viṣṇusūkta*, and the *Vāruṇa*.
On the west, the wise man should recite the *Pavamāna* and the *Hiraṇyaka*. (5)
Likewise, the Jyeṣṭhasāman is surrounded by gods, and the Puruṣa is surrounded by men;
moreover, the Virūpākṣa is specifically surrounded by the Vāmadevya in the north.
One should recite the Agni-śopa-upaniṣad and the Raudra-puraṇa in sequence;
furthermore, one should study the Āgamas in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should then perform the fire-oblation (homa), [reciting] the Bhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Gītā, the Māhātmya, and the Īśvarī. (8)
Prior to the commencement of the oblation, however, there should be the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, fuel, and husks;
likewise, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), *darbha* grass, sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and the cooked rice offering (*caru*).
All the materials for the fire oblation, as well as fragrance, flowers, incense, (10) lamps, vessels for the substances, the araṇi wood, and the water-pot.
When the time for the performance of the oblation has arrived, one should bring the *vardhanī* vessel, the unbroken grains, and the ladle;
having thus gathered the materials for the oblation, one proceeds around the sacrificial pit in a counter-clockwise direction.
The preceptor [should preside] over the primary [fire], while the image-guardians (mūrtipās) attend to the other fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
First, one should perform the consecration of the pit, and thereafter accomplish the Śaiva fire.
An oblation offered in consecrated pits becomes fruitless;
therefore, the preceptor should perform the consecration of the pit with mantras.
The length should be two *tāla*s, the circumference [of the base] that of the little finger, and it should be straight,
of the correct proportions, and dark green in color.
And with [blades] having their tips pointing eastward and northward, upon the eastern and other girdles (mekhalā),
one should place thirty *darbha* grasses each, two *vitasti*s in length.
Furthermore, one should place other [threads] wound around the bamboo staff, joined with seats made of *ādara* grass, and knotted with right-handed turns, upon the middle girdle.
The length of the knot is known to be thirty-six finger-breadths, and its width is said to be four finger-breadths;
it is joined with sixteen *darbha* grass blades at its tip. (7)
The strewing of grass should be performed in this manner; the preceptor should cast the girdle.
He should scatter a handful of parched grain above the girdle in the four directions.

One should sacrifice the entire remainder of the oblation in the sacrificial pit with *vikara*, *elā*, and *puṣpa* flowers; one should worship Brahmā, Acyuta, Rudra, and Ananta on the enclosing stones (*paridhi*).
One should worship the World-Protectors, such as Vajrapāṇi and others, upon the seats and on the mats;
in this very manner and sequence, the supreme instructor should perform the worship. (10)
Having first prepared the primary pit and the Śiva-fire according to the rite in the southeast, one should cast it into those respective pits.
Having prepared a seat in each respective place, one should visualize the corresponding form.
(2) I shall now state, in due order, the names of the fires situated within those respective sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).

In the primary [fire], there should be the Śiva-fire; then, starting from the east, there should be one for each direction. (3) To the east is the Āhavanīya fire, and in the southeast is what is called the Vṛddhāgni.
In the south should be the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; in the southwest, the Yauvanānala fire.
(4) In the west is the Gārhapatya fire; Bālāgni is in the northwest corner.
The northern fire may be alone, but the eastern one is common to both;
having assigned these names, one should perform the respective meditations upon them.
Red in color, endowed with five faces, and adorned with seven tongues;
possessing ten arms and three eyes, he is embellished with all ornaments. (6)
Clad in red garments and seated upon a lotus, he sits in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), equipped with a triple girdle and anklets. (7)
In the right hands are the trident, the thunderbolt, the sword, and the spear;
in the left hands are the mace, the staff, the noose, the lotus, and the discus.
In the upward-facing [face], one should place Sṛjihvā; then Śeṣa, and so forth, in order starting from the east.
One should install Svāhā, O Goddess, and likewise Svadhā in the south, and Vāmana in the west.
The meditation on the Śaiva fire is thus prescribed and proclaimed as being performed in the Śiva-kuṇḍa:
it has one face, three eyes, three girdles, and three feet;
in its right hands, it holds a rosary, a trident, and a sacrificial ladle.
In his left hands, he holds a goad, a hand-drum,
and a sacrificial ladle. One should meditate upon the Āhavanīya fire, red in color, seated comfortably, and draped in yellow garments, within the center of the eastern sacrificial pit.
He has four arms and three eyes, with a single face and matted hair;
he holds a trident and an axe, and is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
One should worship Vṛddhāgni in the fire as having a white luster, mounted upon a bull, with two faces, a golden complexion, three feet, and seven hands. (4)
The four tongues beginning with Hiraṇyā are located in the right face;
the three tongues beginning with Suprabhā are situated in the left face.
He holds the Śakti, the fire, the *sruva* ladle, and the *sruk* ladle along with a vessel of clarified butter in his left hands;
he holds the *tomara* and the axe in his right hands, and is mounted upon a goat as his vehicle.
Having meditated thus, one should place the Dakṣiṇāgni fire in the southern sacrificial pit [kuṇḍa].
[One should visualize the deity] with three eyes, five faces, red limbs, and ten hands.

In his right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and two hands in the gesture of granting fearlessness; in his left hands, he holds a chisel, a noose, a lotus, a discus, and a hand in the gesture of boon-granting. (8)
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Sadyojātā, and Īśānī—these alone constitute the entirety [of the group].
One should place Yauvanāgnī, mounted upon a bull, in the southwestern direction (Nairṛtī).

Red-bodied and adorned with red garments, joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in his upper hands, and decorated with ornaments of pearls. (10)
One should meditate upon Gārhapatya in the western fire-pit as being endowed with seven tongues, having one face, wearing matted hair, and mounted upon a horse. (11)
Two-faced and single-hearted, with four ears and two nostrils,
possessing four horns and mounted upon a bull, he has a radiance equal to the rising sun.
In his right side are the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a rosary, and a spear.
They took up a fan and a vessel of ghee for the left hand.
One should thus place the form of a young fire in the Vāyu-kunda;
it has two eyes, two arms, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Having meditated upon Kevalāgni in the center of the northern pit as being clothed in white garments, possessing an equal brilliance of white and red, adorned with all ornaments, and seated upon a lotus throne; (4)
The two-faced [liṅga], the Veda-peak, the fearless, the spear, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
One should install the deity in the northeastern sacrificial pit (īśakuṇḍaka), who bestows boons and carries a sword and fire in his right and left hands respectively,
and who possesses the nature of the common fire.

Following the very same path previously described, the preceptor, having meditated upon Śambhu as the primary fire within each respective sacrificial pit, should perform the sacrifice with an undistracted mind. (6) 350.
Having prepared a seat for the Pradhāna, one should perform the visualization of the form:
five-faced, ten-armed, with a luster as white as cow’s milk. (7)
One should meditate upon the dweller who bestows all accomplishments and faces the west.
Having invoked Śiva into the Śiva-fire, one should worship Śiva as in the daily rite.
Endowed with the five offerings and accompanied by water for the feet and incense, one should first worship in this manner; thereafter, one should worship the Earth-form and the others.
Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, Water, Wind, the Moon, Sky,
and the End— these eight are the bearers of the forms of the sacrificial pits.
Bhava, Ugra, Śarva, Mahādeva, Rudraka, Bhīma, Paśupati, and Īśāna are his eight forms.
(11) Bhava is in the eastern pit, and Ugra is in the southeast.
And Śarva is in the southern pit, while Mahādeva is in the southwest;
Rudra is in the western part, and Bhīma indeed in the northwest;
Paśupati is in the northern pit, and Īśa likewise in the northeast. (I.21b)

They are three-eyed and four-armed, wearing crests of matted hair, and are described as possessing forms complete with all ornaments and earrings. Thus have the guardians of the images been described; now the Lord of the Images is being told of.
One should worship Puruṣa and the others in the cardinal directions of the sacrificial pit, and Hṛdaya and the others in the intermediate directions.
(3) The Guru should worship Īśāna, Netra, Astra, and the Mūla-mantra in the primary pit; he should worship Īśāna, who has the luster of crystal, in the Śiva-pit. (4)
One should meditate on the Puruṣa in the eastern pit as being endowed with a yellow color,
and on Aghora in the southern pit as having the luster of collyrium.
One should worship Vāra, endowed with a red complexion, in the Saumya kuṇḍa;
and Sadyojāta, white in color and possessing two arms, in the western kuṇḍa.
In the heart is the Fire [deity], impure, three-eyed, and four-armed;
she is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and equipped with a battle-axe and a trident.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing white garments,
one should worship the auspicious heart, which has the luster of the color white, within the fire-pit.
The wise one should place the head, which is said to be yellowish in luster, in the Īśa-pool (northeast);
the crest-lock, endowed with a dark-blue color, in the direction of the Nairṛta (southwest). (8)
The wise practitioner should place the armor, which has the luster of smoke-colored light, in the wind-pitcher;
the eye is dark-hued, and the weapon is indeed black in color.
The best of teachers should then place the two [deities] in the *śiva-kuṇḍa*;

they have three eyes and four arms, beginning with the heart-mantra and ending with the weapon-mantra, and they wear yellow garments while holding the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. (10)
The nature of Sadāśiva must indeed be known by the preceptor.
Having placed these two [deities] in that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should likewise place the Vasus outside it;
and outside that, the Maruts, and further outside, the Guardians of the World (Lokapālas). (I.22a)

If it is devoid of the world-protectors (lokapālas), it is declared to be a middling *homa*. If it is devoid of the Maruts, Vasus, Ādityas, and Asuras, it is considered the lowest. (2) The Guru should place all the deities, beginning with those of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), within the center of the pit.
Then, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual, beginning with the water for the feet and ending with incense.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter in sequence into the *hastaka-māna* pit;
for the principal rite, one should perform the *homa* with *palāśa* wood, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and parched grain (*lāja*).

Then, the officiating priest should offer twenty-five other oblations, such as fuel sticks (*samidh*) and so forth, into the *Śiva-kuṇḍa* for the deity, and subsequently into the other sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*).
One should worship the six limbs of Brahmā starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
having offered ghee into each fire-pit fifty-two hundred times.
Having offered half of that number of fuel sticks (*samidh*), and likewise the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in that same number;
having offered with the substances prescribed for each respective fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the previously stated number.
One should offer all other substances in sequence according to their availability.
Ghee from a tawny cow is excellent; that from any other mixed-breed cow is middling.
Clarified butter from a ram is said to be the lowest; one should avoid ghee from a buffalo.
[One may offer] a thousand, or three-quarters, or even half of a thousand.
The Guru should perform the primary oblation in the principal fire-pit according to the sequence beginning with the *uttamā*;
likewise, he should offer the five Brahmans and the six limbs into the fire-pits located in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Indeed, according to the number of oblations for the principal rite, one should perform half and half again of the oblation; [one should perform] the oblation for the primordial deities and those belonging to the enclosures as previously declared. (10) The principal fire-pit (kuṇḍa) should indeed be known as being one-hundredth part of the total number of oblations.
Four *khārīs* and one *bhāra*, and two *khārīs* are included in the *saṅgraha*.
The wise man should offer oblations at the appropriate times in the sequence beginning with the *uttamā*.
Two *gavyūti*s are held by the forefinger; this is designated as a *bindu*. (i.22b)
Six *bindus* and a half a *sarṣapa* constitute one *vīma*; two *karṣas* make one *muṣṭi*, and two of those make one *prasṛti*. Two of those are called a *kuḍupa*, and two of those make a *dhāraṇa*.
Two *dhāraṇās* are declared to constitute one *prastha*, and thirty-two *prasthas* constitute one *āhuti*. One should then perform a single *āhuti* with clarified butter weighing one *karṣa*.
Alternatively, twenty *māṣas* of *kuñja* [weight] are traditionally recorded as one *dhāraṇā*.
Eight *dhāraṇās* constitute a *muṣṭi*, or alternatively, a *muṣṭi* is said here to be a *vādha*. Another [measure] called *kṛṣṇa* is known as a *kuḍumbī*.
Four *kṛttas* make one *prastha*, and four of those make one *āḍhaka*.
All [offerings], beginning with the nine kinds of grain, should be offered separately with water.
(6) Two *prastha*s of mustard seeds are prescribed, and sesame seeds by the measure of one *añjali*;
in this very same proportion, one should offer them in sequence at each respective time. (7)
The Vyāhṛti-homa with clarified butter is thus described; here the five-fold division is stated:
the Āhavanīya fire is in the east, the Dakṣiṇāgni in the south, the Gārhapatya fire in the west, and the Kevalāgni in the north. (8)
In the northeast, however, the Śivāgni is proclaimed as the Pañcāgni.
In the center, there should be the form of space; in the east, the form of wind;
in the south, the form of fire; and in the north, the form of water. (9)
In the western pit, Kṣmāmūrti is the sustainer of the forms of the pits. (10) I shall describe those respective lords of the forms, starting from the principal one and ending with the westernmost.
And in the fivefold system, the meditation on the forms of the deities is taught here.
For Īśa and Sadāśiva, the meditation on form is said to be as previously described.
The supreme guide should perform worship by means of the path of the five obstructions;
in the eastern sacrificial pit, he should visualize the three-eyed one, who has a single face and a smiling countenance.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a serpent as his sacred thread,
resembling pure crystal, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Holding a rosary, a trident, a sword, and a bell in her right hands,
and an arrow, a water-pot, a lotus, and the gesture of granting boons in her left hands.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord, adorned with all ornaments,
the wise man [should place] Rudra in the southern direction, his body smeared with ashes.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
possessing the manifold luster of rubies, and draped in yellow garments.

In the northern *kuṇḍa*, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who resembles the color of a dark cloud, holding a book and a trident in his left hands, while displaying the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāna*) and a firebrand in his right hands. (7)
Having one face and two eyes, blazing with a crown and tiara, wearing yellow garments, and holding a conch, mace, discus, and lotus. (8)
Endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with ornaments of pearls,
Brahmā is [installed] in the western pit, decorated with a girdle of muñja grass and darbha blades.
Four-armed and four-faced, with two eyes in each face, (10) wearing yellow garments, with a beautiful countenance, and adorned with variegated cloths. 400.
Complete in all its limbs, [bearing] a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot—thus the Lords of Form (Mūrtīśvaras) have been described; now they are explained by means of their mantras.
(I.23b) In the east, the Puruṣa-sruk is proclaimed, and likewise the Ghoraśiras in the south.
The noose (pāśa), the armor (kavaca) belonging to Sadyojāta, and the crest (śikhā) belonging to Vāmadeva are considered to be in the north.

(2) The Eye (netra) and the Weapon (astra) are the deities of Īśāna; having worshipped them primarily in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍaka), one should worship two deities in each pit starting from the east, with the visualization of their colors as before. (3)
Having invoked each [deity] into its respective fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the oblation (*homa*) with its corresponding mantra.
Thus, the fivefold [rite] has been described; the remainder should be performed as previously stated.
(4) If one should arrange a single fire-pit, it may be done according to one's means.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the prescribed materials, offering a tenth part for the limbs of Brahmā.
Thus, the three kinds of fuel-wood have been declared; now the tongues [of fire] are described here, extending from the western (Vāruṇa) to the northeastern (Īśāna) direction. (5–6)
For Hiraṇyā, the oblation is clarified butter; likewise for Madhudugdhā.
For Kanakā, ghee is prescribed, and for Dadhī, sugar.
(7) For Raktā, however, one should offer caru as well as fruits and cakes.
Having offered parched grain (*lāja*) into Kṛṣṇā, one should offer wild rice (*nīvāra*) and chickpeas (*caṇaka*);
likewise, one should offer flattened peas (*niṣpāva*) and *āḍhaka* into Suprabhā;
and having offered barley (*yava*) into Atiraktā, one should indeed offer bamboo shoots (*veṇu*) and mung beans (*mudga*).
One should offer sesame, black gram, white mustard, and cow dung, as well as all other substances, into the fire of Kanaka in sequence.
With a ladle full of clarified butter, one should offer fuel-sticks twelve finger-breadths long once the fire is well-kindled. (10)
One should collect kāśa grass, clay, lotuses, and tālī leaves according to the prescribed rite.
(11) The preceptor should take seven or eight grains of rice and say to the guru: "Whether it be cooked according to the rite or otherwise, he should consume it in a single mouthful. (i.24a)
One should perform the oblation of cooked *caru* rice on the street; this is the refinement of the conversation.
One should cast fried grain (*lājaka*) into the fire with the hand of a hunchback.
One should offer parched rice (*pṛthuka*), *dhanuka*, and barley meal (*saktu*) in portions of one handful each.
One should offer wheat, bamboo-seeds, and wild rice according to one's capacity;
beans are said to be worth nine [units],
chickpeas ten, and a wise man should offer an *āḍhaka* of kidney-beans with five fingers [of the hand].
Having offered kulastha, māṣa, mudga, as well as priyaṅgu and śyāmaka according to one's capacity, one should offer half that amount of barley and mustard seeds.
Having offered sesame and mung beans, one should offer the *vyāhṛti* mantras at the end of the substances;
for the sake of food, it is prescribed that one *āḍhaka* of each be offered separately.

One should cook the rice in due order according to the measurements prescribed for each respective substance. The wise practitioner should offer pure food, mung-bean porridge, milk-rice, kṛsara-rice, and jaggery-rice into the fire with ladles of the size of an akṣa.
Having divided one's own measures of flour-cakes into four parts, one should otherwise offer them.

(8) Having offered the oblation of milk, curd, honey, ghee, meat, sugarcane, and the substances of one's birth, and having performed the full oblation with the *sruva* ladle, [one offers] a portion like the fruit of the *puṃnāga*. (9)
One should perform the oblation with half a section of sugarcane;
having offered mango wood of its own [standard] measure, one should split six coconut fruits.
Having likewise [offered] *likuca* fruit of its own measure, one should cast them into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having divided the breadfruit into thirty parts, one should offer it as an oblation.
One should offer into the fire after piercing with a single Vibhīta fruit the kāla, sūraṇa, bāla, padmakanda, nīlaka, and kunda.
Then, one *caṇa* of sandalwood, two of musk, (2) one of camphor,
one of saffron from Kāśmīra, one of musk, and one of black sulphur.
One should burn an incense of black gram and guggulu, mixed with jujube fruit.
(3) [One should avoid] uśīra, water-piṅga, maruta, and tālaka.
And [he offered] two-finger-long sprouts, a *śrīvatsa* mark, five flowers,
nutmeg, betel leaf combined with cardamom and cloves.
One should offer the substance as an oblation with the hand, or with a ladle filled to the brim;
then, one should perform the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) using the *sruc* ladle filled to the brim of the pit.
One should offer *palāśa* wood with the *sadyojāta* mantra and clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra;
having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *aghora* mantra, one should offer parched grain (*lāja*) with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra;
and one should offer groats (*saktu*) with the *vāmadeva* mantra, while offering the eye of *īśāna*.

Having first offered all the materials for the kindling (*samid*) into the principal fire, one should subsequently offer the remainder of the oblation into the pits starting from the east. Having offered *niṣpāva* and *apāmārga* into the northeast, one should then offer them into the principal fire. (8–9)
In the east, *aśvattha*, wheat; in the south, sesame and *udumbara*;
in the north, *āḍhaka* and *vaṭa*; in the west, *plakṣa* and mung beans; in the southeast, mustard;
and in the northeast, mung and black gram.

The wise one should offer oblations into the Śiva-kuṇḍa with *khādira* wood in the south-west, and *caṇa* and *bilvaka* in the north-west; likewise, *āmra* and *nīvāra* for the Netra-kuṇḍa. For the Atrī-kuṇḍa, one should use *vaiṇava* wood and *dūrvā* grass, and similarly for the Āśiva-kuṇḍaka.
And in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) of the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the respective mantras,
using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), caru-rice, parched grains (lāja), and the substances of the directions in equal measure.
The best of teachers should offer all other substances— whether deficient or even in excess— into the fire according to their available measure.
In the forest, having offered wild rice with its root and the *rājamāṣa* bean,
one should offer *śyāmāka* grain at the crest and *priyaṅgu* and *gulasthaka* at the neck.
One should offer a five-fold oblation of cakes with the Aghora mantra;
having offered milk-rice with the Netra mantra, one should perform the fire-oblation of milk with the Īśa mantra.
