One should offer curd with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, honey with the Vāmadeva mantra, molasses with the Ghoramantra, and a stalk of sugarcane at the root-mantra (Mūlamantra).
One should offer fruits and the like with the Īśāna mantra, and bulbs and the like with the root mantra;
likewise, one should offer sandalwood, musk, and black aloe-wood with the root mantra.
One should offer into the fire, in sequence, gorocanā, kāśmīra, kuṅkuma, mṛganābhi, snow-water, and camphor.
One should offer incense made of *bījamukhya*, *śrībera*, *muśira*, *maru*, and *guggulu* with the ten-syllable mantra; and flowers and *bilva* fruits with the *Pāśupata* mantra.
One should offer betel leaf combined with fragrant substances using the Aghora mantra;
other items suitable for the fire sacrifice, however, one should offer using the Mūla mantra alone. (10)
Having specifically offered the substance and the recitation again and again,
one should perform the fire-oblation ritual starting from the east and ending at the wind-pit.
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should offer oblations in sequence with the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
Afterwards, one should present incense and lamps at the end of that, within the three girdles (*mekhalā*).
Then, one should offer the bali-oblation to Lokeśa and the others with their respective name-mantras,
[offering it] to the deities of the various sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and so forth by way of the channel-union (nāḍī-sandhāna).
Having taken unbroken rice (akṣata) and flowers, one should rise up in due order.
One should unite the supreme [soul] with Śiva, who resides within the fire situated in the Śiva-kuṇḍa.
(4) Having offered the great *pūrṇāhuti* accompanied by all musical instruments and endowed with the resonance of the Vedas, one should then offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*. (5)
Having displayed incense, lamps, and so forth, one should offer the inner and outer bali.
Having performed the salutation to the ears, one should say: "May you grant me protection.
(6) Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having performed the recitation (japa), one should offer it.

And the fire situated in each respective pit should be protected within that very pit. (7) In case of rising, sitting, anger, hunger, spitting, and speaking with those who are uninitiated, one should respectively worship the deities Vāyu and Āpa. (8)
If, due to heat or exhaustion,
there should arise a lapse in the performance of the ritual during the recitation of the mantra as prescribed for the yantra, one should perform an oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Then, having gone to the vicinity of the water-jar from the southern side of the altar,
one should worship with a handful of flowers while reciting the mantra of the three principles (*tattva*).
Thereafter, one should offer incense and lamps, and then perform the great food offering (*mahānaivedya*).
A vessel of four *hasta*s in measure is called a *prastha*;
four *prasthas* constitute an *āḍhaka*, and four *āḍhakas* make a *droṇa*.
The *nitya* [daily] recitation is always performed with two *droṇas* and eight *droṇas*.

(2) However, the *naimittika* [occasional] recitation consists of eight *droṇas*, while the *kāmya* [optional] recitation, which is requested by those according to their specific numbers, consists of twelve *bhāras*. (3)
In this manner, the most excellent preceptor should cause the food offering (*naivedya*) to be presented in due order.
Eight kinds of sacrificial oblations (*havis*) should be offered:

pure milk-rice (*pāyasa*), plain cooked rice (*annaka*), rice with jaggery (*gulānna*), rice mixed with sesame and lentils (*kṛsarānna*), rice with curd (*dadhyānna*), and rice with mung beans (*mudgānnaka*).

Two āḍhakas of rice mixed with various ingredients, accompanied by many side dishes and including cakes and the like; likewise, a single grain of *vrīhi* rice becomes tenfold when it is *śāli* rice. (5–6)

Priyaṅgu is said to be a hundredfold [more meritorious], while nīvāra is a thousandfold; wheat (godhūma) shall be a hundred-thousandfold, and bamboo grain (vaiṇava) is indeed infinite. (7) Edible food is fivefold: that which is chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drunk.
Provided with various fruits and accompanied by cakes,
one should wash the vessel and worship the food offering.
One should fill the top of the rice with side dishes.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a pure wooden tripod, the cook should serve it;
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, he should cause it to enter the sacrificial hall.
Having placed it before Śiva, he should then sprinkle it with water.

Then, with the mantra "devasya tvā," one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented. One should perform the ritual services (upacāra) beginning with incense and lamps and ending with the side dishes.
Having worshipped with the "mantra-flower" (mantrapuṣpa) and other offerings, the preceptor (deśika) should bestow the sacred ash (bhasma).
The food-offering for the three times, the daily festival and other rites,
the performance of the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) and so forth, and the establishment of the kitchen hall—
all these daily festivals should be conducted in the pavilion of the Śiva-sacrifice.
One should avoid using water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) as a causal factor in the Śiva-sacrifice.

(4) From the preparation of the *akura* offerings up to the ritual ablution, one should feed the twice-born at midday, numbering from a thousand to ten thousand, according to the extent of one's wealth. (5)
For the sake of averting all defects, one should perform a feeding of Brahmins with devotion for seven nights, or five nights, or three nights;
or else, on a single night or immediately, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the deity. (6)
One should offer oblations every day with one's own respective mantra and worship Śiva.
In this very manner, according to the prescribed rule, day after day— at evening and at dawn—
one should thus perform worship during the night and when the morning has become clear.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, the preceptor should complete his daily rites;
then, having entered the sacrificial hall together with the officiating priests and attendants,
he should worship Vighnarāja and thereafter perform the formal declaration of intent (*saṅkalpa*).
The preceptor should establish the "auspicious day" rite, the five products of the cow, and the water-pot.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should carry out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth.
One should worship, in sequence as before, from the doors up to the worship of the gurus.
The Guru should place the *śivakumpā* and other vessels;
then, having discarded the *nirmālya*, he should prepare a firm seat.

Having performed the visualization of the form and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the preceptor should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra and offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, incense, lamps, betel, and other offerings.
Then, one should prepare a movable seat either upon a mirror or a *kūrca* [grass-bundle].
Having offered the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) beginning with oil and ending with the *kumbha* [vessel],
one should join that image into the *kumbha* and sustain it with perfumes and garlands.
Holding incense and a lamp, one should cause mantra-food and betel-leaf to be offered.
One should fashion a golden image according to the prescribed rule, and thereafter perform the worship upon the altar,
having presented the ritual offerings by means of the previously mentioned procedure.

One should certainly perform the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the worship of the doors and other parts, and the fire offerings (*homaka*) at both times; however, the offering of food (*naivedya*) together with incense and lamps is prescribed for the other time.
Having dismissed the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*), one should [dispose of] the food offering along with the incense and lamps.

Having worshipped day by day according to the prescribed procedure on the designated days, one should thereafter enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and perform the general sacrifice (*sāmānyayajana*). At the time of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*), however, it should be performed without the *nandyāvarta* diagram. (7–8)
When the work on the ground has been excellently completed but the application of lime-plaster has not yet been done,
one should take a moment and perform the re-consecration.
Having thoroughly sprinkled the Peace Vase (*śāntikumbha*), the supreme preceptor should worship it.
Before the designated day, at the conclusion of the evening oblation.
Having gone to the vicinity of the primary linga, the supreme preceptor should purify it;
having divided the portion of the pedestal into sixteen parts, he should place one part as the nine gems.
One should gradually bind together one-tenth part mixed with sand and one-fifth part;
[the base] should be square, measuring three finger-breadths in size, and made of gold.
One should draw [the design] with the seed-syllable of Śiva and place it within the central cavity;
having placed a ruby in the middle, one should set an emerald upon Indra.
Indranīla should be in the southern direction, and crystal should be in the western;
vajra should be in the northern quarter, and vaiḍūrya in the region of fire (the southeast).
One should place pearls in the south-western region, rubies in the north-western region, and corals in the north-eastern region;
these four should be arranged according to their purificatory rites.
Having worshipped with the root mantra, one should worship the sixfold seat;
then one should display the *mukulī*, the lotus (*padma*), and the *śodhanī* mudrās.
One should perform the placement from the center up to the northeast using the root mantra.
One should then fill the liṅga and the firmly established pedestal with water mixed with milk.
On the front of the temple, on the south, the southeast, or another location, one should then smear two squares with cow dung. (6)
There, a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared, having eight petals and a pericarp;
it should be provided with nine vessels, or else with a single vessel.

One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and sprinkle all the ritual materials. (8) If the five-fold or three-fold stability of the Śiva-liṅga is broken, [one must perform the rite].
One should perform all that worship and so forth in the Śiva-sacrifice,
especially at the root-liṅga, accompanied by the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
[This includes] the food offering (naivedya), perfumes, flowers, along with incense and lamps.
Having fully worshipped the eight substances for the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras) in sequence,
first [worship] the five-fold form and the substance with the three-fold form;
one should consecrate these very substances with this root mantra.
Having performed worship according to the prescribed method, one should carry out the rites up to the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Then, one should sprinkle the mortar and the pestle with pure water.
Having worshipped the six seats, one should place [the pestle] upon them:
the mortar has Brahmā as its deity, and the pestle has Viṣṇu as its deity.
Having adorned the mortar and the pestle with cloths and *darbha* grass,
and having worshipped them with scents, flowers, and so forth, one should offer incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Having summoned two attendants wearing turbans and upper garments,
the preceptor should place that substance inside the mortar.
Then, taking a pestle, one should strike it very firmly again;
having thoroughly pounded it with pestles, the wise man should observe that it is well-dried.
Having performed the sixteen-fold worship, one should offer oblations for atonement in the prescribed sequence.
To remedy defects such as contact with artisans, one should establish a vessel for pacification (*śāntikumbha*).
Having kindled the fire of the vessels, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *śānti* mantra.
(6) Earth should be taken from the root of *darbha* grass, from an anthill, from a sacred field, and from a *karkaṭa* [crab] burrow;
(7) from the horns of a bull, from the root of a *bilva* tree, from a riverbank, and from near an elephant.
The wise one should take eight types of earth and cause them to be placed within a vessel.
Likewise, having taken the five barks—known as those of the *aśvattha*, *māmbu*, *jambū*, *vaṭa*, and *audumbara*—and having placed them in a single vessel; (8)
The sprouts of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *jambū*, and *nyagrodha* trees are declared to be the "five sprouts" (*pañcapallava*); one should place them in that vessel. (9)
Bilva, kapittha, niguṇḍī, saralī, and likewise vāruṇa—
these are known as the "five bilvas," which one should place inside the vessel.
The most excellent preceptor should duly set out the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having placed rice grains mixed with sesame and rice before it. (11)
The wise one should place those respective jars together with mango sprouts;
having worshipped the seat arising from the six [syllables], he should perform the worship according to the *saṃhitā* in due order.
There, the Guru should recite the *vyomavyāpin* mantra and offer incense and lamps;
he should then place rice, together with the two protective amulets (*kautuka*), into the vessel.
Having worshipped the white ashes, the coconut,
and the betel leaf with the ritual substances in their proper order, one should skillfully place them with a sense of wonder.
The wise man should offer the *saṃpāta* oblation accompanied by the sound of musical instruments;
then, joined by the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), he should proceed to the vicinity of the Śiva-liṅga.
Then the wise one should especially perform an oil massage for the deity;
having bathed the area between the liṅga and the pedestal with the five products of the cow in the proper sequence, (5) [he should proceed].

One should consecrate [the image] with the eight types of earth and water, with decoctions, and with small jars; likewise, one should sprinkle it individually with the five sprouts and bilva fruits. Then, having anointed it with sandalwood paste, one should fasten the protective thread.

Thus it should be performed at night; then, in the morning, one should perform the ritual bath. (8) Having then entered the inner sanctum, one should sequentially perform the auspicious-day consecration and sprinkling; having removed the worn-out flowers, along with the protective thread and the cloth. (9)
Then one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and arrange the ritual services (*upacāra*).
Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the six paths (*adhvaṣaṭka*), one should indeed place the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*).
Then, having performed the placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*), one should offer incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having returned once more to the sacrificial hall, together with the officiating priests and attendants,
one should worship Śiva along with his limbs (retinue) according to the method of sacrificial worship.
Having kindled the fire and worshipped it, one should perform the *homa* offering as previously described.
Having first performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should then offer the *jaya* oblations and so forth;
and having offered the *bhūḥ* and other oblations up to the *śiras* oblation according to the rule, one should finally perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Thereafter, one should offer incense and lamps, and then present the inner and outer offerings.
Having performed the salutation to the ears, one should burn the protective enclosures with the *varman* mantra.
Taking up the seats, one should untie the knots;
having brought the spread of darbha grass, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter and burn it.
Having taken that ash, one should wear it on the forehead;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should afterwards worship with recitations.
One should perform the ritual of the body of Kuṇḍa by means of the path of the union of the channels (*nāḍī*).
(7) The wise one should join [the deity] within the *kumbha* (vessel), accompanied by incense, lamps, and so forth.
(8) Afterwards, one should dismiss the fire, as well as the *astrakumbha* and the *vardhanī*.
He should dismiss all the world-protectors, beginning with the gatekeepers.

(9) When an auspicious moment has arrived, the preceptor should perform the rite of departure with ritual offerings; having received the command of the deity, he should especially enter [the city] amidst the joyful sounds of the householders' delight. (10)
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, molasses, silver, and salt— these they call the ten gifts (*daśadāna*).
Furthermore, the gift of a daughter, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and likewise the gift of sacred ash;

A rudrākṣa bead shall serve as a śivaliṅga; one should cause other [liṅgas] to be given as well. Thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and earrings, as well as a bed, a vehicle, female servants, and various kinds of gems.
Having spent a year [serving] the earth filled with crops and one's own body [offered] to the milk-yielding cow,
one should afterwards offer these betel-leaves and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The best [fee] should be thirty niṣkas, while twenty niṣkas would be middling.
The minimum sacrificial fee for the preceptor shall be ten niṣkas;
half of that for the assistant preceptor, and half of that for the one who provides the site and gold.
And for all the officiating priests, there shall be a separate gift for each individual. (5–6)
One should give half of that material as the fee for the craftsman;
half of that to those who recite the Astra-mantras, and an equal amount to the Vedic scholar. One should give an amount equal to the divine command to the reciter of the Purāṇas as well. (7)
One should especially show affection toward the local attendants according to their faith and merit,
as well as toward those who sing, play instruments, and dance, and likewise toward the female servants and other devotees of Śiva. (8–9)
O Guru, perform extensive and distinguished giving in due order;
for satisfaction in what is being practiced is the cause of the gods' satisfaction.
The teacher is the anger of the mind and indeed the anger of the gods. Therefore, the master should satisfy the teacher with every effort. (10)
Even a mere deficiency in the sacrificial fee— such as a load of firewood or ten jars of clarified butter— will lead to the destruction of the performer.
An *ācārya* who is devoid of mantra, a craftsman who is devoid of ritual action, and a donor who is devoid of wealth—these three factors bring about the destruction of the family. (I.30a)
One should perform the rite in this manner according to the prescribed rules and in accordance with one's wealth.
He who performs the sacrifice with a deficiency of wealth perishes through his lack of devotion.

Therefore, having invited two Brahmins according to the path taught in the scriptures and in accordance with one's wealth, the preceptor should perform the purification of the *kalaśas* as refined by the ritual.
Equipped with sacred ash and rudrākṣas, and provided with a head-cloth,
one should lift the principal pitcher and the vardhanī vessel above the head.
Having lifted up the eight jars and the head of the attendant,
the Guru, the preceptor, should touch the root [of the disciple] with his hand-broom and recite the mantra.
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, provided with parasols and fly-whisks, joined by the chanting of the Vedas, and attended by those reciting hymns and auspicious prayers.
Having performed a circumambulation of the palace together with all the devotees,
one should first offer incense and lamps, and then scatter flowers and parched grain.
Having stepped from one footstep to another, he should cause [the disciple] to enter at the doorway;
then, having offered the *arghya*, betel, and the eye-ointment (*nīrāñjana*), the Guru [proceeds].
Having prepared a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice at the base of the liṅga,
and having duly installed the water-pot (kumbha), the preceptor, being serene in soul, should likewise proceed.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, perform the sprinkling with the "Auspicious Day" mantra;
then, having placed the seat and the form endowed with the thirty-eight kalās.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva in the liṅga, the preceptor takes a flower;
(I.30b) taking the seed from the water-pot, he should place it upon the top of the liṅga.
Taking the seed from the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it upon the pedestal;
(2) one should then place the eight jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) in their respective locations.
Having lifted up the auspicious water-pot, one should consecrate the Śiva-liṅgas;
then, having consecrated them in their respective places, one should offer the mantras and the food.
The consecration by means of ablutions with the five nectars and so forth in due order;
[the deity] is provided with garments and ornaments, and all its limbs are anointed with fragrance.
Having adorned [the deity] with all kinds of flowers,
the supreme guru, having prayed to Śiva, should present a great oblation accompanied by incense and lamps.
One should cause a benediction accompanied by the sound of the Veda to be recited;
the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) must be performed, as well as the great food offering (mahānaivedya).
Then, one should perform the festival for the forms of Somāskanda and the others.
On the following day, the wise practitioner should perform the daily bath and other rites.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing there while holding [the vessel] one thousand and eight times,
or alternatively, one should perform a hundred and eight oblations for pacification.
One should perform sacrifices for three fortnights, two fortnights, or one fortnight in succession;
one should daily offer the *śānti-homa* and complete eleven recitations of the *Rudra*.
One should especially perform the recitation (*japa*) with the Astra-mantra and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Brahma-mantra;
one should daily feed Brahmins according to the extent of one's means.
Day by day, having fully honored either a thousand or fifteen Brahmins, one should afterwards satisfy them with food alone.
In this very manner, for the sake of propitiating Śiva,
for the purpose of avoiding faults, and for the removal of the defect of heat.
In this very manner, the preceptors should act regarding both auspicious and inauspicious matters.
Afterwards, one should worship the teacher with garments, gold, and rings.
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks a son obtains a son.
One who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth; one who seeks sacrifice shall obtain sacrifice.
Having attained happiness in this world, he shall at the end attain union (*sāyujya*).
Thus ends the "Rite of the Eightfold Bond" in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Sahasratantra*.
I bow to Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods and leader of the worlds, whose chest is marked with the saffron from the full expanse of the breasts of the illustrious Pārvatī. (i.31b)
The fourfold installation has indeed been declared with certainty by the best of sages;
now it is demonstrated according to the procedure taught in the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas,
in the sequence of *āvarta*, *punarāvarta*, and *anāvarta*.
And finally, "intervened" (antarita); thus it is declared by the wise to be fourfold.
O Six-faced One, listen as I shall describe its nature as Anāvarta:
there is no village where a temple or a *liṅga* has ever existed.
In that regard, whatever shrine or emblem is established by men there is declared to be "non-returning" (*anāvarta*); now, the "non-returning" shall be further explained.
If the linga should be uprooted by the ocean or by rivers,
or where it is [damaged] by wild animals, it should be reinstalled elsewhere.
It was renowned as Āvarta by those learned in the Kāmika Āgama;
for there, even the temple and the liṅga had long since fallen into ruin.
If the ālaya is established there as a sign, those sages who are experts in the scriptures call that too a whirlpool. (8)
Where there is no abode, yet a mark exists, they call this the "revolving" [state].
Where there is no abode and no cool mark, it is declared to be the "non-revolving" [state]. (9)
This is called "the whirlpool" (*āvarta*); it is further described as "the returning whirlpool.
[It occurs] in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that is devoid of color, or on a pedestal (*pīṭha*) that is devoid of its binding structure.
Where a new [verse] is composed, it is called *punarāvarta*; thus has *punarāvarta* been described. Now, *antarita* is being described.
If [the water] has been touched by Caṇḍālas, those who have fallen from their caste, or even by robbers,
men perform the sprinkling of the traveler for the sake of pacifying that defect.

That is declared by the wise who have reached the further shore of the scriptures to be "interposed" (antarita). Installation is said to be of three kinds: interposed, non-interposed, and [the third].
Now, regarding the distinction between *pratiṣṭhā* and *antarita*, it is as follows: (5) That in which there is a perfect drawing-in (*ākarṣaṇa*) is called *pratiṣṭhā*.
Where there is no drawing [of the deity], that is called "intermediate" (*antarita*).
(6) In all three cases here, one should perform the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the manner of the *bālālaya* rite.
(7) I shall now describe the procedure for the non-returning (*anāvarta*) installation according to the tradition.
Having mastered all the authentic scriptures through the grace of his guru,
the preceptor, who was a righteous Brahmin and a priest, [performed the rite] with auspicious songs and instrumental music on a propitious day at an auspicious moment. (8–9)
Having gone to the mountain and seen the stone, one should meditate upon the mountain as consisting of Śiva.
Where the preceptor breaks the stone fragment into half a disc,
there the Guru should perform the worship and invoke Śiva.
Having invoked that deity from the stone into the pitcher, the best of teachers [should proceed];
whatever kind of stone-liṅga the practitioner desires to fashion, that should be its asterism and its measurement, while for a wooden or small liṅga, it should be smaller. (2–3)
Having caused a mobile liṅga to be fashioned according to the scriptures,
the preceptor should indeed invoke Śiva into a wooden liṅga placed within a pitcher.
The Guru should bring such a wooden *liṅga* to his own country;
with a vigilant mind, he should worship it perpetually according to the prescribed sequence.

Once a block of stone has been brought from the mountain, the artisan should bring it under his control. Whatever linga is to be fashioned from that stone, it should be made of silver and of those same proportions. The wise should have a linga made of wood in accordance with the scriptures.
The wise sages have declared this to be the *bāla-liṅga*.
Having installed this *bāla-liṅga* in the *bāla-ālaya*, the Guru should duly invoke Śiva from the mobile liṅga (*cara-liṅga*) into the ritual pitcher (*kumbha*). (8–9)
Having properly invoked Śiva from the pitcher into the *bāla-liṅga*,
the preceptor should consecrate the *bāla-liṅga* with the sixty-four rites.
After the artisan has had the preceptor fashion the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rule, (I.33a).
Then, having entered the temple, one should install this *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite.
For within this stone *liṅga*, one should invoke Śiva, beginning with the [deity] Bāla;
in the same manner, one should perform the ritual for the retinue of the gods in due order.
Thus has the rite of non-return been definitively proclaimed by the best of sages;
it is certain that this installation of non-return does not exist at all in the Kali age.
The procedure for the *kalāpanāvarta* is proclaimed as the *bāṇaliṅga*;
alternatively, it is also proclaimed as the *anāvarta* made of crystal and other materials.
(5) The sequence of the *anāvarta* procedure applies to the deities of the retinue and so forth. (6)
Having brought a piece of stone from the mouth of a craftsman, the Guru [should perform the rite] according to the rule.
Having invoked the deity upon the stone slab according to the previously mentioned method,
the Guru should likewise invoke the deity from the stone slab into the water-pot (kumbha).
One should invoke the deity into the pitcher and other vessels as previously described for the *bāla-liṅga*.
(8) Now I shall explain the procedure for the *āvarta*; listen with devotion, O Six-faced One!
(9) [The site may be] by the ocean, by rivers, or by wild animals native to the forest.
One should join that uprooted *liṅga* to the *kumbha*.
Having established the *bālālaya* according to the ritual manual and the prescribed rule,
one should subsequently invoke [the deity] into the *kumbha*, and thereafter into the former *liṅga*.
This Āvarta has been described; now another is being told. Where there is no sign of the letter *a* and so forth, they call this the [other] Āvarta.
(3) Here, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, I shall certainly explain the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having worshipped the clay *liṅga* here according to the prescribed rule,
the Guru should then invoke it into the water-pot (*kumbha*) as before, into the small *liṅga*.
This is known as the *āvarta* [rite] by those learned in the traditions of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Now, O Six-faced One, hear again concerning the re-establishment [of the deity] so that there is no return [to worldly existence]:
having invoked [the deity] from the *liṅga* into the *kumbha*, one should then [invoke it] from the *kumbha* into that young *liṅga*.
Listen now to the detailed procedure for the consecration of a temple for children.
One may perform the consecration of another temple as a substitute for a temple dedicated to the gods.
Or else, one may perform it within a temple according to what is available; O Six-faced One, whatever banners exist there in that temple, [one should use them]. (8)
Having invoked [the deity] upon painted cloths, variegated garments, swords, mirrors,
and likewise upon wooden images, one should perform the rites as appropriate.
A *vimāna* is said to be the gross [form], while the subtle is that which consists of the primary *liṅga*.
The gross is the vehicle, while the subtle is the subtle;
there is no difference between the two here, as they exist in a relationship of part and whole. (2)
Having properly drawn out the gross form as well as the two subtle forms according to the rules,
the most excellent preceptor should thereafter have the work of the artisan performed.
In the case of a small temple, there should be a connection with the vimāna [architectural plan].
But in the absence [of these], one should perform the rite as appropriate for a cloth painting (*paṭa*) and so forth.
Thus has been stated the summary of the re-consecration (*punarāvarta-pratiṣṭhā*), the secret cave. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the re-consecration.

I always salute Śiva— the Lord of Kailāsa, the Lord of Gaurī, who is compassionate toward his devotees, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Viṣṇu and others, and who is auspicious. Having condensed all the Āgamas, I shall describe the sequence of consecration.
The patron, being satisfied and possessing an abundance of wealth and grain,
should choose through his discernment preceptors who have reached the further shore of all the scriptures;
the patron, the most excellent of twice-born sacrificers, should then proceed with the sacrifice.
While the sacrifice is being performed, one should cause the preceptor to complete [the rite] in sequence;
likewise the officiating priests, the practitioners, and the seeker.
One should first honor the preceptor according to the method prescribed in the Āgamas. (5–6)
The permission of the gods, the permission of the twice-born, and the worship of the Lord of Obstacles.
The wise man, acting as the purifier, should perform in due order the collection of materials, the purification, and the distribution of portions for all those who have been initiated.
In the rites concerning the honey-group, the purifiers, and so forth,
the instructor should perform all of them correctly in the preceptor’s residence.
The consumption of honey-preparations is proclaimed as the first [rite]. (9) Anointing with oil, shaving, bathing with clay, and the Varuṇa-bath [are the subsequent rites].

Mental bathing, ash-bathing, the inner bark of the *tvaksāra* tree, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the royal consecration ending with the water-pot—these are the ten types of bathing in their respective order. (I.35a)
Having performed the oil-bath at home, one should complete the remainder on the riverbank.
One should perform the ninefold bath beginning with shaving, followed by the *pañcagavya* bath and more.
Having always concluded the special libations, the twilight prayers, and the honors to the gurus, [one may proceed].
Then, having placed [the image] upon a palanquin, one should have the preceptors brought to their homes.

The most excellent of preceptors should perform the gift of the procession and the rite for the delight of the household. Having gone to the temple, he should seek the permission of the deities. (4–5)

The learned preceptor, for the sake of the rite to destroy demons and for the rite of the entrance-offering (*praveśabali*), should select other teachers for the peace of the village. (6) Having caused these three tasks to be performed by the teachers, he should abandon them with the *tribha* [mantra]. (7)
The setting of jewels upon the image and likewise the opening of its eyes.
The purification of the image is its cleansing; the consecration of water, grain, and so forth; then the circumambulation of the village, and finally, the resting of the image is prescribed. (8)
In the inner sanctum, one should perform the placement of the footprints and the installation of the pedestal with mantras;
[then follow] the hair-jewels of the image, the installation of the image, and its binding.
In this very manner, one should have [the temple] constructed with celestial palaces and so forth;
prior to that, for the sake of purifying the sacrificial ground, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
One should perform the work of the artisans and afterwards dismiss the artisans;
for the sake of pacifying the site, the preceptor should engage a master teacher as before.
The principal consecrated preceptor shall not perform the rite for the pacification of the site;
rather, he should carry out the purification of the temple and the image, as well as the collection of the clay.
Having consecrated the sacrificial hall, one should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds;
one should then carry out the binding of the protective thread for the image and for all the officiating masters.

Having adorned [the disciple] with grains and other items, he should don the initiation garment. (5) For the sake of the image-oblation (*mūrti-homa*), he should indeed perform the generation [of the deity] therein.
(6) Then, he should perform the propitiation worship (*prasanna-pūjana*) as well as the decoration of the ritual jar (*kumbha*).
The wise preceptor should first perform the *mūrtihoma*, the *diśāhoma*, and the purification through the recitation of the *trikhaṇḍa*; then he should perform the *tattvasaṃyojana*,
the *nāḍīsaṃdhāna-homa*, and finally offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.
One should unite the deity residing in the fire with the act of protecting the fire.
From the image [of the deity], one should properly unite it with the pot through the mantra of the oneness of the Śiva-tattva.
(9) One should lead the sacrificial vessel from the place of sacrifice, along with the pilgrimage oblation and the gifts. (i.36a)
In that aforementioned fire of the form, the wise one should perform the expiatory oblation.
Then one should perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), as well as the extraction of the deities from the sacrifice;
likewise, the sacrificial oblation (yāgahoma), the oblation to the directions (diśāhoma), and the consecration with the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha).

Upon the *liṅga* known as the three-sectioned (*trikhaṇḍa*), one should perform the worship of the principles (*tattva-pūjā*). Then, having performed the *nāḍī-sandhāna* and the *homa*, one should offer the great final oblation (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*).
Having joined [the deity] to the vessel in the form of fire, one should perform the homa for the journey;
there, the wise one should cause all the ritual gifts to be given according to the rules.
Having led [the deity] from the pitcher to the primary abode, one should perform the unification with the Śiva-principle.
(5) According to the path taught by the Guru, one should properly join [the deity] from the image into the pitcher.
In the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of Mūladeva should also be performed in due order.
(6) Having returned again to the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), one should offer the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
(7) Then, having concluded the sacrifice (*yāga*), there is the dismissal of all protective deities (*visarjana*).
Having bathed and awakened [the deity],

all those initiated [priests] should immediately thereafter proceed to the temple of all the gods and perform the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) for the deities; after that, they should conduct the festival (*utsava*).

Having received their respective shares of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), all the preceptors (*ācāryas*) there should perform the bestowal of the fruit of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā-phala-dāna*) as well as the festival for the initiate (*dīkṣita*). They should conduct the three-fortnightly sacrifice (*tripakṣa-yajana*) according to the scriptures and according to the prescribed rules.
This alone is proclaimed as the sixty-fourfold offering of parched grain (karmalāja).
These sixty-four ritual acts constitute the foundation for the three days [of the rite].
[They include] the opening of the eyes, the placement of jewels, and the circumambulation of the village.
Having performed these four tasks— the bringing of water, the gathering of grain, the preparation of the site, and the consecration—
there is no returning again once this cave has been established.
Having brought [the disciple] from the teacher's house, one should bestow blessings.
(3) The garland of sixty-four rites is now described here in their proper sequence.
Indeed, from the selection of the preceptor until the end of the three fortnights here, the selection of the preceptor is complete;
the second [stage] is the permission of the deity.
The third is the permission from the Brahmins; the fourth is the worship of Vighneśa (Gaṇeśa);
the fifth is the offering of the remainder of the portion of materials, namely the madhuparka.
The seventh is the tenfold bath, the eighth is the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
and the ninth is proclaimed to be the special libation (*tarpaṇa*).
(6) The tenth consists of the pilgrimage, the gift, and that which is accompanied by the satisfaction of the household.
The eleventh is the rite for destroying demons, while the twelfth is the offering of the *bali*.
The thirteenth is the pacification of the village, and the fourteenth is the deposition of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*).
The reality (*tattva*) is said to consist of ten [chapters], and herein is the opening of the eyes (*netronmīlana*).

The purification of the image consists of sixteen stages; thereafter follows the cleansing of the image. Then comes the consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*) as prescribed by the mantras, which is designated as the eighteenth.
The nineteenth is declared to be the circumambulation of the village;
the twentieth is the seating of the deity, while the twenty-first is the installation of the pedestal.
The wise have declared the placement of the twenty-two jewel-locks;
the mantra for the installation of the image is said to be the twenty-third.
The binding of gold and other materials is declared to be the twenty-fourth rite;
the establishment of the sacrificial hall is proclaimed as the twenty-fifth.
The twenty-sixth [chapter] is declared to be the dismissal of the artisans;
then, the twenty-seventh, the pacification of the site (*vāstuśānti*), should be performed by another preceptor.
The twenty-eighth is proclaimed by the learned as the purification of the image (*bimbaśuddhi*).
The taking up of the clay is said to be the twenty-ninth;
the well-consecrated sacrificial hall is called the thirtieth;
and the rite known as the thirty-first is that which is taught in the mantra for the planting of sprouts. (3–4)
This rite of binding the protective thread is known as the thirty-second;
the installation of the sacrificial grain is proclaimed as the thirty-third.
(5) This thirty-fourth rite is the wearing of the initiation garment.
This thirty-fifth rite is known as the production of the physical form.
The thirty-sixth rite is proclaimed as the *prasannapūjā*.
This thirty-seventh rite is indeed the adornment of the ritual jar (*kumbha*).
The offerings for the forms (mūrti-homa) and the offerings for the directions (diśā-homa) are declared to be thirty-eight;
this constitutes the purification of the thirty-nine principles (tattvas).
And this fourfold [measure] is well-yoked to the jar and the tube;
then, the fire of the full oblation is likewise properly and well-yoked to the form.
From here, there are forty-one [verses] for this [section], and one for Śiva;
beyond this, there are forty-two verses concerning the well-joined application of the *bimba* into the *kumbha*.
This rite of the journey-homa consists of forty-three [verses];
this bestowal of the journey is declared on earth to consist of forty-four.
The entry into the sacrificial hall is said to be forty-five [steps].
(2) Therein, one should offer the expiatory oblation into the fire of the previously mentioned form.
One should cause that very fire to rise; this [is] the forty-sixfold [rite].
And this forty-sevenfold [rite] shall be the production of the sacrifices.
The sacrifices, the fire-oblations, and the directional oblations are proclaimed to be forty-eight;
this [total] of forty-nine constitutes the peaceful vase-consecration.
The purification of the three sections is called the fiftieth rite;
the proper joining of the channels of the image is said to be the fifty-first.

Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* into the fire, one should well-unite the protective deity within the *kumbha*. Having protected that fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the wise know this [rite] to consist of fifty-two [parts].
This rite of fifty-three is proclaimed as the *yātrā-homa*.
This rite of giving for the journey is said to consist of fifty-four [elements].
The entry into the temple of sacrifice is said to be fifty-five [units];
this sixth [unit] from the pitcher onwards constitutes the joining to the image.
Then, after proceeding to the sacrificial hall, the Guru should perform the *kumbhābhiṣeka* (water-pot consecration);
therein, in the previously mentioned sacrificial fire, he should offer the oblation for atonement (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
One should cause the single fire to be removed; this is said to be the fifty-seventh.
Afterwards, the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice is said to be the fifty-eighth.
After that, the Great Consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) is designated as the fifty-ninth;
this sixtieth rite is proclaimed as the festival.
They know the giving of the teacher’s fee (*ācāryadakṣiṇā*) as the sixty-first.
The sixty-second is said to be the bestowing of the fruit of consecration.
(3) The wise declare the sixty-third to be the festival of the preceptor;
the sixty-fourth is proclaimed as the sacrifice of the three fortnights. (4)
The Āhāryakarma-jāla is proclaimed to consist of sixty-four [elements];
this same sixty-fourfold set is also proclaimed for the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
The opening of the eyes, the placement of gems,
the circumambulation of the village, and the consecration of the water and grain.
All the sages who know the sacred tradition declare that these four types of karma do not exist within the cycle of rebirth.
The Table of Contents for the Pratiṣṭhā is completed.
May there be auspiciousness.
This definition of a teacher, as agreed upon by the scriptures, will now be stated:
"One who knows the scriptures, is true to his word, and has mastered all the traditional teachings. (I.38b)
One who is free from disease, though lacking wealth, yet possesses devotion and a family;
who is learned in the Vedas, endowed with virtuous conduct, and devoted to daily ritual bathing.
Compassionate, peaceful-minded, handsome, and possessing the five auspicious marks;
accomplished in the study of the Vedas and devoted to the worship of Śiva.
One who has been initiated, accompanied by his wife, devoted, with no missing limbs, not a child,
(4) neither too emaciated nor too old, standing on level ground, and skilled in ritual action.
Having properly sought out such a guru, the master should serve him;
he should then gradually serve the previously mentioned preceptor who is authorized in the Dharma.
If a virtuous Brahmin should choose a teacher, he may do so himself;
but if he is a Śūdra, he must have a Brahmin choose a preceptor for him, as the Brahmin is his master.
One who has received initiation and is most learned in the scriptures should choose [a wife] just as a householder does;
having bathed in the morning and become pure, he should be surrounded by his own kinsmen.
At an auspicious moment during the rising sign (lagna), accompanied by songs, musical instruments, and the like,
one should place unbroken rice, food, and flowers into a golden vessel according to the prescribed rite.
Taking [the staff], the wise and highly intelligent one went very quickly to the teacher’s house; having arrived, he fell properly at the feet of the teacher. (9)
"O Knower of the true nature of Śiva from the beginning, O Beloved of all sacrifices,
establish the Lord of the World in every way for the sake of protecting the people.
Having thus entreated the Guru, [he offered] two coconut fruits.
Having offered his face to the feet of the guru, the most righteous one should speak.
Upon seeing him, the wise teacher should reply:
"So be it; I shall perform this rite exactly according to the rule."

Immediately thereafter, the righteous patron should worship the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the instructor (*bodhaka*), and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) with devotion, each according to their respective order.
The teacher (*ācārya*) has the Creator as his deity, while the instructor (*bodhaka*) has the Guru as his deity.
The righteous ones, having consecrated the sacrificial ground as belonging to the deity Brahmā, the officiating priests as belonging to the deities of the mantras,
and the assembly hall as belonging to all the deities,
[performed the rite] under an auspicious constellation, on a Wednesday, in a favorable conjunction, and at a propitious moment. (5–6)
One should perform the consecration with Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and who possess divine knowledge...
In a vessel made of gold or other precious materials, [he places] grains of rice resembling the color of a cow's udder.
A beautiful coconut fruit, saffron resembling a gem,
fruits, garlands of flowers, betel leaf, and likewise turmeric;
(7) sacrificial grass with the auspicious marks, mango sprouts, and likewise the *praṇava*.

Having gathered these materials— scented substances, flowers, gold and the like, as well as a pair of fine silk garments (dukūla)— and accompanied by dance and song, one should perform the ritual circumambulation amidst the chanting of auspicious benedictions. (8–9)
Having gone to the temple of all the gods, having devoutly washed his feet,
and having performed three circumambulations according to the rules with a concentrated mind,
he entered the assembly pavilion while reciting the *Rājātamantra*.
On this excellent and beautiful seat, the Guru faces the north.
One should meditate upon Śiva seated facing either east or north;
then the wise practitioner should pray to the true Guru, who brings auspiciousness to all actions.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is Rudra the Great Lord;
the Guru is the manifest Supreme Brahman—to that Śrī Guru, salutations.
Salutation to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, using the collyrium-stick of knowledge.

Having thus meditated correctly upon the Guru for the sake of attaining success in the temple of mantra, the wise one should strike his own head; thereafter, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the worship of Vighneśa and then carry out the formal resolve (saṅkalpa);
then, in due order, the proclamation of auspiciousness (svastivācana) and the sprinkling for the holy day (puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa).
Having purified [the vessel] by means of gazing and other rites, the wise one should worship the substances and deities;
and having washed the cooking pot according to the rule with the *astra* mantra.
One should apply a coating of turmeric, and thereafter place the vessel level;
then the preceptor should deposit all the ritual substances into that vessel.
The cooking pot, the spear-form, the rice grains whose deity is the stars, Sarasvatī in the flower, and the leaf whose deity is Gāyatrī; (9)
The preceptor should worship, according to the prescribed rite, the unbroken grains, the great mantras, the *dukūla* cloth whose deity is Śakti, and the saffron whose deity is the Sun. (10)
Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should consecrate them with the Brahma-mantras and the ancillary mantras (*aṅga-mantras*).
Then, taking the vessel with both hands, one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
The Preceptor (*deśika*), having performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*), should perform self-purification and worship.
Having placed the *arghya* according to the rules, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances.
(2) One should worship the deities of the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*) and so forth, in sequence, ending with the worship of Śakti.
Then the Guru should perform the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) as prescribed. (3)
One should worship with incense, lamps, food offerings, and the eight flowers;
then, having offered a golden flower and prostrated with the eight limbs,
one should take the vessel together with *darbha* grass in both hands in the presence of the deity.
O Agni, having recited the mantra, the Guru should offer the prayer prescribed by that mantra.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, cause of the world’s joy!
O Lord, I have set out for the rite of Śiva; grant me your permission.
Then, having gone to the abode of Śakti, one should worship her according to the prescribed rite;
taking the previously mentioned vessel along with darbha grass into the presence of the deity.
O Goddess Gaurī, O Sovereign of the World, O Bringer of Joy to the Universe!
(7) I have set out for the sacrifice of Śiva; it behooves you to grant me your permission.
Having gone to the assembly pavilion, the preceptor, facing north,
should take the vessel with both hands and request the Brahmins in due order.
Having given betel and sacrificial fees to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule,
one should properly entreat the Brahmins for the successful accomplishment of the performance of the rite.
That illustrious Brāhmaṇa had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
(10) he was a knower of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, and was well-trained in all the scriptures.
"O you who have been well-purified by the initiation of Śiva and are devoted to the worship of Śiva,
please deign to grant permission for me to perform the sacrifice of Śiva."
The Brahmins should speak to the Lord and the Preceptor with all haste, saying:
"If you wish to perform the Śiva-sacrifice, may there be the accomplishment of the necessary qualification."
The Worship of Vighneśa—Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the worship of Vighnarāja.
For the sake of completing [one's undertakings] without obstacles, one should worship him during those respective rites. (I.40b, 2–3)

Having gone to the temple of Vighneśvara, which is equipped with the king of weapons (the Astra-mantra), one should have the *puṇyāha* (declaration of an auspicious day) recited there by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
(4) The most excellent preceptor should perform the bathing and the fire-oblation (*homa*) using products of the cow (*gavya*). (5)
Having worshipped the deities of the doors, one performs the worship of the inner enclosure.

One should perform the fivefold oblation and the oblation for the removal of obstacles; then one should carry out the consecration, beginning with the bathing in oil and ending with the final ablution.
One should offer incense for the garments, perfumes, and ornaments according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, one should offer cakes, various kinds of rice dishes, sweetmeats, and parched grain.
Having offered parched grain, mung beans, and groats according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor [offers] fruits, sugarcane, and rice mixed with molasses.
One should offer the *urvāruka*, *kaṅka*, and the three fruits (*triphalā*) according to the prescribed rule.
I shall now explain, according to the rule, the characteristics of the coconut:
that which is white belongs to the Brahmin caste, while that which is red belongs to the Kṣatriya caste.
One of the Mañjiṣṭha color belongs to the Vaiśya caste, while one that is dark-complexioned belongs to the Śūdra caste.
It should be well-rounded, filled with water, shaped like a cart, neither too long nor too thin, beautiful, not too thick, and free from defects. (i.41a)
Having thus examined the coconut in many ways for its auspicious characteristics— whether it is unblemished, rich in its ridges, possesses a beautiful crest, and has fine eyes—
the wise man should strike one that has a crest and announce the one without a crest.
With the *Tṛyambaka* mantra, O best of gurus,
[the practitioner attains] perfection of action through the first [recitation], the accomplishment of action through the second,
and when the third striking occurs, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If the fourth striking occurs, the ritual action becomes fruitless. When the action is split into two parts, it is successful; otherwise, it is a mere fragment that destroys the efficacy of the rite.
If the principal eye of the preceptor is pierced, fear shall arise;
if the right eye is pierced, the destruction of the king is proclaimed.
If the left eye is pierced, the village perishes instantly;
to pacify that defect, one should again perform worship of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Furthermore, the procedure for worship here shall be described in accordance with the scriptures:
one should strike a hundred coconuts there for the Lord of the Gaṇas.
O elephant-faced one, best of gods, son of Śiva, obeisance to you!
I strike this coconut; be gracious to me so that there may be freedom from obstacles.
(9) One should offer pieces of coconut, betel leaves, and other such items.
Having worshipped with the eight flowers, one should cause a golden flower to be offered.
Having performed worship according to the Veda, Drāviḍa hymns, and the rhythmic dances of Gaṇeśa,
and having honored [the deity] along with all its limbs and sub-limbs and praised it, the Guru should offer this prayer.
Wherever an action is commenced, one should strike with the two fists at the region of the head five times while recollecting Vināyaka.
That nectar which was released from the ocean by Sāgara flows through the Suṣumnā.
The Guru should indeed satisfy Vighneśa, who resides in the *mūlādhāra*, with that [liquid].
(3) The Guru should form the *muṣṭi-mudrā* with his left and right hands;
then, with the middle fingers, he should strike [the disciple] upon the head. (4)
One should sprinkle the bodies with the nectar located in the head.
O foremost among all gods, O most excellent one, O Lord of Obstacles, O Leader of the Gaṇas!
"Having worshipped you, make that ritual action fruitful.
When this is done with devotion, the Lord of Obstacles becomes well-pleased.
Taking the vessel of authorization along with darbha grass into the presence of the God,
[he spoke] to Skanda’s elder brother, the Lord of the Gaṇas, together with his beloved Goddess.
"O Lord, I have set out for the auspicious sacrifice; please pacify all obstacles.
[I offer] laddukas, modakas, forest fruits, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite. (7)
Having offered all the things known to Śiva outside the city to Vighneśa,
one should give all of that to the celibate students (brahmacārins) along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having circumambulated Vighneśa, the bestower of boons, the Guru—
should the king be the presiding authority over dharma— may take the materials according to the prescribed rule.

If he is wealthy, he should give for the sake of protection according to his capacity by the grace of the gods; if he is unable, the righteous man should give wealth after having requested it [from others]. (10)
Whether one is wealthy or poor, one should not practice stinginess regarding the offerings. (I.42a) If stinginess regarding the offerings is practiced, the ritual act will certainly become fruitless.
With reference to the Śivadharma, there are donors as well as beggars,
practitioners and teachers, and even men who provide sweetmeats.
Furthermore, the instigator, those incited by him, and the people associated with them—
all shall attain union with Śiva through the grace of Śiva.
Where the preceptor is filled with mantra, filled with wealth, and righteous,
and where the artisan is perfected in his craft, there shall be the presence of Śiva.
By the mere presence of Śiva, the home of all shall become [holy].
If the preceptor is devoid of mantras and lacking in wealth, yet righteous;
and if the artisan is devoid of skill—therein, O God, there is no presence [of the deity].
Due to the absence of the God, there is the destruction of the lineage of all. (5–6)
Whatever substance is given for the sake of the Śivadharma,
the righteous preceptor himself should take that substance in a copper vessel and,
having performed the rite of offering it to Śiva, place it into the hand [of the recipient]. (7)
Immediately thereafter, the Guru should perform the purification of the materials according to the prescribed rite.

He should sprinkle the wealth with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) consecrated by the *puṇyāha* formula; he should then recite the root mantra one hundred times and the Brahma-aṅga mantras fifty times.
By that very [act], there shall be purity of substance; the pure substance is offered to Śiva.
The agent should divide the portion according to his means, following the prescribed rule.
(10) The sequence for dividing the substance: re 15540.
"I shall describe the sequence of the distribution of the substances; listen in detail, O Six-faced One.
One should divide the substance of Śiva and the reality (tattva) again into ten parts. (I.42a, 10)
Three parts are for the purpose of sacrifice, while one part is for the consecration;
in that regard, a triad beginning with the Guru has been proclaimed.
In this rite for the complete satisfaction of Brahmā, two parts are prescribed;
of those two parts, one is for the purpose of recitation, and the other is for abundant giving.
One part is designated for the construction of the sacrificial hall and the artisans;
two parts are proclaimed for the rites of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, ending after three fortnights.
(3) I shall now describe the sequence for this; listen with focused attention.
The wise man should divide the sacrificial materials previously mentioned into two parts:
(4) there, one part is for the purpose of binding [the deity], including the matted hair, jewels, and so forth;
[the other part consists of] jars, water-pots, vessels, bowls, and ladles. (5)
The *pālikās*, the *ghaṭikās*, and whatever other varieties of vessels there may be—
all these are said to be made of gold, or alternatively, they are prescribed as being made of silver.
Even in that case, however, if one lacks the capacity [to afford them], one should employ vessels made of copper.
Alternatively, one should prepare vessels made of silver or gold;
even there, in the absence of such means, an earthen vessel is prescribed.
These include the arghya vessels, the nāḍī, and the vessels for incense, lamps, and so forth.
These bell-metal vessels have been described by the lords of sages,
as well as the *kūrca* grass, the coconut, and the mango sprout.
These they call the Kāñcanātyas, or else the Rājanas;
(9) as well as the Hemotpalas, the Hemaśūlas, and the Hemapaṅkajas.
And for these [grains], nine parts are prescribed;
two parts are proclaimed for rice and grains.
O Six-faced One, three parts are declared for the purpose of clarified butter. (I.43a)
Now, with reference to the materials for the *homa* sacrifice, one part is prescribed;
for *śāli* rice and other grains, half a part is prescribed. (2) Furthermore, there are the cloth for the altar, the cloth for the water-pot, and also the silk thread.
And that thread which is five-colored, half of it is one part.
One part shall be silver, and one for the consecration;
the food offering shall consist of half a part—thus they are remembered as twelvefold.
This rule is proclaimed according to the sequence of the eightfold binding.
Furthermore, another procedure for the binding of gold and other substances will now be explained.
Two bhāras of ghee are prescribed for every three parts of gold.
One should divide the aforementioned materials for the consecration into sixteen portions.
Half [of the total] is prescribed for the mantra-recitation and the ritual bathing;
one part is prescribed as the fixed substance for the consecration.
One portion shall be for the cloth and one portion for the food offering;
the remainder is proclaimed to be allocated for the festival.
Having personally divided this substance into two parts, [one] part is for the Great Consecration and likewise for the Prasanna consecration. (8)
The preceptor, possessing unerring intelligence, should perform the ritual application (viniyoga).
I shall now explain, according to the rules, the sequence for the three parts beginning with the Ācārya.
Two parts are prescribed for the garments, ornaments, and vessels; one part, it is said by the best of sages, is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (10)
And having respectfully divided this substance into nine parts, the Guru [should take] one-third for the Teacher and two parts for the officiating priests. (I.43b)
The portion for the assistant preceptor (parivārācārya) is proclaimed to be two shares;
the portion for the awakening preceptor (bodhakācārya), however, consists of one share for the goal (sādhya) and one for the practitioner (sādhaka).
The two parts prescribed for the satiation of Brahmā shall be divided fivefold;
and from the gift of food to the Brāhmaṇas, four parts are to be given.
One should give the remaining single portion as the fee for the ritual enjoyment (*bhukti-dakṣiṇā*).
Now, the application of the single portion intended for recitation (*japa*) is described here.
The preceptor himself shall divide that substance into six parts according to the rule;
four portions are prescribed by the wise for those learned in the four Vedas.

One part [of the time] should be devoted to the recitation of Śiva-mantras, and half a part to the Purāṇas; (6) one quarter should then be spent on the recitation of the Navagraha-mantras, and the remainder on the worship of the Sun.
Indeed, for as many teachers and officiating priests as there are,
that same number of Veda-reciters are prescribed.
That one portion which was previously set aside for the purpose of extensive giving—
having divided that very portion into four parts— one part is intended for the purpose of giving.
One should assign the remainder for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for all;
that which was prescribed as two parts for the purpose of worshipping during the three fortnights [is also included].
The wise and most excellent preceptor should divide that [water] into seven parts;
three parts are prescribed for the daily consecration (*nityābhiṣeka*), while one part is prescribed for the satiation of Brahmā. (10)
On the third fortnight day, there is the division for the consecration;
one portion is proclaimed for the satiation of Brahmā. As for that which is called the "great consecration" (*mahābhiṣeka*), it occurs when the consecration has become serene.
Likewise, regarding the consecration of the vessel (*pātrābhiṣeka*), the tradition has been proclaimed:
"The procedure that was previously described for the propitiation of Brahmā (*brahmasantarpaṇa*), the wise one should perform it here as well during the propitiation of Brahmā. (3)

I shall describe the sequence of the *madhuparka* offering according to the scriptures and according to rule. (i.44a, 3) The seeker of realization should prepare the honey-mixture in the house of the Guru. (4)
First, one should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* rite; then, one should prepare rice grains of the *śāli* variety.
(5) Having drawn a lotus there, the wise *bodhaka* should place a shallow bowl in the center of the pericarp, filled with plantain fruit. (6)
To its right, one should place a shallow bowl filled with honey;
on its left side, having set down a shallow bowl filled with clarified butter,
one should properly perform the four purificatory rites beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*).
One should properly perform the strewing of grass all around the outside of that.
One should worship the *śivatattva* in the plantain vessel situated in the center;
the wise one, having worshipped the *vidyātattva* in the honey-vessel.

Having worshipped the principle of the Self, the wise one [should recite] the Rudra-sūkta, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Brahma-sūkta according to the prescribed rule over a vessel of clarified butter. (9)
Having recited [the mantra] together with the Brahmins, the awakener should offer his own lower lip;
then the awakener should bestow sacrificial fees upon those Brahmins.
Having mixed ghee with honey, one should place that mixture in a plantain fruit;
then, with the mantra "āpyāyasva," one should fill the fruit with milk.
With the mantra "madhu vātā," the wise one should nourish everything with his hand;
having worshipped the three principles, he should effect union with Śiva.
Having offered it according to the rules with the *tattva-mantra* to the preceptors in the prescribed manner,
one should personally give [the remainder] the size of a jujube fruit (*badarī-phala*) as a token of that [instruction].
The preceptor should consume that [mixture] three times;
thereafter, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). This indeed is the sequence for the madhuparka.
Now, the procedure for bathing is being stated; listen with a concentrated mind.
Having consecrated the oil through the rites of inspection and so forth according to the rule, the Guru—
One should chew betel leaf, perform an oil massage,
and bathe with warm water or cold water.
Then, either on that very day or on the following day, the preceptor and the officiating priests—
all those who perform the protection rites— for them the shaving of the head is prescribed.
One should perform the bath in river water or else in the water of a pond;
thereafter, the bath with clay from those very same sources is prescribed for them.
There, on the riverbank, the instructor should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
he himself should bathe with that same sacred water, for this bath is indeed a protection.
Afterwards comes the mental bath, and after that the ash-bath. Then the wise man should cast the fire into the tree [of the body] which is filled with water.
Having recited the *pada-mantra* over the vessel, one should then perform the bath;
or else, one should perform the bath with water containing the five products [of the cow] or with the essence-water (*sāratoya*). (I.45a)
The *aśvattha*, *jambū*, *nyagrodha*, and *audumbara* trees—
these five barks are called "bark-essence" (*tvaksāra*) in the treatises.

Thereafter, bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is known as the royal bath (rājasnāna). Following that, one should sit down in order, using either four parts or three parts of the [mixture] for the first [two].
One should bathe even with warm water mixed with the substances for the impressions (*vāsanā-dravya*).
Those learned in the Āgamas call this the "Royal Consecration" (*rājābhiṣeka*).
Then, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and likewise the preceptor (*deśika*) should perform the "Vase Consecration" (*kumbha-snāna*).
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite in a pure place on a riverbank,
and having duly established the *pāśupatāstra* vessel there according to the ritual procedure,
the instructor, after worshipping it according to the rules, should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
There, the *bodhaka* should perform recitation (*japa*) together with the Brahmins using mantras such as the *Rudrasūkta*, after having given them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
With that very water from the jar, everyone should perform their ritual bath.
This is known as the "consecration by weapons" (astrābhiṣeka), which surpasses the ritual bath from the water-pot (kumbhasnāna).
(8) The offering of honey-mixture (madhuparka) is prescribed for the purpose of removing the fault of disparagement;
the wise have declared the oil-bath (tailasnāna) to be for the sake of bodily health. (9)
Shaving the limbs is prescribed for the pacification of improper conduct;
bathing with clay is declared for the self-purification of all.
The bath with the sap of the bark is prescribed for the purpose of removing the defects of disease;
here, the ash-bath is prescribed for the sake of prior rites such as the daily obligatory duties.
For the sake of removing the fault of attachment, there should be a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
for the removal of mental defects, there is the consecration of a king as prescribed by mantra.

The consecration by the water-pot (kumbhābhiṣeka), as prescribed by the mantras, is for the sake of attaining oneness with the nature of Śiva. (2) The purification of speech is proclaimed to be achieved through the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus, the tenfold fruit of bathing has been declared by the wise.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the tenfold bath. (3) [Now follows] the special libation (*tarpaṇa*).
I shall explain the special libation (*viśeṣatarpaṇa*); listen in detail, O Six-faced One.
Having first performed the Vedic rite, one should subsequently perform the Śaiva rite.
Immediately thereafter, one should begin to perform the libation known as the "special" (*viśeṣa*).

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) first, one should thereafter perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). Alternatively, the purification of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) or the purification by water (*jalaśuddhi*) is prescribed.
One should then perform the libation to the deity (*devatātarpaṇa*) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Each of the three principles (*tatva*) consists of five parts (*kalā*), and there are three Śivas;
likewise, each of the limbs of Brahmā consists of three principles (*tatva*). (7) Subsequently, it is declared that there are one hundred and eight [parts] beginning with the root-Śiva (*śivamūla*).
The Guru who knows the Āgamas states that for the Manonmanī [level], it should be half of that.
(8) One hundred and ten [offerings] are prescribed as the libation with the limbs of Śiva;
thereafter, the triad of principles (tattva) was proclaimed by those who have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas. (9)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Rudra;
Rudra is declared as the eleventh, and the Suns are celebrated as twelve.
(10) The Vasus are declared to be eight, and the Maruts are indeed seven.
The nine planets, the world-protectors, the zodiac signs, and likewise the stars;
the seven sages are thus proclaimed, as well as the four beginning with Sanaka;
and the twelve great sages beginning with Dūrvāsas are also fully enumerated.
In the same manner, the eleven [libations] for the ancient teachers have been proclaimed;
from the gurus, seven in number, the libation for the ancestors follows from the mouth of the lion (the west).
Indeed, one should perform the ancestral libation here just like the libation at the New Moon sacrifice.
One should perform the libation for the gods at the *devatīrtha*, for the sages at the *ṛṣitīrtha*,
and for the ancestors at the *pitṛtīrtha*.
For the gods and the sages, one should do so with the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), and for the sages, with it worn around the neck (*nivīta*).
It has been declared by the ancestors that in the rite of ancestral libation (*pitṛtarpaṇa*),
unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) are for the deities, while both sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains are for the sages (*ṛṣis*). Indeed,
in the libation for the ancestors, only sesame seeds alone are prescribed.
The satiation of the gods is declared to be performed with the utterance of "svāhā.
A wise person should perform the satiation of the sages with the words "I satiate.
The satiation of the ancestors should be performed with reverence, using the word "svadhā" at the end.
The Brahmāstra, the Pāśupatāstra known as Ghora,
the Pratyaṅgirāstra, and the Rudrāstra— these are called the five weapons.
One should perform the libation for each weapon ten times.
One should perform the libation with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* using the *devatīrtha* [finger-tip] (10).
A wise person should perform the libation for the weapons (*astras*) using the tip of a *kuśa* blade.
Thus has the libation for the installation of Śiva been described. (i.46b)
In the case of an installation [of an image], one should perform a different libation;
indeed, for its surrounding deities as well, one should proceed in this very sequence.
This specific procedure for libation has been proclaimed by the sages.
The best of teachers should then perform the special twilight ritual (viśeṣa-sandhyā).
(3) Subsequently, the Guru should mutter the Rudra-hymn, the Camaka, and the Padamantra;
with a well-composed mind, he should also mutter the five-syllable mantra one thousand times. (4)
The Guru should recite the mantra of Manonmanī one hundred and eight times;

for the Brahma-mantras and the limbs [of the deity], it should be half of that, and for the weapons, half of that again. (5) Having thus performed the recitation, thereafter, being composed, he should proceed according to the prescribed rule.
At whatever time the libation (tarpaṇa) is to be performed, one should meditate upon this Śakti with reverence.
Immediately thereafter, the most excellent of beings ascended the palanquin,
properly supported by the officiating priests and adorned with dances and songs.
Having brought [the image] to his own home, he should perform the rites of domestic affection there;
then, accompanied by dance, song, and other such arts, he should offer the gift of departure.
Having gone there to the temple, the Guru should worship the deity;
(8) having worshipped, prostrated, and praised [the deity], the Guru should offer a prayer.
The learned preceptor should choose other [priests] for the rite of expelling demons, for the rite of the entrance-offering,
and for the peace of the village.
Having caused another preceptor to perform these three tasks, the guide should afterwards relinquish them;
the guide himself should not perform these three tasks. (10)
The preceptor should perform the expiation or cause it to be performed.
O Skanda, the Rakṣoghna rite, which wards off all obstacles, will now be described.
One should perform the Rakṣoghna rite to the southwest of the temple. (1.47a–2)
There, the preceptor should construct a pavilion for the purpose of exorcising demons;
it should be provided with four doors, adorned with altars and sacrificial pits,
decorated with colorful garlands, and beautified by various ornaments.
The preceptor, who had previously been enjoined by his teacher for the purpose of slaying the rākṣasa,
maintained his resolve; accompanied by singing and instrumental music,
and placing the deity of the weapon at the forefront, he was joined by brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
Having installed the Astra-deity in the northeast corner of the pavilion,
one should there, in the pavilion, recite the *puṇyāha* for the purification of the structural defects (*śalya-śodhana*).
Then, the preceptor should install five water-pots (*pañca-kumbha*) upon the altar there.
There, the preceptor himself should properly worship the five weapons;
likewise, having worshipped the five weapons in the fire according to the ritual rules,
he should indeed employ those weapons for the purpose of exorcising the rākṣasa.
One should perform a fire sacrifice there with all [the aforementioned] substances using neem oil,
with cotton seeds, balā, and karavīra flowers;
one should offer oblations there with the fuel-sticks of the red arka tree while reciting the Astra-mantras.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras for each of the weapon-deities (10).
The preceptor should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the scriptures;
having taken up the form of the Fire-god, he should sequentially unite it with the ritual jar (kumbha). (I.47b)
Taking up the form of the pitcher, one should unite it with the deity of the weapon (*astradeva*).
Having offered incense and a lamp to the deity of the weapon with a concentrated mind,
one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins who have performed the recitation of the *rakṣoghna* [mantra].
Having given [the offerings] and gone to the temple, the preceptor [should worship] with the Weapon-deity (Astradeva).
Thereafter, this preceptor should perform his bath according to the prescribed rule;
he should perform the rite for the destruction of demons at night, but the preceptor should not do so during the day.
If the Rakṣoghna [rite] has not been performed, the Rākṣasas, who feed upon flesh and blood, will create obstacles to the sacrifice; therefore, one should perform the Rakṣoghna rite.
O Six-faced One, today I shall speak of the entry-offering (*praveśabali*) at the beginning of the entry-offering ritual—
that which was previously enjoined by the Guru for the performance of the entry-offering rite. (I.47b, 5)
When the preceptor has emerged from the *sacala* [mandala] by means of the deity of the weapon (*astradeva*),
he puts on a new garment accompanied by song and instrumental music.
Having gathered the offering substances there from the beginningless [tradition],
