one should indeed perform the bali offering to Brahmā and the other deities in the ten directions according to the ritual rule.
Having first accomplished the *sthala-siddhi* (the mastery of the site), the wise practitioner should offer the *bali* there;
he should also perform the worship of the various *piśācas* residing in each direction with fragrant flowers.
Having offered the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite, saying, "I give the bali to the bhūtas," [he should offer] food,
edibles, fruit, coconut, and other fruits,
as well as the flower-cluster of the betel-nut tree and the cluster of the coconut.
And one should place there a lamp soaked in neem oil;
likewise, incense combined with guggulu, as well as red meat and blood.
In its absence, however, there should be a *kūṣmāṇḍa* mixed with saffron.
(11) Thus the most excellent preceptor should offer the oblation in every direction.
"O Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and whoever else creates obstacles,
accept this as your sacrificial offering and depart today by the command of Ajaśiva."
Having spoken thus, one who is departing for another land should worship the deities of the directions there with incense and lamps;

having offered a *bali* oblation to the deities of the directions ending with the word "svāhā," he should then command those deities of the directions to grant him protection and circumambulate [the site] clockwise.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], the most excellent teacher should go to the temple and bathe.
At night, the *niśīśekhala* must be performed; that is the ritual of the *praveśabali*.
If the *praveśabali* is not performed, Rākṣasas will constantly cause obstacles.
An obstacle to the sacrifice may arise; therefore, one should perform the offering for entry.
(4) Regarding the peace of the village:
O Guha, I shall describe the procedure for the peace of the village, which is dear to all the gods. (i.48a, 4)
One should perform the rite for the peace of the village in the western part of the courtyard;
listen with an attentive mind as I shall describe the procedure.
Having made the ground level, free from depressions and elevations, it should be nine cubits, five cubits, or even seven cubits in size. (6)
Having caused a square pavilion to be constructed, provided with four doors and equipped with twelve pillars, one should build it there.
Having divided this field into two parts, one should construct an altar in the middle. (8) One should construct that altar there so that its height is equal to its width.
In the middle of the eastern part of that [area], there is a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
There, on the northern portion of the altar (vedi), one should place nine jars.
In the northeast, one should place the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), and in the southeast, the Auspicious Day (Puṇyāha).
To the south of that is the station of the Guru, and in the southwest is the Five Products of the Cow (Pañcagavya).
In the western quarter, one should place a handful of *darbha* grass tied with *audumbara* wood and other materials;
that is declared to be the Vāyavya [quarter], the chamber for the *upasādhana*.
Having decorated it according to the prescribed rule, likewise with plantain trees—
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and adorned it with colored garlands and the like,
(2) enriched with *cīta* sprouts and flowers, and perfumed with fragrant substances—
having done this, the wise man should then perform the rite for the peace of the village. (3)
The preceptor who acts as a teacher for the sake of peace,
having put on a new lower garment and an upper cloth, being pure,
and having performed his daily rites from morning until he is no longer naked— (4) [should proceed].
Placing the deity of weapons at the forefront, accompanied by dance and song.
At the end of the first watch of the night, equipped with the substances for pacification,
he should depart from the temple and go to the pavilion of pacification.
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, one should prepare the *pañcagavya*.
To prevent the destruction of the rice crop, one should perform the consecratory rites for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
Having worshipped the Astra-deity, one should offer incense, lamps, and other offerings.
(7) Thereafter, one should draw the maṇḍala upon the altar for the Guru.
Having drawn the outer square, the doors, the pairs [of lines], and thereafter the circle; (8) [one should proceed].
The wise one should draw an eight-petaled lotus within the space between two circles.
Having drawn a square consisting of nine compartments,
the wise one should delineate it there with flour-powders of white, yellow, and other colors.
Alternatively, one may fashion a wheel out of rice grains or sesame seeds;
here, the sequence for the worship of the wheel will be described according to the scriptures.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla in the central square according to the prescribed rite;
in the eight squares starting from the east, one should worship the eight Bhairavas.
One should worship Mahendra and the other eight Śaktis on the eight petals;
one should worship Asura and the others at the four gates of the outer enclosure (*bhūpura*).
Having worshipped Kṣetreśa and the others, the preceptor should perform the fire-rite in nine jars; there he should worship the lords of the fields.
There, one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, parched grain, and so forth, according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the offering of the omentum, or, if that is not possible, the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblation.
The cook, having split that fruit in two with his hand,
should cast out its seeds and, being wise, offer the seed-vessel into the fire.
Taking ghee for sprinkling, one should perform the *sandhāna* oblation.
(6) One should offer blood as food for the *bali*, or otherwise, beans (*māṣa*).
(7) Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should present incense and lamps.
After that, the wise one should join the fire of the hearth with the [deity’s] form.

Having joined it from the wheel into the pitcher, and from the pitcher into the mind of the preceptor, he should take the tips of *darbha* grass and a collection of fuel sticks of *udumbara* wood. (8–9)
Having kindled [the fire] with songs and instrumental music, the wise one, acting as the attendant,
should perform the ritual circumambulation and the rite of encircling with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
[He should do so] with many *divikās* accompanied by the deities of the weapons.
The wise one, having performed the ritual sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *puṇyāha* rite,
should dismiss this fire-brand toward the southeast.
Having led it to the edge of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should perform his ablution.
Thereafter, one should perform expiation for the Lord of the Asterism (*Astreśa*).
If the village-peace rite (*grāmaśānti*) is omitted, there will be suffering here for the protectors. Furthermore, impurity may arise here for the villages, cities, and inhabitants.
Famine shall therefore arise; hence, one should perform the rite for the peace of the village.
(5) Regarding the ritual for the deposition of jewels:
O crusher of the stars, listen as I describe the ritual for the deposition of jewels. (i.49b, 5)
Those skilled in the traditional systems of the Ratna-nyāsa will describe it as being of two kinds:
one is the Aṅga-ratna-nyāsa, and the other here is the Jaṭī-ratna.
Hereafter, the Jaṭī-ratna will be explained prior to the binding.
Now the ritual placement of the precious limbs (*cāṅgaratnanyāsa*) will be described; listen to this.
The five substitutes for the [divine] image are declared by those most learned in the scriptures:
[an image] made of metal, stone, wood, clay, or even [a painting]. (8)
In the *Paṭhakāmika* and other [tantras], these are the causes for the presence of the five deities.
Having placed the image facing east and performed the *puṇyāha* rite before it, the Guru should respectfully prepare a nine-square grid there with rice grains. (i.50a)
Having placed the pitchers upon the nine auspicious spots,
the wise one should worship the eight Nāgas in the eight pitchers and then worship Śeṣa. Upon the head of the image, however, one should place a ruby, and on the forehead, a sapphire.
The wise one should place a diamond at the heart and lapis lazuli at the navel;
(3) crystal at the two knees and ruby at the feet;
(4) pearl at the pair of ears and emerald at the two arms.
The preceptor should place coral on the palms of both hands in succession;
he should then place a pair of jewels upon each limb over the fragrant paste.
One should worship Śeṣa, beginning with Mūrdhāra, on the head, and Ananta on the forehead;
one should worship Vāsukī at the heart and Takṣaka at the navel;
Kārkoṭaka on the pair of knees, and likewise Padma on the pair of feet.
Upon the pair of ears is Mahāpadma, and upon the two arms is Śaṅkhapālaka.
(8) On the hands is Aṅgulika; now the placement of the Liṅgas is described: Māṇikya should be on the head, and likewise the Liṅgas in the eight directions. (9)
Having placed the eight jewels, the Guru should perform worship as before;
the Guru should then reverently sprinkle each of those jars upon the corresponding limb [of the deity].
(I.50b) Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, he should also present betel-leaf. (2)
The best of teachers should meditate upon this image made of jewels.
The procedure for the deposition of the jewels has been declared; now the opening of the eyes is described.
(3) The preceptor should perform the opening of the eyes of the image in front of it, and there he should recite the "Auspicious Day" formula. (i.50b, 3)
One should place three water-pots for the three-eyed deities;
for the two-eyed deities, there should be two water-pots there.
The number of faces need not be taken into account here; the number of eyes alone is the determining factor.
And for the eyes, one should worship Bhu, Sūrya, and Pāvaka in sequence.
(6) Therein, the preceptor should worship the two eyes as the Moon and the Sun.
One should perform the fire-oblation with pleasing materials such as parched grain (*lāja*) and others, just as in the case of the water-pot (*kumbha*).
There, the preceptor should offer a garment to the artisan who has bathed, which is not inferior to those of the gods.
And ornaments such as grapes and the like should indeed be offered;
furthermore, the Guru [should provide] gold, silver, and there, implements made of stone.
One should immediately sprinkle [the site] with auspicious waters from the ocean.
Having taken hold of it there, you yourselves, along with the master craftsmen and the preceptor, [should perform the rite].
Having carefully placed a screen all around the image,
one should first [visualize] the eye of the forehead, and after that, the eyes of the sun.
Immediately thereafter follows the sequence of opening the eyes of the moon;
for deities with two eyes, the eye of the sun comes first,
and immediately thereafter the eye of the moon— such is the sequence of opening the eyes.
Likewise, for those with additional faces,

the artisan, meditating on the deity with a concentrated mind, should open as many eyes as there are, along with the mouth, the nose, the pair of ears, and likewise the anus and the generative organ. (3–4)
One should fashion the navel, the tip of the nose, and the nine apertures;
then one should perform the purification of the image with the *puṇyāha* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having consecrated the previously mentioned jars upon the eyes [of the image], one should proceed according to the sequence.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, the wise person should personally perform the twelvefold visualization there as the instructor.
Then, [he should offer] milk, ghee, honey, grain, and a mirror. (6–7)
An elephant, Brahmins, as well as a maiden, a lamp, and likewise a lattice;
Thereafter, one should cause the patron to behold the cow and the ārārtika ceremony, preceded by their respective mantras. (8)
There, the preceptor indeed cast aside the curtain;
he caused everyone to see [the image] properly with devotion, and not merely at the opening of the eyes according to the ritual for the placement of jewels. (9)
The image attains fullness, yet through that very [image] there is no fullness.
(10) Now, O child, the purification of the image will be explained; for here, indeed, is the purification of the image. (i.51a, 10)
After opening the eyes, one should perform the purification of that image.
Whatever defect has arisen from the hands of the artisan is to be known by its cause;
by that very means, the wise man should purify it according to the sequence to be described. (I.51b–2)
If the image possesses the aforementioned characteristics yet is struck by poison or smeared with ghee,
that image must be abandoned and another image should be fashioned.
In the case of stone images, one should smear them with butter along with the *vṛtra* [protective substances].
The wise one should cause an application of collyrium to be made upon the metal image.
(4) Having thus purified the images according to the rule, the Guru himself should accept a flawless image and reject one that is defective. (5)
Purity of the Image:
I shall now proclaim the purity of the image; listen to this with respect, my child.
That purity is considered to be of two kinds, distinguished by the specific and the general. (I.51b, 5–6)
Now, O Six-faced One, I shall explain in detail the brief purification;
one should perform the consecration with the oil of tamarind fruit. (7)
Then, with the water of the Puṇyāha rite and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [he should sprinkle] the trees:
the Aśvattha, Jambu, Nyagrodha, and Udumbara.
The wise preceptor should add the five barks, the heartwood, water,
and the navel [of the tree] from those aforementioned trees— along with their sprouts—
to the water in the pitcher, mixing them all together. (9–10)
And having recited the Saṃhitā-mantra, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
The most excellent of instructors should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Now, O Guha, the preliminary consecration with water (jalādhivāsa) will be explained in detail. (I.52a)
Having led the image to a pond or a river amidst the sound of dancing and musical instruments, the wise preceptor should construct a pavilion in the midst of the water.
Having placed a pedestal below, he should set the image upon it.
Then, facing eastward, the wise one should pray to the image;
if it is an image of a female deity, the preceptor should pour water up to the ears, but if it is an image of a male deity, the most excellent of preceptors should pour it up to the breasts. (3–4)
One should worship jars on the banks of the seven rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā;
and with the water from those very jars, one should perform the external consecration.
The preceptor, having entered within, should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings;
then, preceded by song and instrumental music, he should lead the image to the temple.
The consecration of the grain follows the consecration of the water; one should indeed perform the dwelling of the grain.
(i.52a, 7) Having purified the grain according to the rule, one should sprinkle it with the waters of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha). (8)
When the grain reaches the height of the ear, the wise one should place a female *bera* there;
the best of preceptors should place a male *bera* at the level of the breasts.
(9) Having worshipped it with the eight flowers, he should offer betel leaves and other items.
Having thus paused for a moment, he then circumambulated the village.

Having adorned the image with ornaments, garments, and flowers, the wise man, having placed it upon a palanquin or an elephant, proceeds in circumambulation of the village accompanied by songs and instrumental music. (I.52b–2)
One should perform a circumambulation of the village and carry out the rite for the relief of the threefold suffering.
Having established the doors of the gate-towers, the consecration of the image and the release of the gaze [should be performed].
(3) The best of preceptors himself should perform these with cotton and other materials.
Then, having performed the great rite of adoration (*mahārārtika*), one should lead [the image] to the temple.
The wise man should have a bed prepared upon either a fivefold or a sevenfold layering of cloths;
it should likewise be beautified with perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Then one should offer milk, water for the hands, and fruit as the food offering;
there, the wise preceptor should especially cause songs to be performed.
The Procedure for Placing the Footprints:
O Guha, listen as I explain the placement of the footprints in detail.
Having made the inner sanctum twenty [parts], one should make the *garu* three parts. (I.52b, 6–7)
One should indeed install Śiva in the center of the inner sanctum;
the area in front of the deity must be avoided by the wise. (8)
The Liṅga is the western part, while Vidhi and Viṣṇu shall be the feet;
O child, that western foot belongs to Gaṇeśa and to you as well.
That which is to the west of Durgā is declared to belong to Lakṣmīpāṇi;
(10) that western portion should always be avoided by the wise at all times.
To the west of that, there is the face of Caṇḍeśa, which is the station of the devotees; (I.53a) to the west of that is the station of Maheśa, beginning with Bhairava.
That which follows is declared to be the word beginning with "Cāmuṇḍā" and so forth;
after that, there shall be the word "nilayam" (abode), referring to the dwelling place of minor deities and the like.
Having thus performed the placement of the steps, the best of teachers should proceed.
(3) Listen, my child, to the installation of the pedestal; the installation of the pedestal is now described in brief. (i.53a, 3)

One should perform the excellent installation of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) when the ascendant is stable. (4) Having declared it an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should carry out the purification of the pedestal. One should install therein that deity whose specific station (*pada*) has been prescribed. (5)
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should then present the food offering (naivedya).
Now I shall explain that which was previously set forth as the "Placement of the Crest-Jewel" (jaṭiratnanyāsa);
listen, O Piercer of Krauñca!
In the central region of the pedestal, at the nine openings,
the wise and most excellent of teachers should place nine jewels.

Regarding the placement of the jewels: one should place a ruby (*māṇikya*) in the central cavity, and an emerald (*marataka*) in the [cavity] of Indra. Indeed, one should place lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) in the southeast, and sapphire (*indranīlaka*) in the southern [cavity]. (I.53a, 7–8)
A pearl should be placed in the northwestern region, and likewise crystal in the western;
a *gomedhaka* gem in the northwestern [region], and coral in the northern.
In the northeast, one should place the vajra; in this manner, one should arrange the jewels.
One should place the eight world-protectors at the feet and Brahmā in the center.
If it is a male form, it is called the head; if it is a female form, it is likewise said [to be the head].
O best of teachers, one should worship Brāhmī within the central aperture.
The preceptor should worship the wives of the guardians of the directions in the eight cardinal points;
having inscribed the syllables of the mantras of those deities upon a golden plate.
The wise one, being composed, should place that plaque in the central region,
[adorned] with various flowers, bilva fruits, and those fashioned of gold.
Having placed [the mantras] upon the nine limbs, the wise and most excellent of teachers,
preceded by the four Vedas, should perform the installation of the image at an auspicious time and under an auspicious lunar mansion. (i.53.4)

The preceptor, accompanied by Brahmins with songs and instrumental music, should place the image upon the pedestal according to the method prescribed in the treatises on iconography (śilpa-śāstra). Then, the wise one should offer incense, lamps, and other offerings in accordance with the scriptures. (5–6)
I shall describe the procedure for consecration; listen to it in detail from the Six-faced One.
For the threefold classification of consecration is indeed as previously stated.
Now I shall describe its ritual; listen with a concentrated mind.

Where there is no festival for Brahmā, nor even a fortnightly festival, and where there is not even the worship of Śiva—one should not settle one's mind there. In that village, there is neither a ruined temple, nor an ancient one, nor a new one. (8–9)
One who desires their own welfare should not reside in that village where there is a dilapidated temple, or where a *liṅga* is deficient,
or where the pedestal is missing, or where the temple lacks structural integrity. (10)
In that case, all [acts] such as worship and the like are proclaimed to be fruitless.
Through its defects, it perishes in the village; through the destruction of the kingdom, it perishes.
O Six-faced One, listen to the fruit when the binding of the *pīṭha* is properly performed. (2)
Whatever merit is found in all sacrifices, whatever fruit is found in all holy places,
and whatever merit is found in all acts of giving— from all that, this [rite] shall become a bond for liberation.
(3) It is the pacifier of all diseases and the increaser of all good fortune.
Therefore, one should perform the binding of the pedestal with every effort.
One should bind it with gold or silver, but never with lead.
Binding in eight ways has been declared by the wise who have reached the further shore of the Āgamas. (4–5)
In that regard, the fourth [type] is the giver; binding is considered by the Sages to be of four kinds:
single binding, triple binding, five-fold binding, and beyond that, eight-fold binding—so it has been declared by those who have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas. (6)
That bondage is said to be of two kinds, yet you have also stated that it is "ripe."
That which is cooked is said to be *pācita*, while that which is uncooked becomes *mardana*.
Having understood this as "cooked-uncooked," the wise one should bind it very firmly.
That which is unripened is said to be divine, while that which is ripened is called human.
(8) I shall describe the sequence of its bondage; listen with a concentrated mind.

Having adorned it with golden ornaments and satisfied Jalandharaguhā with water offerings, the wise practitioner should properly place [the vessel] all around that pedestal so as to be completely sealed without gaps. (9)
One should make it equal in all four directions, for indeed there must be no deficiency or excess;
that cave-like space surrounding the liṅga and its pedestal should be like a ring-finger.
One should indeed apply the weapon to that which is embraced by the *liṅga*.
Then, this very "golden bond" (*svarṇabandha*) is called "cooked food" (*pakvabhukti*) by the wise. (I.54b)
Now, the binding of unrefined gold is described; listen with faith.
(2) Having taken molten gold, one should strike it repeatedly like cotton.
One should strike it correctly and must not encircle Śiva on all sides;
one should rub [the site] with the weapon-mantra "Hūṃ" inside, outside, and in the four directions.
The wise physician should thoroughly lubricate the area all around the *liṅga*.
This is described by the learned exponents of the scriptures as the "unmatured gold-binding" (*apakva-svarṇa-bandha*).
This very same sequence has been prescribed for *apharāja* and *atasī*.
Now, O Six-faced One, listen as I describe the method for a single-bond (*ekabandha*):
one part of *kundariṣka* and half that amount of oil is prescribed.
Having properly mixed both together, the wise should cook them in fire.
Then, taking that which has been declared cooked, the intelligent one should mix it with water and *kundariṣka*. (6–7)
First, the wise one should rub [the stone] against a fragment of stone on a grinding slab;
thereafter, he should gradually rub it with oil as before. Having made it smooth, he should carefully bind that mass to the pedestal.
In this very manner, it is called "bandha" when it is not yet cooked. (9) Now, the procedure for the three-fold binding (*tribandha*) as approved by the scriptures is stated:
sugar, *kundariṣka*, and fresh butter—this is the sequence. (10)
Two parts of sugar are prescribed, and three parts of *kunduriṣka*;
with two parts of clarified butter or oil is it proclaimed.
Having properly mixed these three on the fire and satisfied them, the wise man [should proceed].
With that very [substance], one should perform the "cooked" binding; this is the triple-binding of the cooked.
(2) The wise person should grind the aforementioned triad of substances upon a stone;
by means of that same "cooked" binding, this becomes the "uncooked" triple-binding. (3)
Immediately following that, my son, the fivefold binding is described;
it is proclaimed as *kāṣāya*, *śarkarā*, *lākṣā*, *kundariṣka*, and *taila* or *navanīta*—this is the cooked binding. (4)
Lac, fresh butter, and three parts of *rida* (red lead);
(5) one part of *kāṣāya*, and likewise sugar outside;
two parts of *kundariṣka*—this is remembered as the sequence of the portions. (6)
Having respectfully gratified the aforementioned five substances in the fire,

one should perform the "fivefold binding" (*pañcabandhana*) upon the cooked [substance] by means of that very [mixture]. (7) One should thoroughly rub the aforementioned five substances together with a stone.
By that very means one should perform the binding; this is called "unripe" (apakva).
Now, the tradition for the "cooked binding" (pakvabandha) will be explained:
sugar, red cotton, ochre, and *kunda-riṣka*. (8–9)
Beeswax, lac, fresh butter, and guggulu;
sugar is said to be three parts, and likewise kunduriṣka.
Lac is one part, and half of that is said to be cotton.
Two parts of beeswax and half of that amount of ochre;
likewise, there should be butter and vermilion—this is said to be the sequence of proportions declared by the ancients who were experts in the traditional scriptures. (1.55b–2)
Having crushed all this with a pestle in a mortar,
the time for this crushing is proclaimed to be ten *yāmas*.
Alternatively, it is described in another way as the eightfold binding.

Two parts of sugar are prescribed, three parts of *kunduriṣka*, one part of lac, and three-quarters of a part of *kāṣāya*. One part of resin (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) and half of that [one part] of red cotton should be used. (4–5)
Fresh butter is said to be three-quarters [of the weight], and vermilion is said to be half;
however, a binding that is devoid of vermilion is lacking in strength.
One should indeed pound all of this in a mortar with a pestle;
then the wise practitioner should perform the binding according to the scriptures.
This period for rubbing [the ointment] is proclaimed to be one hundred watches;
having rubbed it for one hundred watches, one should thereafter perform the binding.
Afterwards, one should smear the top of the binding with powdered *hiṅgu*.
Now, the lifespan granted by the aforementioned bindings will be explained.
The lifespan of gold jewelry is recorded as one hundred years;
for silver, its lifespan is proclaimed to be half of that.
Half of that is said to be the fixed proportion for lead-binding;
half of that again is declared by the wise to be the binding for tin and lead.
The "binding by the sun" and so forth are proclaimed for the establishment of the abode of the ignorant (bālālayapratiṣṭhā).
However, among the bindings previously mentioned, the binding occurs during the middle of the lifespan.
If anything should become broken, one should perform the rite of re-binding;
that very binding is known in the world as "immediate binding."
Bondage has been declared to be threefold by the ancient masters who had reached the further shore of the Āgamas:
instantaneous bondage, gradual bondage, and absolute bondage.
The immediate binding has been described; now the sequential binding is explained here.
When the separation [of the fingers] exceeds the thumb, the sequential binding is proclaimed.
(4) But when it is entirely devoid of binding, it is remembered as the "exceedingly triple" binding.
"Without performing *ākarṣaṇa*, the wise one should immediately perform *bandhana*.
(5) "Those who have mastered the scriptures say that this is according to the sequence of *prāyaścitta*.
Having performed *ākarṣaṇa*, the wise one should perform *bandhana* in due order. (6)
Those learned in the scriptures say that there is no abode of power (*balālaya*) here;
however, for the sake of purifying any defects of the artisans, one should perform the rite of pacification (*vāstuśānti*) once again.
One should effect the ultimate binding precisely through the sequence of the *bālālaya*;
the distinction regarding the lifespan of the *bālālayapratiṣṭhā* is now being described.
In the case of a water-jar (kumbha), it shall last for one month; in the case of a sword (khaḍga), it is recorded as two months.
In the case of a mirror (darpaṇa), it is declared to be six months, while in the case of a cloth (paṭa), it is recorded as one year.
It is declared elsewhere that [the gift] bestows [the fruit] for three years, while in another tradition, twelve years are recorded.

If the deity is invoked elsewhere than in the *kumbha*—such as in a sword (*khaḍga*) and so forth—the wise say that the sequence of sacrifice does not exist [in that way]. For one bound for a year, [the initiation] is for one year; for one bound for three years, it is for three years. (I.56b)
The lifespan for one with five bonds is likewise proclaimed to be six years;
if the Bālālaya is made of stone, the lifespan is twelve years.
(2) When the Liṅga is to be fashioned from wood in the Bālālaya, [the same applies].
With nyagrodha, bakula, aśvattha, punnāga, and udumbara trees;

Having fashioned the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rules, one should perform the ritual of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). If it is a stone *liṅga*, one should perform it upon the stone; if it is a *bāṇaliṅga*, one should perform it upon the *bāṇaliṅga*.
However, for the rite of summoning all images, Guha should proceed with the previously mentioned substances, whether on a cloth or upon the image itself. (4)
They say that one should recite [the mantra] while obstructing the paths of those who wander;
(5) here, in this ritual of worship, a certain distinction exists which shall now be explained.
(6) A wise person should perform the consecration of the paintings with devotion.
The installation in the abode of the ignorant, however, lasts for exactly twelve years.
(7) The construction of the sacrificial hall and the characteristics of the sacrificial hall shall be described; listen, O Six-faced One! (i.56b, 7)
There, for the sake of the sacrifice, one should construct a pavilion either beside the temple or on its side;
[it may be located] in the direction of Indra, or Agni, or Yama, or even Rākṣasa (Nairṛta);
or in the region of Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, or Īśāna. (8–9)
Or, O Goddess, the sacrificial field is praised as being in a corner of the house;
the site for sacrifice may also be determined by the very path previously described, or it is fixed on the left side of the temple of Śiva. (10)
If, in the instruction regarding indolence, there should be a sacrificial hall;
It is certain that the purification of that site must be performed correctly;
where the sacrificial hall is constructed within the interior of the laziness [of the ground]. (I.57a)
In that regard, it is certain that the purification of the ground need not be performed at all.
(2) O Six-faced One, one should properly purify the ground to a depth of one's own height.
Likewise, this [measurement] with one cubit is proclaimed to be square;
it is the superior *manusūtra*, while the *ravisūtra* is the middling.
And the lowest [measurement] is ten threads; such is the determination of the threads. (4) The Manu-thread and the hands have been declared to be twenty-one finger-breadths.
The Ravisūtra is said to be seventeen cubits long;
in this treatise, the Daśasūtra is recorded as being fifteen cubits.
In the three previously mentioned sūtras, there should be hands with intervening spaces;
that intervening space here should be equal to the width of the altar, or it may be at the end.
Therefore, this intermediate space shall be described according to its possibility:
first, by means of the western arrangement, there is a thread consisting of a number of *manus*. (7)
In the same manner, one should construct the southern and northern lines according to the measurement of the sūtra;
thereafter, one should make the Maghā-laya square.
One hundred and nine squares have been described;
now the application of all these squares is being stated.
(9) In the center, there is a nine-square altar (*vedi*), which is the principal [area]; there, one should place the *vardhanī* [vessel].
O God, the wise one should place [the deities] in the central square according to the scripture.
Outside of that are the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), and outside of that is the sixteenth square.
This is said to be the place of worship in the four cardinal directions; in the intermediate directions, it is called the pillar.
In the remaining eight squares, the eight auspicious signs (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) are said to be placed here;
outside of that, twenty-four squares are declared for the purpose of movement.
Beyond that, the wise declare there are thirty-two square cells.
And outside of that, forty *pada*s are proclaimed by the wise.
(3) Within these *pada*s, the wise should perform the ritual for establishing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*);
the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) are prescribed [for this].
The remaining three steps are called the "Teacher's Steps" (ācāryapada);
beyond that, the wise declare it to be the "Eighty-four Steps" (aṣṭacatvāri pada).
The preceptor should place twenty-seven jars there;
or he should place ten pillars in the four directions.
In the remaining twenty squares,
the wise and discerning practitioner should construct four gates in the four directions equally, according to the scriptures.
And outside of that, the intermediate space is proclaimed to be in the four directions.
By this much of the text, the *manusūtra* has been fully described.
The sequence of the sun’s thread:
the sun’s thread should have its tip pointing east, and likewise its tip pointing north.
It is declared to consist of one hundred and twenty-one divisions of the square.
In the center, there is one square for Brahmā, which is the primary [square], and likewise the Vardhanī;
in the divine squares, there are the Kumbhas, and the sixteenth is Paiśāca.
For the purpose of worship, pillars are said to be placed in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions;
in the remaining eight squares, the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) are prescribed.
Beyond that, at a distance of fifty-six [units], the human station is proclaimed.
One should perform the ritual specifically according to the rules in each corner.
One should cause nine [circles] starting from the east to be made, with an eighth pit in the center;
(2) between the Rudra and Khaṇḍala [circles], one should make the primary circle.
Outside, at the fortieth step, there is a gateway with a water-pot for the Rākṣasa;
it should be a refined space suitable for the movement of the teacher and the disciples.
The pillar-station is outside the foot; thus the station is established.
(4) The sequence of the ten lines begins from the east; likewise, there are ten lines toward the south and the north. (i.58a, 4)
The eighty-one placements of the squares and their ritual applications are now described:

(5) In the center is a nine-square altar; outside of that are the eight auspicious symbols; outside of that are the compartments for the sacrificial pits; and outside of that, the gateway is said to be located. (6)
Alternatively, the procedure for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is described in another way:
if it is less than nine cubits, the wise man should construct it in this manner.
Having divided the sacrificial field into three parts, the altar (*vedikā*) is placed in the middle portion.
Having divided that [space] externally into three parts, one should arrange the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in its center.
(8) It should be provided with sixteen pillars and endowed with four gates;
O wise one, one should also place an altar (*vedi*) with four pillars in each of the four directions. (9)
Outside the pavilion, twelve pillars should be arranged here;
O brother Ṣaṇmukha, listen as I describe the characteristics of the altar.
The divine [section] consists of nine squares, and the Piśāca [section] consists of sixteen squares;
having multiplied these by twenty-five, one should fashion the altar of squares.
The height is said to be one cubit, and the width is likewise;
one should fashion the small altar with a width of three cubits. (I.58b)
Above that, one should construct the secondary altar (*upavedī*), which is two cubits higher;
its height is said to be six finger-breadths, and its width is likewise.
One should arrange it there so that it is joined with the two side-boards at the front and the back of the base-board;
or else, the characteristics of the altar (vedī) are described in another manner.
Its height should be equal to its width, or even half of it;
resembling a mirror or water, this is known as the characteristic of the *vedikā*.
(4) The *vedi* should be properly provided with a pedestal (*pīṭha*), and there should be a secondary altar (*upavedi*) for the ascetic (*yati*).
It is known as the Mahāvedī by those proficient in all the Āgamas.
(5) That altar which is devoid of a pedestal is called a common altar in the world. (6) [Now follows] the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O child, the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) will be described in brief.
(i.58b, 6) One should fashion the pits in the nine fire-sanctuaries located in the eight directions.
(7) The primary pit is said to be situated between Indra and Īśāna.

In the case of the five-fire ritual site (*pañcāgnyāyatana*), one should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in each of the four directions. (8) However, in the primary [site], the pit is prescribed for the northeastern quarter. In the case of the single-fire ritual site (*ekāgnyāyatana*), one should place the pit to the west of the altar (*vedi*). (9)
In the direction of Indra (the East), it is square; in the South-East, it is of the form of a *bhaga* (womb);
in the South, it is called the half-moon; and in the South-West, it is triangular. (10) In the West, it is circular in shape; and in the North-West, it is hexagonal.
In the north, the lotus-shaped [kuṇḍa] is prescribed; in the northeast, the eight-cornered kuṇḍa. Between Indra and Īśāna, the circular kuṇḍa is the primary one.
Just as the shape of the kuṇḍa has been described, so is the primary kuṇḍa designated.
The preceptor should indeed make the field of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) square;
having laid a single thread from east to west and from south to north, the wise one, free from distraction, [should do so] through the center. (3)
That thread should be one cubit in length, and that [thread] consists of twelve finger-breadths.
There is a fish-mark at the eight directions of the forest [grid], and upon those [points], four threads are laid out.
From these six threads, there arise four squares.
The entire cave-pit should be ninety-six finger-breadths in length;
it is proclaimed that its height up to the girdle is one cubit, and there should be five layers.
Here, the three girdles shall have a height of nine finger-breadths each.
That [measurement] has been declared according to the sequence; the strike is fifteen finger-breadths.
At the final point of the *meghalā*, one should establish a limit of nine finger-breadths.
Above the ground, O wise one, one should fashion the neck (*kaṇṭha*) as one finger-breadth. (7–8)
The upper girdle is declared to have a width of four finger-breadths;
the middle girdle is remembered to have a width of two finger-breadths;
and the final girdle is proclaimed to have a width of two finger-breadths. (9)
Above that, on the girdle, either to the south or to the west,
the wise man should fashion the *yoni*, twelve finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width, shaped like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.
Beginning from the throat at the top of the womb and extending upward to the waistband,
this [structure] one finger-breadth in height is called the *kalpa-yoni*.
In the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), there should be a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
The length is twelve finger-breadths, and the pericarp is four finger-breadths.
The height of the pericarp and the petals shall be four finger-breadths.
The measurement of the base of the pericarp is said to be two finger-breadths;
this is declared to be the characteristic of the quadrangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The field, having been divided into two parts, is designated as the base and the tip.
Having divided that field into five parts, one portion is placed outside at the front. (5) Having divided the base portion into two, the right and the left are spoken of.
One should fashion the ear-threads on both the right and the left foot.
(6) One should rotate the pair of horns at the sides of the ends of the half-area. Starting from that point, by means of two threads, one should add one unit outward. (7)
And this [mandala] called the Yonikuṇḍa has the shape of a vulva;
one should fashion it as a half-moon from a field divided into nine parts. Leaving two squares at the base and at the tip, one should perform the circumambulation.
This is called the *candrarāka* (moon-shaped) pit by the wise.
(9) Having divided the field into six parts, one should place two parts on each side;
then, from the root, there should be a pair of lines extending to the front of that single part. (10)
When one extends that cord at the front as three cords, it forms a triangle;
having removed the eight-cornered portion of the field divided into nine parts,
and having rotated the remaining corner, the pit becomes circular in shape.
The field is divided into six parts, with two parts each at the top and the base.
Having divided one part into two, one should place them to the south and north.
This is called the "sixty-cornered" [mandala] by the experts of the Kāmikāgama. (2–3)
The lotus-pit known as *vṛttavat* is said to have eight petals on the outside.
The pericarp (*karṇikā*) has a width of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and a height of half that measure.
Each petal is five finger-breadths long and one finger-breadth in height.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), resembling a lotus, is said to be two finger-breadths wider than the girdle (mekhalā).
The field divided into eight parts, one part should be placed outside.
Then, in each corner and in the middle, a diagonal line (karṇasūtra) is drawn across three squares.
According to the Sūtra, the elevenfold [fire-pit] shall be octagonal;
in the lotus-shaped pit, one should fashion a navel, but one should not construct a womb.
For the other types of pits, one should fashion both a navel and a womb.

One should construct a *bhūpura* (enclosure wall) on the four sides of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*). It should be one cubit in width and six finger-breadths in height. Then, one should arrange three altars (*vedi*) in the northwest, northeast, and southwest corners. (8–9)
The supreme preceptor should fashion the fire-pit (chulli) dedicated to Agni,
with a height equal to that of the protective square (bhūpura) and a width of one cubit.

Indeed, the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), altars (vedi), and pavilions (maṇḍapa) have been described in detail. Prior to the construction of the sacrificial pits, a meal for the Brahmins should be provided in that field.
Having performed the dismissal of the blue jay [image] as many times as required, one should thereafter perform the rite for an auspicious day.
O Six-faced One, listen with respect as I describe the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
The preparation of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is likewise made from nine types of trees.

The fig tree (*vaṭa*), the holy fig (*aśvattha*), the palāśa, the *jambu*, the udumbara, the mango (*cūtaka*), the *plakṣa*, the *śrīvṛkṣa*, and the *khadira*—these are proclaimed as the nine trees. (2–3)
One should have four *sruk* ladles made of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *aśvattha*;
this set of four *sruk*s should be like the face of a calf at the front.
One should have four *sruva* spoons made of *plakṣa*, *khadira*, *jambū*, and *cūta*.
O child, one should conceive of this tetrad as being like a bee-hive.
A wise person, not being bound by ritual constraints, should prepare a single sacrificial ladle from either *gaja* or *bilva* wood;
and by whichever tree the discerning practitioner makes the ladle, [so shall it be]. (5)
A wise person should fashion the *sruva* ladle from a piece of wood of that same kind.
(6) There should be nine *sruc* ladles and likewise nine *sruvas*;
according to the sacrifice, each *sruc* and *sruva* should resemble its respective sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (7)
Now the characteristics of the trees previously mentioned are described: one should select mature trees that are free from cracks and hollows. (8)
Having understood the root and the tip, the wise one should fashion the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
They declare that the characteristic of the *sruk* is a length of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The handle is said to be four finger-breadths at the base, while the shaft is measured according to the sun (*mārtāṇḍa*), [twelve finger-breadths].
The Veda-altar is said to be one Veda (four) finger-breadths [in height], and the neck should be one finger-breadth.
The great altar in the center should be eight finger-breadths [in width] between the altar and the neck.
The mouth is declared by all experts in the science of architecture to be seven *aṅgulas* in measure.
On the rear portion, the great altar (*mahāvedī*) and the two altars (*vedi*) are said to be located.
Below that, a lotus is described, and likewise above it;
the great altar (mahāvedi) is said to have a width of three finger-breadths.
The diameter is said to be five finger-breadths, and the rim should be one-quarter of a finger-breadth. The center of the cavity is equal to the pericarp, and outside of that are eight petals.
The height of the pedestal for the feet should be equal to the width of a toe;
the teacher should then fashion the neck and the altar as square.
The thickness of the staff should be one finger-breadth (rasāṅgula), and the tip of the ghaṇṭī should be four finger-breadths wide.
The channel for the flow of clarified butter should be the measure of the little finger.
The wise man should fashion the mouth of the spout to resemble the face of an elephant or the face of a deer.
O Mahāsena, listen now; the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle are being described.
(6) Its length is said by the wise to be twenty-four *aṅgulas*, and its tip should likewise have a width of three *aṅgulas*. (7)
The neck is one finger-breadth, and the staff is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
The base is one finger-breadth, and the base of the neck is said to be three finger-breadths.
It is stated that the circumference of the two necks should be one finger-breadth.
O Guha, this [liṅga] fit for a staff should be the size of a thumb;
the pit should be made like a city gate, and the back like the head of an elephant.
One should construct an archway using *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* trees.
On each of these trees, one should place a single crossbeam (*teraṇa*).
Its height should be five cubits and its width three cubits.
The thickness of the plank is declared to be three finger-breadths.
The width of the four [spikes] is six finger-breadths, and their characteristics are equal.
Three upward-pointing spikes are prescribed—one in the middle and one on each side—and their height is clearly stated to be nine finger-breadths. (2–3)

That pair of two *dhana* finger-breadths is declared to be the characteristic of the arch (*toraṇa*). The length of the tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*) is said to be one cubit (*hasta*), while its width is said to be equal to that; its mouth (*āsya*) shall be four finger-breadths (*vedāṅgula*). (4)
The four legs are three finger-breadths [in length], and it is said that the tail and other parts are one finger-breadth. Having divided the width into five parts, one part shall be its thickness.
Its face is described as having the form of a serpent; such is the characteristic of the tortoise.
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Sumukhī, Tilottamā,
Sundarī, Kāmukī, and Kāmavardhanī— these are the eight types of women.
And their height is now stated to be thirty-two finger-breadths;
one should fashion the image according to the correct characteristics as prescribed by the scriptures.
(8) [One should also depict] a mirror, a full water-jar, a bull, and a pair of chowries.
The Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, and the lamp constitute the eight auspicious signs.
(9) A mirror was assigned to Urvaśī, Menakā a full water-pot, Rambhā a bull, and Tilottamā a fly-whisk. (10)
The *śrīvatsa* is said to belong to Sumukhī, while the *svastika* belongs to Sundarī;
the *śaṅkha* is said to belong to Kāmukhī, and the *dīpa* belongs to Kāmavardhanī.
(I.62a) It is stated that mirrors and other such objects are held in the hands of the aforementioned women.
The Vajra, Śakti, Daṇḍa, Khaḍga, Pāśa, Dhvaja, Gadā,
Triśūla, Padma, and Cakra—
those who bear these ten weapons are the ten deities in embodied form. (2–3)
They should have the colors of their respective world-protectors (dikpālas) and bear the ten weapons placed upon their heads;
all are described as having two arms and joining their palms at the heart.
In the absence of a physical image, however, one should perform a painting;
the previously mentioned arches and so forth should be made according to the measurement of the preceptor’s fingers.
The preceptor should have effigies made there for all [the deities];
the wise one should decorate the sacrificial hall according to the scripture. (i.62a, 5)
One should construct four archways at the four directions of the sacrificial hall:
at the eastern gate a *nyagrodha* tree, likewise an *udumbara* at the southern gate, an *aśvattha* at the northern gate, and indeed a *plakṣa* at the western gate. (6–7)
Above the door, one should place eight banners in the four directions;
on both sides of that, one should place sixteen slender banners.
Or, at the twelfth [stage], one should fix the *sṛṣṭi* on both sides of the pillar.
On the banners one should depict eight elephants, and on the small ones, great bulls;
on the two types of flags, one should draw lotuses with two colors.
Now, the distinction between the cloths for the eight large banners is described.
In the east is the banner with blue cloth; in the southeast, one with red garments;
in the south, there should be one with black cloth; and in the southwest, one with smoke-colored [cloth]. (10)
In the northwest there should be a conch-shell garment; in the west, a variegated cloth;
in the north, a golden garment; and in the northeast, a yellow cloth.
Above the altar there should be a canopy, with a fringe on the four sides;
and upon that canopy, there should be a lotus endowed with a thousand petals.
The wise one should fashion a secondary wave on all four sides of the altar;
the wise one should also fashion a wave upon the upper pedestal of the great altar.
On both sides of every door, however, there should be plantain trees and coconut palms.
With betel nuts, sugarcane, dates, and likewise various fruits;
with garlands of *darbha* grass, mango leaves, and flowers of many colors;
and outside and in the intervals between them, also with various kinds of leafy vegetables. (4–5)
The wise man [should offer] with pumpkins having the appearance of watermelons, as well as jackfruit, mangoes, vārtāka, and jambīra, along with various other branches,
diverse ears of grain, and many kinds of lamps. (6)
Having adorned [the site] well with water and so forth, one should thereafter perform the sacrifice.
(7) Having satisfied the artisan with wealth, ornaments, garments, and other gifts, one should thereafter perform the rite for the pacification of the site (*vāstuśānti*). (8)
The Procedure for the Pacification of the Site:
Now I shall explain in detail the unsurpassed pacification of the site (vāstuśānti), [to be performed] at the time of consecration, sprinkling, festivals, and other auspicious occasions. (I.62b, 8–9)

For the sake of averting all defects, one should perform the *vāstu-śānti* (propitiatory rite for the site). Outside the city gate, in front of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) within the sacrificial pavilion (*yāga-maṇḍapa*),
or in any of these locations, one should diligently perform the *vāstu-śānti*.
Having constructed a pavilion there, one should perform the rite for the pacification of the site (*vāstuśānti*).
Indeed, the characteristics of the pavilion for the pacification of a village have already been stated; the expert in this field should construct the pavilion here in that same manner.
The highly intelligent preceptor, accompanied by the deities of the weapon-mantra and provided with song and instrumental music, should perform the rite for the pacification of the site. (I.63a)
Having reached the sacrificial pavilion (*vāstu-maṇḍapa*), one should place the deities of the weapons in the northeast;
having performed the *puṇyāha* rite, the purification of the site (*sthala-śodhana*) is to be carried out as before.
The Vāstucakra has been declared in two ways by those who have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas:
namely, as the Maṇḍūkapada and likewise as the Paramaśādhika.
The arrangement of the frog-step (maṇḍūkapada) for all the gods beginning with Śiva, as well as the supreme station of all the Śaktis, [is established]. (4)
I shall describe the procedure for the Maṇḍūka [maṇḍala]; listen with respect, O Six-faced One!
One should draw nine lines so that there are sixty-four squares.
Having drawn two diagonal lines, there will be a square at each corner.
And at its side, the wise one should draw a line through the ears (the diagonal).
Then, from the two points where the ear-lines intersect, he should proceed with two bamboo-lines (diagonals),
resulting in a design endowed with twelve lotuses and four corner-tridents.
The wise practitioner should draw a circle in the four directions, starting with the east;
in its center, he should depict a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having combined the six-word [unit] within the two rules,
the wise one should thus correctly grasp the definition of the *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap).
Now, the characteristic of the state of supreme rest is described with reverence:
from the east to the west, and from the south to the north. (10)
One should draw ten threads so that there are eighty-one squares.
As before, one should mark the diagonal lines and four lines for the central axis (*vaṃśa*).
The instructor should likewise fashion twenty squares with the armor-line (*varman*).
In the center is a nine-square lotus with eight petals and a pericarp;
in the eight directions there should be a trident, while at the corners it is mixed.
O God, this indeed is called the *paramaśāyika* in this time.
Having performed the ritual identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with Brahmā, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Having worshipped the object of the wheel, [one should worship] those situated in the ten directions beneath the wheel:
Lakṣmī, Yaśas, Patikāntā, Supriyā, Vimalā, and Śivā.
Subhagā, Sumati, and Sārā are situated in the east and the other directions according to the Sūtra.
One should worship Dhanyā, Prāṇaviśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Arajā, Vibhavā, and Cetanā, as well as the Rakṣasūtra and the others. (4)
One should worship this Śakti and Maṇḍūka within the lines of the diagram:
(5) Śāntī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Vimalā, Prāṇanāhinī, Satrī, Sumatī, Nandā, Subhadrā, and Manoramā. (6)
One should worship, in due order, within the ten threads starting from the east:
Hiraṇyā, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Sthirā, Dharā, Jvālā, and Viśokā;
and [the goddesses] beginning with Iḍā in the west and the others.
Thus, O King, those numbering eight were established in the supreme state by him:
Kīlinī, Madanī, Suvṛttā, Anivṛttakā, Sadbhāvā, Rājanī, Pakṣiṇī, and likewise Yakṣiṇī. (8–9)
The wise one should worship Durjaya and Durdhara upon the stakes and on the bamboo pole;
O gods, by the command of Śiva, let Vāstupuruṣa also be worshipped at the junctures.
Having placed the *kūrca* [mantra] upon the lotus, one should worship Brahmā there;
the Guru should then worship Ananta and the others on the eight petals according to the prescribed rite. (10)
A wise person should also worship Marīci, Vivasvat, Pitāmaha, and Dharaṇīdhara;
and in the mixed positions beginning with the east, one should worship as previously stated.
Āpamāvakavatsa, Savitra, and likewise Sāvitraka;
Indramijaya and Rudra—these one should then offer.
One should worship at the corners for the removal of misfortune, and likewise in the four cardinal directions:
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Mahendra.
Āditya, Satyaka, Bhraṃśa, Antarikṣa, Tadhānika, (3) Pūṣan, Gṛhakṣa, Yama, and Gandharva.
One should worship Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛgādhīśa, and the chief Nāga according to the prescribed rite,
as well as Bhallāṭaka, Soma, Ṛga, and Āditi.
One should cause this wheel to be taken up and worship these according to the ritual;
beginning from the position of Īśāna, one should worship them according to the ritual.
Worship Maḍūkī at the half-step, and Tāpī at Paramaśāyikā;
[worship] Carakī, Vitārī, and Pūtanā, the sinful rākṣasī.
Having worshipped Etaśūla, Skanda, Aryaman,
as well as Jṛmbha, Bali, and Piñcha, one should honor these in the circular enclosures.
One should likewise worship the wheel of the supreme couch upon the spikes;
then, one should place ten water-pots on the northern part of the sacrificial altar.
One should worship Brahmā, Bhāratī, and the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas), and so forth.
(9) Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should present the bali-oblation in the proper sequence.
(i.64b) Milk-rice should be given to Brahmā, along with wood-apples (*kapittha*).
The offering of cooked rice (gulonna) to the gods, such as Marīci and others, is declared to be bali.
One should offer a bali-oblation of cooked rice to the Āpāda and other deities;
(2) one should offer a bali-oblation of sesame and rice to the Īśāna and other deities;
(3) one should offer a bali-oblation of meat and rice to the eight deities beginning with Carakī.
For the sake of the meat offering, one should present an oblation mixed with black gram according to the prescribed rite:
to Brahmā in the center of the square, to the Marīcis in the space between the feet, to the Āpas and others at the corners, and to Īśāna and the others along the lines.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the eight deities beginning with Carakī during the Śūlavṛtta rite;
one should perform the fire-ritual and worship Brahmā and the others therein.
Having offered the sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and other substances with the Brahma-mantras and with a well-disciplined mind,
[he should offer] another substance according to the rules, following the thousand oblations of clarified butter.
One should perform ten oblations of clarified butter for all the deities of the enclosure;
according to each respective deity, one should offer an oblation of the corresponding food.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations for atonement with the Pāśupata and other mantras.
The preceptor should then perform oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras for the deities such as Carakī and the others.
Thereafter, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should perform the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth.
Then, the wise one should unite the form of the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with its [respective] station.
Therefore, having joined [the mantra] into the jar, and from that [jar] into the deity of the weapon;
having worshipped the deity of the weapon, one should perform the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth.
Then, having respectfully given the sacrificial fee and other offerings to the preceptor of the site,
and having given betel-leaf and sacrificial fees to the reciting Brahmins;
Having fashioned a torch from dried *palāśa*, *darbha*, and other such materials, or from dried wood of the *palāśa* and *udumbara* trees,
and having burned it in that fire according to the measurement of a staff;
Having sprinkled it with clarified butter, one should then worship those three principles;
then, having given clothing as well as wealth to that Brahman who is consciousness, ||| (4) ||| [one should proceed].
Having placed a firebrand in his hand, preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
and honoring the deity of weapons, he was followed by attendants carrying lamps.
For the sake of purifying the sacrificial site, for the purification of the primary liṅga and so forth,
and for the sake of purifying the entire abode, one should perform circumambulation within the temple.
Then, having performed the ritual procedure for the removal of delusion, one should cast the firebrand outside.
(7) Thereafter, the preceptor, having bathed, should perform the rite for a day of merit.
Having performed the expiation and the rite for the weapon-deity according to the rules and according to tradition, this must certainly be done;
otherwise, hear the result.
Due to the defect of the *vāstupuruṣa*, an obstacle to the sacrifice will certainly arise.
Therefore, the pacification of the site (*vāstuśānti*) must necessarily be performed here according to the prescribed sequence.
Regarding the purification of the *bimba*, I shall explain the sequence of the purification of the *bimba* in detail; listen, O son!
[This may be done] in a pavilion, or even in the sacrificial ground, the city, or the outskirts.
One should construct a pavilion there, provided with a sacrificial pit and an altar;
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and perform the rite of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
At the base of *darbha* grass, at an anthill, at the roots of a rose-apple (*jambū*) or banyan (*nyagrodha*) tree,
at the root of a wood-apple (*bilva*) tree, at the root of *tulasī*, and at the root of an *aśvattha* tree.
The wise man, having taken earth from the root of an *audumbara* tree, [should perform the ritual];
if that is unavailable, the intelligent one may take it from five other trees:
the *aśvattha*, the *vaṭa*, the *rājādana*, the *bilva*, and his own native tree.

The sprouts and likewise the bark of the *tulasī* and the *udumbara* trees—(5) the preceptor himself should place all these uncrushed together into one vessel; the most excellent preceptor should place all the barks into another vessel. (6)
One should place all the sprouts in another vessel;
in an earthen vessel, the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), and in the sprouts, the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
And the wise one should worship the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) according to the rules in the skin-vessel;
likewise, he should recite the Namaka, the Camaka, the Śrīsūkta, and the Viṣṇusūkta.
The Brahmins should perform the recitation of the *Brahmasūkta* and the *Pañcaśānti*;
the preceptor should recite the *Padamantras* and the *Tattvasahasra*.
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the mantras of Viṣṇu and the other deities.
Then, having performed the weapon-oblation (*astrahoma*), one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
The preceptor himself should then unite the form of the fire within the vessels.
To eliminate defects in craftsmanship, one should perform purification and consecration for the primary linga of the temple,
as well as for other images, using the previously mentioned water from the pitcher, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and so forth. (I.66a, 2)
If this rite is to take place, how can there be purity of the image?
And in the absence of purity of the image, how can there be the presence of the deity?
Furthermore, in the absence of the deity’s presence, the sacrifice would indeed be meaningless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the purification of the image.

(4) [One should use] the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), excellent water, fruit water, scented water, leaf water, and likewise water with grains and jewels. (5)

Then, the wise one should place eleven jars filled with the previously mentioned waters— iron water, washed water, weapon water, root water, and water from a *kūrca*— one by one in sequence. (6) Having established the jars, they should be filled with the aforementioned liquids.

Having recited the Rudra-mantra for the sake of Rudra by means of Brāhmaṇas, the Preceptor himself should then perform the consecration for each individual at the proper time. This consecration with the water-pot (kumbha-abhiṣecana) should take place prior to the daily sacrifice (nityayāga).
Upon the completion of the daily sacrifice, however, there is the rite of peace and the consecration with the water-pot.
In this manner, the preceptor should perform [the rites] every day according to the rule.
(9) Thus, the purification of the image has been proclaimed to you in detail.

Henceforth, O Guha, I shall explain the collection of clay. For the rite of collecting clay, that which comes from the northeast is said to be the best; the west is considered middling; and the south is declared to be the lowest.
On a riverbank, or by a pond, or in a field at the root of *darbha* grass; or in a cow-pen, or on a mountain, or even at an anthill or a termite mound. (I.66b)
Alternatively, the wise one should take clay from a pure location;
having constructed a pavilion there with plantains, betel-nut trees, and other such plants.
Likewise, having placed Vighneśa, Astra-rāja, and Caṇḍeśa before him,
he should proceed equipped with a spade.
Then, proceeding to the pavilion accompanied by the sound of song and instrumental music,
one should place Vighnarāja facing east on the western side of the pavilion,
and the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) facing west on the eastern side.
One should place Caṇḍīśa facing south on the gentle (northeastern) side.
(5) The best of preceptors should deposit the spade in the northeast direction;
in the south [he should perform] the preceptor’s *svasti*, the *puṇyāha* rite, and the purification of the *śalya*. (6)
In the center, the preceptor should draw the Earth Goddess in a variegated form,
with her head facing east and her face turned upwards, adorned with their respective colors.
Then, in the western portion, he should arrange nine squares.
One should place seven jars in the western part of the square.
(8) One should worship the boundary lines here and sacrifice to Brahmā and the other deities within the squares.
The preceptor should offer curd-rice as a bali-oblation and pray to Brahmā. (9)
"O Goddess Earth, by the command of the Immortal One, I shall take clay for the purpose of the Lord's ritual;
you should perform the strewing of grass on the outer ground."
One should worship Indra and the other deities there, and cause an offering of mung-bean rice to be presented as a bali.
(10) O guardians of the world, listen indeed for the sake of the sacrificial rite!
"I take up the earth; let it be given to me... (I.67a).
Having thus petitioned the world-protectors, one should worship the Goddess Earth.
Having recited the Bhūsūkta, one should then offer incense and a lamp.
For the sake of pacifying impurities, one should cleanse the spade with a mixture of oil and cow-products.
Having adorned the handle of the spade with tufts of wool, mango leaves, flowers, and also with garments and other ornaments, one should worship Keśava and the others.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should worship Śakti in the vessel.

Having taken up the small spade with the mantra "devasya tvā," the wise preceptor should dig into the region of the belly of the Earth Goddess while reciting the sword-mantras. There, the preceptor should deposit the earth into the vessel three times.
If the earth crumbles at the site of the womb, it is another kind of clay that causes loss.
Having leveled the ground to eliminate defects arising from excavation,
one should consecrate that spot with seven jars filled with water from the oceans.
Then, having scattered rice grains there, the wise one should cause all [the materials] to be sprinkled with water.
Having placed kūrca-grass, flowers, and unbroken rice upon the clay, and having covered the Guru with silk garments, he should consecrate him with the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras.

Having placed the sacrificial fee upon the heads of the attendants— either on a palanquin or upon an elephant— for the sake of the knowers of reality, the reciters, and the Brahmins, the wise preceptor,
having touched it with *kuśa* grass, [should take it] from the earth. (9)
Then, one should enter the temple by proceeding in a clockwise direction.
The preceptor, having gone to the sacrificial hall, should perform the rite for an auspicious day;
he should perform the eighteenfold consecration for the removal of the thorns [of defects].
The Procedure for Planting the Sprouts: I shall describe the sequence for sowing the seeds; listen with a concentrated mind, my child.
(i.67b) It is proclaimed that the commencement of the sacrifice begins with the planting of the sprouts.
From the seedling stage up to the final consecration, there are thirteen days;
those who know the Ādityāgama have declared this to be the procedure for the supreme sacrifice.
Nine days is declared to be the middling [period], while seven days would be the lowest.
They say that three or even five days constitutes the lowest of the low.
Upon immediate sprinkling, one should not perform the rite of germination;
however, after thirteen days have passed, one should perform the consecration and the *acaracara* rite.
Before the day of the ritual of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), the preceptor should perform the preliminary rite of the auspicious thread (*kautuka*).
Prior to the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), he should do so three or five days in advance.
One should obtain the permission of the deities and perform the binding of the pedestal;
thereafter, one should perform the pacification of the site and the purification of the image.
Between the *anujñā* and the *aṅkura* [rites], if there occurs the passage through the new moon day (*amāsa*) and so forth,

(7) provided that the lunar day (*tithi*) remains constant therein, no fault regarding shaving (*kṣaura*) exists. (8) Between the *pratiṣṭhā* and the *aṅkura* [rites], [if there occurs] the passage through the new moon day and so forth...
A wise person should act in such a way that no obstacle arises; however, O Six-faced One,
if obstacles such as initiation, festivals, sacrifices,
or transgressions should occur, they will not lead to any fault.
In any other auspicious rite, one should perform the offering of the ritual sprouts;
however, on the day of the summoning, it is prescribed that this be done only once.
On the day of consecration as well, there is likewise only one session;
however, on all the intermediate days, there shall be two sacrifices.
Even during the thirteen days, the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) is performed for one day;
for the remaining twelve days, the duration is said to be twenty [units].
In the case of the eleven-day rite, the time is declared to be eighteen;
for the nine-day sacrifice, the time is stated to be fourteen.
In seven days, one should perform ten fire-oblations; in five days, six;
in three days, two; and in a single day, one oblation in heaven.
The Guru, devoted to devotion and meditation, should perform the *homa* according to the scriptures.
The wise practitioner should perform the rite of planting the sprouts at midday.
(5) The time of the sun is declared to be day, while the moon is the leader of the night.
(6) Because the moon nourishes medicinal herbs, the sprout is said to belong to the moon.

Therefore, when the sun has set during the first watch of the night and an auspicious moment is present, the wise man should perform [the rite] during that first watch; such is the determination of the scriptures.
The *pālikā* should have a height of eight *aṅgulas*, and its mouth should likewise be circular.
Its width should be half of that, and the lip should be one *aṅgula*.
The cavity is said to be three finger-breadths deep; this is the characteristic of the *pālikā*.
One should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts in the northwest corner of the hall.
One should likewise draw five lines from east to west and from south to north;
there, upon the altar, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains.
Having drawn a lotus in the center, one should place three jars there;
the preceptor should then place the two-faced jar in the middle.
Having properly covered the opening of the *pālikā* with straw, the preceptor, the instructor,
should wrap it with threads, mango leaves, and *darbha* grass; then,
having filled it with clay, he should place it in the outer compartments.
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, one should carry out the purification of the grains.
(2) One should fashion a seat within the pitcher and worship the Lord of Herbs (*Oṣadhīśa*).
One should also worship Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī on either side of the two pitchers. (3)
In each individual *pālikā*, one should worship the six deities who arise from their seats:
Vaikartana, Vivasvān, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, (4) Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣī, and Trivikrama. (5)
And Āditya, the great Sūrya, and Aṃśumān, the maker of day.
One should indeed worship these twelve Ādityas in earthen bowls;
[one should offer] sesame, mustard seeds, mung beans, black gram, peas, and *āḍhaka* beans.
The instructor [should take] horse-gram, barley, and wheat— the nine types of new grains—
and first wash them with water, and afterwards sprinkle them with milk.
One should have the Brāhmaṇas recite the *Oṣadhī-sūkta* mantra;
or, one should sow the succession of seeds with the specific mantra of each respective deity.
Thereafter, one should perform the sowing of seeds with auspicious flowers;
then the preceptor, having pervaded the *pālikās* with water from the moon-jar, [places them] there.
Again, having filled the jar with water, one should perform worship once more;
one should offer milk-rice, molasses-cakes, and betel-leaf.
In this way, one should perform the worship every day until the conclusion of the sacrifice.
O Guha, when the sprouts have attained growth, only auspiciousness will prevail.
Furthermore, if the sprouts are stunted or if a sprout takes on the appearance of smoke, [it portends otherwise].
The wise man should perform the expiation according to the prescribed rules.

(2) He should likewise offer betel leaves and sacrificial fees to the Brāhmaṇas who have recited the medicinal mantras, as well as to those who are highly auspicious, in accordance with the ritual injunctions. (3)
Having given betel-leaf and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to all the Brahmins,
