Now hear this rite of binding the protective thread from Kārttikeya.
(I.69a, 4) Having placed the water-pot dedicated to Varuṇa, one should perform the recitation of its hymn.
(5) Having performed the winter [rite] with the mantra, one should carry out the purification for protection.
The instructor, taking the root of the protective [mantra] with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand,
should perform the cleansing with ashes,
reciting the mantra "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ" while using the thumb and ring finger for protection. (6–7)
Having performed the protection ritual with the [mantra] facing upwards, one should dismiss [the deity] with the heart-mantra.
Betel, coconut, fruit, ash, and rice—these, as well as the protection, should be placed in a golden vessel by the hand of the Guru. (8)
Having purified [the site] with the *Vikṣaṇa* and other mantras, the Guru should perform worship for protection.
(9) In the midst of that, he should worship Ananta and the others, as well as the respective substances.
Having worshipped the three principles (*tattva*), he should perform the oblation of union (*sandhāna-huti*). (10)
Having performed the recitation of the *Āyusūkta* for protection together with the Brahmins,
and having placed the fire into the jar, one should perform purification at that sacred ford.
Then, having placed this vessel upon a palanquin together with the Brahmins— (I.69b) (2)
Having performed the circumambulation of the sacred site, the wise one went to the temple.
Having worshipped the six seats of arising and meditated upon the deity, one should perform the full worship.
On the Rudra portion of the *liṅga*, on the pedestal, and in the middle of the stalk— there, on the right hand,
is the binding of the deities beginning with Maheśvara.
One should perform the binding of protection upon the left hand of the Śaktis,
on the middle petal of the trident, on the central pillar of the pavilion, at the base of the horns of the bull,
and on the pole of the chariot. (4–5)
The instructor should bind the protective amulet at the wrist;
the preceptor should likewise perform the binding of the protective amulet for the officiating priests.
(6) This same procedure that was prescribed for the sprinkling is also prescribed for the binding. (7)
One should perform the binding of the protective thread with the Tṛyambaka mantra.
Having placed ashes upon that knot with the Astra-mantra, the preceptor [performs] the binding of the two Soma-pitchers; this, however, is the inferior method.
The binding of the protective amulet (*kautuka*) should be performed on the night prior to the day of the ritual attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*);
or, in its absence, one should perform it on that very day before the attraction.

The tying of the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) upon the deity is a constituent part of the festival of installation; the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) as prescribed by mantras is for the purification of the self of the preceptor.

By means of which the preceptor is purified from the defects of death-impurity and birth-impurity; that consecration which is performed by the wise even when it is devoid of the binding of the protective thread. (I.70a)
Because that [previous method] is fruitless, the best of preceptors should perform protection;
the most excellent of preceptors should perform the protection with gold, as prescribed for all cases.
Alternatively, it does not shine at all; therefore, the best of all iconographers should fashion it with a tail and a hood.
Likewise, the forearm should be half a finger-breadth [in length], equal to the wrist.
"O child, listen specifically to the storage of grain; the storage of grain is now being described.
(i.70a, 4) Barley, rice, wheat, and likewise beans—one *āḍhaka* each. (5)
Mustard, mung bean, chickpea, sesame,
and also pulse-free grain— these are proclaimed as the nine types of new grain.
A barley grain is said to be half a *yava*, and it is proclaimed that a *taṇḍula* consists of thirty such parts.
(6) Now hear concerning wheat, rice, black gram, green gram, and also *niṣpāva*; this shall be the measure for each respective grain. (7)
Of the six grains previously mentioned, one-third each of sesame and mustard seeds (8)—
the wise man should place these individually upon lotus leaves on the altar;
for each grain, there shall be a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp (9).
Then, having drawn lines with sesame seeds, one should thereafter place vajras;
this is declared to be the fourfold placement (*nyāsa*). Above that, having scattered fried rice, sandalwood, white mustard, ashes, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken grains—
Pure parched grains (lāja) and clarified butter (sudhi) should be poured there in succession.
The offering of garments, ornaments, and so forth for those who have been initiated is prescribed here.
The sun-god’s garment is the lower robe, and the upper garment is equal to it.
The garment for the body should be of three pieces, while the head-covering should be six cubits in length.
Silk is declared to be the best material, while woven cotton cloth is considered middling.
The cloth is declared to be of the Virgo (Kanyā) sign by those who know the Kāmikāgama;
indeed, a rite performed without a new cloth shall be fruitless.
To each initiate, however, one should cause a yogapaṭṭa to be given;
it should be four finger-breadths in width and six cubits in length.
Then, one should perform the ritual separately for the lower garment and the upper garment;
likewise for the rudrākṣa garland around the neck and the garland on the head.
Likewise, there should be arm-garlands for all the officiating priests as well.
(7) On their hands, they should wear fine rosaries that hang down as far as the region of the navel.
(8) A single-bead rosary is prescribed, adorned with jewels and gold.
And also earrings for the ears, or else ear-ornaments.
The purifier, the index finger, the bracelet, and the ring;
(9) as well as the thumb-seal, all adorned with the Śiva-mantra.
The wise one should draw the Śakti-mantra together with the Tāraka using the index finger;
likewise, he should draw a golden sacred thread and a golden waist-band.
Sandals fashioned from pearls and coral, adorned with various gems; a sandal-bag made of gold, resembling a water-pot;
and a tiger skin, or perhaps the skin of a black antelope.
The gods also delighted in the *barhāsana* seat upon the earth.

(3) Having thoroughly purified all these garments with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, the wise teacher should subsequently cause them to be bestowed upon those who have been initiated. (4)

I shall explain the production of the sacrificial fire; listen with reverence to your guru. The wise one should perform the oblation in the perpetual fire (nityāgni), or in its absence, the preceptor [should do so].
Having generated the fire according to the rules, he should perform the homa therein.
One should specifically procure the fire from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*); or one may produce it by friction using kindling sticks (*araṇi*) from the house of a twice-born;
or a wise person should perform the rite of *puṇyāhavācana* for the purpose of producing the fire.
Having recited the fire-mantras together with the Brahmins,
the wise preceptor, facing the sun, should display a sun-crystal.
Having placed a small amount of cotton there upon the lower fire-wood,
the wise man then generates fire therein and takes it up.
Fire produced from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta) is commended for all ritual acts; likewise, that which is born from a moonstone (candrakānta) is declared commendable by the wise. (10)
Having thus produced the fire and offered the fee for recitation,
that which is called the "eternal fire" (nityāgni) is described by the learned as the "fire of the form" (mūrti-agni).
The ritual for the Prasannapūjā—the procedure for the consecration of Prasanna—is now described here:
(i.71b, 2) In a beautiful pavilion for the assembly, smeared with cow dung and other [purifying substances]... (2)
Adorned with garlands of colors, beautified by canopies and banners, provided with plantain pillars, and decorated with clusters of betel-nut trees.
In the center of the pavilion, upon a platform spread with nine kinds of grains,
one should place jars that have been washed, fumigated with incense, encircled by three threads, filled with water,
and adorned with *kūrca* grass and sprouts. (4)
Coconut [vessels] with hanging tufts, adorned with cloth, perfumes, and so forth—(5) either a thousand or even a hundred jars;
or, at the very least, ten jars should be installed by the preceptor according to the prescribed rite. (6)
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should perform the *pañcagavya* rite;
then the wise practitioner should perform the worship according to the procedure prescribed for the bathing ceremony.
Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) before the water-jar (*ghaṭa*) in accordance with the rules, the preceptor—

Having offered one hundred oblations with the *mūla-mantra* and a tenth part with the *saṃhitā-mantra*, (8) and having offered one hundred oblations with the *aghora-mantra*, the wise practitioner should offer parched grain (*lāja*) as an auxiliary oblation (*brāṅga-āhuti*). He should then offer other substances with the five *mūla-mantras*, five times each. (9)

The preceptor should perform five oblations for each of the five [weapons] with each weapon, and he should also offer oblations with the *jaya* mantras and so forth; then he should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Wherever there may be one hundred or even a thousand jars, [the same procedure applies].
The wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to these numbers.
One should worship [the deities] from Śakti up to Śaktiparyanta within the root-liṅga;
one should worship Śiva with the five-fold enclosure-pūjā as previously described.
One should perform the consecration with the waters of ablution as previously described;
one should also offer the great oblation as a food offering, along with incense, lamps, and so forth.
Thus the best of instructors should perform the Prasannapūjā.
(3) Regarding the ornamentation of the jar, I shall now describe the ornamentation of the jar; listen with respect. (i.72a, 3)
Then, having gone to the inner sanctum at the top of the palace,
the wise man should perform the "heating of grain" (*dhānyastapana*) here as before;
for barley has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and mustard seeds have the *saṃra* [or *soma*] as their deity.

Mudga has Varuṇa as its deity, and caṇaka has Vāyu as its deity; niṣpāva has Soma as its deity, and sesame has Īśāna as its deity. (6) These grains and others should be offered to the gods, performing worship with their respective mantras.
The wise one should arrange everything, including the lines and the placement of the vajra, as before.
(7) There, the best of preceptors should deposit the full water-pot;
having filled it with two *droṇas* of water, it is proclaimed as the *śivakumbha*. (8)
The *vardhanī* jar is half that size, and the jars of the Knowledge-Lords (*vidyeśas*) are half that again.
Twenty-seven jars are thus proclaimed, with half of those [for the remaining deities].
The weapon-jar (*astrakumbha*) is declared to be equal in size to the Knowledge-jar (*vidyākumbha*).
The *vardhanī* should be half the size of that; this is proclaimed as the "two-faced" (*dvimukhī*).
All the jars (*kumbhas*) should be described as being new and without cracks. If clay jars are used according to one's means, one should avoid those of black color.
Having purified all the jars with the Astra-mantra,
the Preceptor should likewise wrap them with three threads, a single thread, and three threads.
The best [circumference] is indeed the size of a sesame seed; the middling is the measure of a barley grain;
the lowest is like the eye of an elephant—thus should the wrapping of the thread be.
Having wrapped a sixteen-petaled lotus around the Śiva-jar,
the wise one should wrap a twelve-petaled lotus around the Vardhanī vessel.
For the pitchers of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśa), there should be an eight-petalled lotus;
for the twenty-seven pitchers, it is proclaimed that there should be a four-petalled one.
The wise one should beautifully wrap [the object] with threads of five colors;
the wrapping is done with lead, using the *tantra* mantra as the armor-thread (*kavaca-sūtra*).
Having taken incense smoke with a formidable mantra into the jar,
the wise one should place the jars and other vessels upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using the *hiraṇyapātra* mantra.
[He should also prepare] a purifier (*pavitraka*) consisting of two blades of *darbha* grass joined at their tips with a knot in the middle.
The Guru should place [the water] into the jars using the thumb and ring finger.
(8) The filling of the jars with water is performed with the mantra "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.1.1).
Likewise, the sprinkling over the hands is performed with the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" (Ṛgveda 10.9.1). (9)
Having cast away the *kūrca* and the knot, one should worship the Lord of Waters (*Jaleśa*).
One should consecrate that water with the mantra "āpaḥ prāṇa.
[Then one should add] cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg leaf, and its fruit.
Uśīra, cavaka, hribera, and likewise rocanā.
Having combined all these and ground them into a powder, the wise one should cast it into the water of the ritual jar while reciting the mantra *gandhadvāram*.
Having filled the jar with snow, water, and the waters of the Gaṅgā,
the wise one [prepares] the *kūrca* for the Śiva-jar, characterized by thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass. (I.73a, 3)
Twenty-five *darbha* grasses are declared to be the *kūrca* for the *vardhanī*.
The *kūrca* for the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), however, is provided with fifteen *darbha* blades.
For all others, beginning with the attendants (*parivāra*), the *kūrca* is similar to that of the Lords of Knowledge.
The tip is said to be one *vedāṅgula* (four finger-breadths), and the knot is declared to be two *aṅgulas*.
The *kūrca* (brush-like base) is wound to the right, and the stalk is eighteen *aṅgulas* long.
The characteristic of the interior of the *kūrca* is that its beginning and end measure one cubit;
the stalk is fourteen finger-breadths long and consists of twenty-five blades of *darbha* grass. (7)
The characteristics of the *vardhanī* and the *kūrca* are as follows:
(8) The knot at the tip (*agragranthi*) is said to be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), while the tip (*agra*) is said to be three finger-breadths.
(9) The stalk (*nāla*) should be twelve finger-breadths; this is for the Vidyeśvaras.
The tip [of the *darbha*] should be directed upwards for the *pratiṣṭhā*; then the tip becomes the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
O Pārvatī, Vāgdevī resides at the knot of the *kūrca*, while at the root of the *kūrca* are all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and Sāvitrī is the presiding deity at the tip of the *kūrca*.
With the mantra "yo rudra," one should place the *kūrca* inside;
[it should contain] diamond, lapis lazuli, ruby, and likewise crystal;
(2) sapphire, emerald, pearl, and coral.
And one should also cast gomedhaka and the nine gems.
The wise one should place these five jewels— ruby, diamond, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and coral— into the vardhanī vessel.
One should place coral, pearl, and sapphire into all the jars. (4) For the jars beginning with that of Vidyeśa, one should deposit materials of their respective colors.
(5) One should deposit all the gems along with the jewels [of the deities] while reciting the mantra.
In the Śiva-pitcher, there should be a golden lotus; in the Vardhanī vessel, a golden *utpala* lily.
For the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), there is a golden trident, and for all [the other deities], a golden fillet (*paṭṭaka*).
Having inscribed their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should cast them into the center of the water. (6–7)
The water is situated in the middle of the pitcher, and the lotus is in the middle of the water;
within the lotus are Pārvatī and Parameśvara.
One should place a golden plate with the *Hiraṇyavarṇā* mantra.
Having placed wealth in all the water-pot sanctuaries (*kumbhatīrtha*), the preceptor (*deśika*) should place mango leaves, equal in number to the tufts of grass (*kūrca*), within the pots;
and he should place long, lifeless [blades of grass] in the outer regions. (I.74a)
The coconut-shaped vessel with an upward-pointing crest and a face in the middle is proclaimed to be the most excellent among all types of water-pots.
A pot lacking a crest should not be known here as a coconut-shaped vessel.
The preceptor himself, learned in the scriptures, should place it facing Śiva.
(3) Those who know the Āgamas have declared that a seat made of *kuśa* grass is the best, a red silk cloth is middling, and cotton cloth is the lowest. (4)
For the Śivakumbha, a silk cloth measuring six cubits is prescribed;
for the Vardhanī, half of that; for the Vidyeśas, half of that again.
For the twenty-seven [other] jars, half of that is prescribed.
For all the jars, a pair of cloths is prescribed.
(6) One should place a hanging tuft of wool inside, similar to the *kūrca* [used for purification];
one should place the hanging tuft with the mantra "tvam agne" (O Agni, you...). (7)

The wise preceptor should place the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) according to the prescribed rite into the *śiva-kumbha* (the auspicious vessel), along with a golden *bilva* leaf, adorned with various ornaments;
he should also [anoint it] with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), sandalwood paste, and the six fragrant substances (*ṣaḍgandha*). (8)
The wise one should make it free from smoke with flower garlands;
having carefully adorned and bound it, the best of preceptors [should proceed]. (9)
The Image Oblation:
"I shall now describe this image oblation; listen with interest, my child.
After first having the learned man proclaim an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), he should then perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). (I.74a, 10)
One should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityāgnihoma) and the worship of the Form and the Lord of the Form,
either in nine ways, or in five ways, or even as one alone.
It is taught that there are nine [types of] enclosures, and likewise five sacrificial pits;
alternatively, the wise have taught the performance of the image-oblation (mūrtihoma) in close proximity.
One should offer a thousand oblations or half of that at the base of Śiva;
half of that again for Manonmanī, and ten oblations with the limbs of Brahmā.
It is taught that for each Brahmā there are ten oblations;
following this sequence, one should offer to the respective deities in the sacrificial pits located in the intermediate and cardinal directions in due order.
One should offer three hundred oblations for each individual deity;
alternatively, the most excellent of teachers may perform one hundred oblations.
One should offer the substances such as fuel-sticks, food, and clarified butter according to the prescribed rules;
this is the sequence for the offering to the forms (mūrti-homa) proclaimed by the learned.
The purification of the three sections: having divided the Śiva-pitcher into three parts, one should likewise do so for the liṅga;
this triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra is called the "three sections."
Above the portion belonging to Śiva is the middle portion belonging to Viṣṇu;
the portion below is declared by those learned in the scriptures to belong to Brahmā, in the case of both the liṅga and the pitcher. (8)
One should worship the five principles in the portion of Rudra as the Śiva-tattva;
there, in the portion of Viṣṇu, one should perform the worship of the seven principles.
In the portion belonging to Brahmā, the wise one should worship the twenty-four principles;
likewise, in each of the three sections, he should perform the worship of the thirty-six principles.
Having worshipped each section as well as the deities and their presiding lords,
the Guru should worship [the principles] starting from the Śiva-tattva down to the earth-element.
One should worship on the pedestal in this very manner according to the path previously described.
(2) The Fire Offering for Joining the Channels:
O Guha, I shall describe to you the ritual known as the fire offering for joining the channels. (i.75a, 2)
The best [tube] should be made of gold, and likewise the middling one of silver.
A tube made of cotton is called the lowest by the wise.
It should be attached to the tip of the *liṅga* where the hair-tuft is located, and likewise to the tip of the water-pot.

Having bound the channel (nāḍī) by means of the path of investigation, the preceptor should bring the self, the pitcher, the fire, and the linga together, and cause [the rite] to be performed through the channel. He should place a single pitcher upon every part of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus, this sequence of scriptural injunctions applies to the fire-pit of Kuṇḍāgni.
(6) In other cases, for all the fire-pits, there should be a single jar for each;
and the Guru should worship the Support Power within that jar according to the prescribed rite. (7)
Having worshipped the three principles (tattvas), one should present incense and a lamp;
the wise practitioner should also worship [them] in the Ādhāraśakti pit.
Having worshipped the five kalās, this is the procedure for all the pits.
Having worshipped the three principles (tattvas) in the primary sacrificial pit (kuṇḍaka), one should honor the Guru.
In the intermediate and cardinal directions, in the sacrificial pits, one should also offer oblations with the weapon-mantra for the sake of channel-union to the embodied deities and their lords. (9)
One should worship the twenty-four principles in the small sacrificial pit (kuṇḍaka) representing the deity's form.
(10) The Guru should perform worship as before in the pits located in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
He should perform the fire-oblation (homa) there and offer one hundred oblations with the root mantra. (i.75b)
Then, having performed the *puṇyāha-vācana* rite, the preceptor should offer the remaining clarified butter into the *śānti-kumbha*,
present incense, lamps, and other offerings, and address a prayer to Brahmā.
Taking up the *śānti* jars, the most excellent of all preceptors, the wise one,
should go near the *śiva* jar and recite [mantras] in the *brahma* portion.
The wise preceptor, having respectfully performed the oblations with their respective mantras an equal number of times,
should then sprinkle the Śiva-kumbha with the waters from the Śānti-kumbha.
The wise one should perform worship as in the *homa* rite and pray for the reality of the self.
(4) Having taken up the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*), the Guru proceeds to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The wise one should worship as before and should properly honor the *vidyā-tattva*.
In the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions, the Guru should worship in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) as before.
One should also offer oblations as before and then perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
One should likewise join the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*) to the jar in due order.
The best of teachers should likewise perform the Śivatattva rite;
and upon the pedestal of Caṇḍikā, he should offer the oblation of touch.
Earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, wind,
the moon, and space— these nine are called the sacrificial pits, and these are the forms (mūrtis) intended for the sacrifice.
Bhava, Ugra, Śarva, Mahādeva, Rudraka, Bhīma, Paśupati, and Īśa—these are the eight forms that he assumed. (9)
Tamā, Mohā, Jayā, Ghorā, Rakṣā, Niṣṭhāmayā,
and likewise Rudrā— these eight powers of the *piṇḍikā* have been proclaimed.
In this very manner, one should then perform the oblation of touch (*sparśāhuti*).
Then one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and offer incense and lamps.
One should properly unite the form of the deity residing in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the primary *liṅga*. Afterwards, the Guru, remaining vigilant, should protect the fire.
I shall explain the method of attraction; listen with an attentive mind. One should perform the rite of attraction either in the forenoon or at midday.
One should not perform the drawing [of the yantra] either in the evening or at night;
however, for an immediate consecration, the drawing may be performed day or night.
One should perform the drawing of the site and the construction of the children's quarters during a movable ascendant;
the consecration of the root-temple is prescribed for a single fixed ascendant.
Then, from the *liṅga* [in the heart] to the *kumbha*, one should perform the drawing forth (*karṣaṇa*) and the installation (*sthāpana*) into the *liṅga*.
Having conceived the rising (*āsana*) within the *kumbha*, one should worship in sequence up to the *Śakti*.
By means of the path of investigation, one should invoke the form into the vessel;
having drawn forth the partless deity, the wise one should worship the manifest form.
That which is without limbs is declared *niraṅga*, and that which possesses limbs is called *sāṅga*. Above the digit of *śāntyatīta* is the lotus-face of *śānti*.
Knowledge is the chest-limb according to the rite; the secret maṇḍala is the foundation.
Cessation is the knees, shanks, and feet; the path of the worlds is the body hair.
The skin of colors, the blood of mantras, adorned with flesh;
(9) the marrow that is the end of reality, the white and other elements—the true enjoyment and liberation.
That light which extends to Śiva, to the end of the principles (*tattva*), which is all-pervasive and eternally auspicious, and whose limbs are undivided, is called "partless" (*niṣkala*).
But the "with-parts" (*sakala*) is said to have divided limbs and a body consisting of *vidyā* and the rest. (10)

That very [reality], when partless (*niṣkala*), is to be known as certainly becoming manifest with parts (*sakala*). That which is called "with parts" by the gods is indeed the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*) itself. The sixfold path is said to be twofold, according to the distinction between emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
The wise one should perform the placement starting from Śāntyātīta and ending with Nivṛtti;
this is declared to be the sequence of emanation by those who have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas.
Beginning with Nivṛtti and so forth, one should install [the kalās] up to Śāntyatītā according to the rule;
those who know this scripture call this "withdrawal" (saṃhāra) in this treatise.
In each of those arts as well, the wise one should place the respective principle, such as the worlds and so forth, and therein he should also join that particular form.
Having divided these Kalās into three, they consist of the natures of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The Śaivī-kalā is indeed called Śāntyatītā, and the Vaiṣṇavī is called Śānti.
One should join the remaining [principles] with the portions of Brahmā and this form;
Śiva is said to be the *tattva*, and Sadāśiva is the form itself.
The form that arises from the union of those two is called "existence" (bhāva).
Because it is the continuous state of Śiva-nature, it is described as being named "giving" (dāda).
For the sake of meditation and worship for all, the formless becomes manifest;
a guru should perform all this with devotion and even with a sense of awe.
(8) O God of gods, Lord of the world, Cause of the cause of the universe!
O All-pervading Lord, I have come to this jar for the sake of supporting the seat of Your liṅga;
yet I do not know the mantras and tantras, nor the scriptures or the meaning of the scriptures, nor the Āgamas that awaken one to Your true nature.
O Lord of Gods, out of compassion for me, come to this jar through the power of my recitation;
endowed with all coverings and possessed of all powers. (10)
O All-pervading Lord, come into this jar endowed with all sovereignty;
even the Vedas and the yogis do not clearly know your true nature.
O All-pervading Lord, how do I know the sages beginning with Sanaka?
And how is it that the Vedas proclaim Your form through the abandonment of [all] parts?
I know how the gods, being of deluded intellect, fill their bellies;
therefore, O ocean of compassion, come to this jar by the power of my merit.
Having thus offered prayers to the Lord of Gods, the Guru, endowed with devotion,
should meditate upon the God who is free from worldly taint (*nīrāñjana*) and is the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution—
resembling a thousand suns and resplendent like a mass of lightning. (4)
Having meditated upon Śiva as consisting of light and composed of *nāda* and *bindu*,
one should loudly recite the mantra according to the path instructed by the Guru.
By means of the yoga of the departure of Brahma and Āditya, one should properly join [the consciousness] from the *liṅga* into the *kumbha*.
The most excellent of teachers should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) upon the pitcher;
he should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and carry out the ritual services (*upacāra*).
Thereafter, having circumambulated the liṅga himself, the preceptor should pray to the deity within the pitcher and perform the *yātrā-homa* (the fire-sacrifice for the procession).
Whatever action has been performed by me now, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
and whatever was done either deficiently or excessively— forgive it, O Treasure of Compassion!
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should perform the *yātrā-homa* (the fire-offering for the procession).
(10) Regarding the *yātrā-homa*, this rite known as the *yātrā-homa* shall now be described; listen, O Six-faced One! (i.77a, 10)
After the drawing [of the deity] from the *liṅga*, the wise one should perform the *yātrā-homa*.
First, he should perform the *homa* for the houses beginning with the Sun and ending with Ketu,
according to the years, months, fortnights, seasons, and solstices.
By means of the *tithis*, days (*vāsara*), yogas, and *karanas*; by means of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), zodiac signs (*rāśi*), ascendants (*lagna*), and *horās*;
(3) and by means of the *dhāmas*, *muhūrtas*, moments (*kṣaṇika*), and even *nimeṣas*, the Teacher [perceives].
The wise practitioner should perform the fire oblation with *kāṣṭhās* and *kalās*. Furthermore,
for all the aforementioned *adhipatis* and *pratyadhidevatās*,
he should specifically perform the oblation preceded by the formal dedication (*uddeśa*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Those deities who are deprived of the journey-offering (*yātrā-homa*) become obstructors.
Therefore, a wise person should perform the journey-offering with every effort.
(6) The Giving of the Journey-Offering.

I shall now describe this gift for the journey; listen with interest, my child. (i.77b, 6) One should perform the gift for the sake of the journey for those initiated Brahmins. (7) Thereafter, the wise man should perform the house-consecration rite according to the rules.
One should perform the tenfold gift and carry out the offering of the *kaṇṇikā*.
Therein, one should properly perform various kinds of gifts.
The preceptor himself [should select] a young man who has been initiated and possesses a firm body. (8–9)
Having respectfully summoned him and bound a cloth upon his head, one should worship the bull after marking its forehead with scents and flowers;
then, with a mind full of vigilance, one should place the water-pot there. (10)
One should perform this same procedure for the other jars as well.
The Guru, whose form is the light of the sun and other luminaries, [should enter] the temple in that sequence,
scattering flowers made of silver and gold.
With parched grain, unbroken rice, and fragrant waters mixed with snow and sandalwood paste,
preceded by various musical instruments, and with umbrellas, chowries, and the foremost [attendants],
accompanied by Brahmins chanting the Vedas and singers playing the flute. (3)
And by those skilled in the art of drama, who were blowing conch shells and uttering the cries of courtesans,
they caused the jars— adorned with lamps and accompanied by men wearing turbans— to be carried forth. (4-5)
When the Śambhava [fire] has been spread out step by step, the Preceptor and the officiating priests, having taken darbha grass in their hands together with the Brāhmaṇas,
should indeed recite the root mantra while the Principal Preceptor himself presides. (6)
Having touched those jars while reciting their respective mantras,
the officiating priests performed a circumambulation of the sacred site and went outside the house,
preceded by all the ritual services beginning with water for the guest-offering and water for washing the feet. (7–8)
The Guru should enter the sacrificial hall by way of the path of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
Having brought the sacrificial altar and the water-jars, he should worship and install Ananta and the other deities.
Then, the Guru himself, having placed the *vardhanī* vessel on his left side, [proceeds].
And one should place all the jars facing toward Śiva.
[One should also offer] milk, molasses, pure parched grains, and fruits.
Having presented the food offering to them, one should perform the benediction.
Then, having gone below the temple, the most excellent teachers should first [perform the rite].
In that aforementioned fire of the form, one should offer the expiatory oblation;
(2) one should also offer the oblations of the *jaya* and other mantras, as well as the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire.
Having performed the ritual removal of the fire, one should perform the production of the sacrificial fires;
one should perform the production of the fires according to the very path previously described.
After sunset, the preceptor should begin the sacrifice.
Because of its fullness, one should perform this at night;
since the day is a deficient time, one should not begin a sacrifice during the day.
The best of teachers should perform the commencement of worship at the onset of evening.
On the following day, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) both in the evening and in the morning.
It is a settled rule that the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) should be performed during the day and not at night.
If the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) is to be done immediately, one may perform it either by day or by night.
The ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) shall be performed in the same manner; thus is the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) remembered.
(7) I shall describe the procedure for the sacrifice and worship; listen specifically, O child!
The preceptor (*ācārya*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having bathed in the evening and being composed in mind, (8)
Having entered the sacrificial hall, one should perform the daily worship.
One should respectfully carry out the ritual for the daily worship and the rite for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) therein.
[One should also perform] the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*), the offering of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the dismissal of the floral remains (*nirmālya*).
By means of the path of channel-union, through the application of the brush upon the mirror.
The preceptor himself should perform the consecration upon a mirror;
thereafter, having joined the channel (nāḍī) together with the beard [of hair] into the divine jar.
The wise one should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings as in the daily rite.
(11) The most excellent preceptor should place four water-pots in the four corners.
To the east of this southern door and to the west of the fire-pot,
one should place a pair of pots in that middle space and cast the fuel-wood into them.
The wise one should place the remaining pitchers here at the center of the door-sides;
he should also place twenty-seven pitchers in those positions.
In the northeast, at the center of the altar, he should place a pair of pitchers.
Adorned with the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) extending from the altar (vedī) to the end of the north,
one should place the ten weapons and then perform the rite for a "holy day" (puṇyāha).
At night, there is worship of Soma, while during the day, there is worship of the Sun.
The best of preceptors should first perform the worship of those two;
having performed the adoration of the Moon and the Sun, he should go outside the pavilion.
Having washed one's feet and hands, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and apply the sacred ash (bhasman).
Then, returning once more to the sacrificial hall (yāga-śālā), one should perform the general offering of water (sāmānyārghya).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground in the midst of that, one who has transcended peace (śāntyātīta) should worship [it].
One should worship Sadāśiva, Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, and Astra in the intermediate space.
The preceptor should first worship the southern and western ends;
likewise, he should worship according to the rules at the arches and the door.
At the western gate of strength, there is peace, the oblation, and likewise health;
and also Bhadra, Vijaya, and Nīlalohita. (8)
And one should worship the Vajra in the western quarter, as well as the presiding deities;
one should likewise perform the four Vedas at the four gates and the four-limbed ritual.
One should worship Vasu, Marut, and Guru upon the tridents;
as well as Praśānta, Śiśira, Parjanya, and Jayantaka. (10)
One should worship these eight attendants— Dhanada, Śrīprada, Bhūta, Amṛta, and Jīvana— in the center of the banners.
One should worship the Lokas and others at the base of the branch, and Soma and others at the tip;
one should worship the letters from the *ka*-group to the *kṣa*-group upon the cloth of the banner.
On the left side of the doors, one should worship the Kalākumbhas;
(3) in the middle of the doors, one should also worship Maheśa and the other deities of the mantras.
(4) [One should worship] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.

One should worship Śaṅkhukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita above the door; one should constantly worship the door itself. Furthermore, one should worship the deities of the door outside the western door.
Bhuvaṅga and Pataṅga are located in the upper and lower regions of the nose;
between those two, one should worship Ramā, Vāṇī, and Vighnarāja.
And one should worship Nandin and Mahākāla, as well as Gaṅgā and Kālindī, on the right and left of the door; [furthermore,] the worship of Daṇḍin and Muṇḍin.
Having worshipped the bull at the front of the door, the moon and sun on the two door-panels, the Earth upon the stone slab, the deities of the mantra within the cavity,
the Vasus in the pegs, and the Maruts from the region of the base; (9) [one should proceed].

One should worship all the deities and offer incense and lamps. With the weapon-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ," one should stamp the ground with the heel to ward off the hosts of obstacles in the earth, the atmosphere, and heaven. (i.80a)
The wise practitioner should perform the trampling of the heel three times with the root mantra. Having gazed at heaven, he should likewise act in the intermediate space.
He should cast a flower with the forefinger while reciting the Astra-mantra ending in "hūṃ phaṭ."
Having worshipped Vighnarāja, one should secure the other doors.
(3) One should touch the threshold-stone with the left foot while reciting the Varma mantra;
then, taking hold of the left door-post, one should proceed with the right foot foremost. (4)
Having entered within, the preceptor should worship at the door with the *astra-mantra* and the root mantra;

having performed the circumambulation of the sacrificial site, he should then, from the south-western direction, worship the grass and other materials for binding the cloth with the *kṣiti* and other mantras. (5) The Guru should perform the worship with the *kṣiti* and other [mantras].
One should worship Dharma and the other [deities] within the pillars, proceeding clockwise. (6) Outside of that, on twelve pillars, one performs the worship of the twelve Ādityas;
having worshipped the eight banners, one performs the worship of the eight auspicious signs (aṣṭamaṅgala). (7)
The wise practitioner should visualize the pavilion as pervaded by the state of Sadāśiva. On the southern side of the altar, upon seats made of tiger skins and similar materials,
the Guru should sit properly, facing north.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having performed the internal sacrifice and worship, one should perform the purification of the site (sthānaśuddhi).
Having established the arghya water there, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances (dravyaśuddhi).
Relying upon the hand of Śiva, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
One should fashion a sword of knowledge joined with thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass. The wise one should form a knot in the shape of a braid at the end of the handle.
The tip is said to be four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula); two hands shall constitute one *gula*.
(2) The two feet are to be made in the same way, while the neck is six *aṅgulas*.
The wise say that the remaining limb measures twelve *aṅgulas*. (3)
It should be made from the root to the tip, measuring exactly one cubit in length;
for the sword of knowledge, one should consecrate the weapon-mantra seven times. The preceptor, with an undistracted mind, should hold it against his own right hip.
In the southwest, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and immediately thereafter, having gathered parched rice,
sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, flowers, kuśa grass,
and unbroken grains into a shallow bowl, one should cast in the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga).
Having purified this [site] through inspection and other rites according to the rules, the Guru himself,
as the instructor, should properly worship it with the *saṃhitā* mantras.
For the purpose of removing defects (*śalya*), he should purify the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇṭapa*).
The best of teachers should perform eighteen preparatory rites (saṃskāra).
He should place the substances contained in the shallow bowls within the sacrificial pavilion.
Having sprinkled the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should consecrate them in the sacrificial pavilion.
The wise and learned practitioner, for the sake of pacifying obstacles in the intermediate space, should sprinkle pure parched grains (*lāja*), *kuśa* grass, and water for honor (*arghya*) together.
He should place the *arghya* vessel and the *pāśupata* weapon at the boundary of the *vardhanī*.
The wise preceptor should place the sword of knowledge motionless in his hand. Having grasped it and held it as before, he should worship according to the ritual rule in the southwest.
He should then worship Mahālakṣmī in the southern jar of Vāyu.
Alternatively, one should worship the Kṣetrapāla or the weapon-mantra in the northeast,
as well as the Pañcavardhanī of the weapon, according to the procedure for the movable seat.
One should worship Bhūtanandī and the others in sequence as the second enclosure;
one should worship the ten jars from Indra up to Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped the ten weapons, the Guru should proclaim the command of Śiva.
(4) The Ācārya, holding the *vardhanī* vessel and the weapon-vessel (*astrakumbha*) from the disciple, [should proceed].
Chanting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), the wise one continuously poured a stream from the spout of the *vardhanī* vessel into the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) all around the sacrificial hall.
Having performed a circumambulation, the wise one should establish a firm seat for it in its former place;
likewise, having fashioned the sword of knowledge, he should deposit it within the *vardhanī* vessel.
Indeed, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice, one should cause the two of them to hear the command of Śiva.
(7) One should worship Gaṇeśa at the pitcher of Vāyu in the eastern direction. (8) One should worship the seven Gurus at the pitcher situated before the pitcher of Soma.
Having formally requested permission from the gurus, the wise practitioner should make the following petition:
(9) "The names of the jars, as approved by the scriptures, shall now be stated.
On the northern side of the eastern gate are Sva-yaṃ-bhū, Nandi, and Śānti. (10)
On its very right flank is remembered Kāśīndravaras;
to the east of the southern gate, however, Bhṛṅgin and Agni are remembered.
At the western side of that same gate are Heramba and Yamaveghasa.
Nairṛti, Viṣṇu, Vṛṣabha, and Nivṛttikā—these are proclaimed to be on the right side of the western gate. On the northern side of the gate are Vāyu, Āpa, Varuṇa, and Guru. (3)
O Goddess, Pratiṣṭhā and the Vighnas are in the western part of the northern gate;
and in the eastern portion of that [gate] are Caṇḍeśa and those who honor the Guru.
Thus, twenty-seven names of the *kumbhas* have been proclaimed;
these are the names of the *kumbhas* for this Śiva-sacrifice.
In non-auspicious sacrifices, these pitchers are likewise approved:
Sūrya, Kalā, Brahmā, Lakṣmī, Vighneśa, and Deśika; and Astra and Astravardhanī, according to the sages who are experts in the scriptures. (5–6)
The knower of the scriptures, possessing double wisdom, should worship the third and fourth enclosure of this deity, Kumbheśvara. Then,
having gone to the southern side of the altar, the best of preceptors [should proceed].
Having sprinkled the altar with water, the preceptor should worship it according to the rules.
(8) Having worshipped the five seats, he should worship the form of Śiva;
and on the left side of the deity, he should worship the *vardhanī* vessel. (9)
The gate whose face is directed eastward has a human face;
having worshipped that [gate] and likewise the heart and other [limbs], the wise one should perform the worship of the second enclosure and so forth, beginning from the east. (10)
Having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, and ritual services, the face of the abode of Maghā was turned toward the west;
thus it is said, "O child, listen, and hear the reason for this. (2)
The western door is proclaimed as Sadyojāta;
and because of the Lord’s state of cessation (nivṛtti), that face is considered Tatpuruṣa.
Not seeing the connection between these two as it has been proclaimed,
Śambhu exists with his mouth made turbid by the venom of the serpent’s fangs.
I shall describe the procedure for the fire-rite; listen, O child, with attention.
Having taken the vessel of fire in the hand, one should circumambulate the altar clockwise.
Then, having sat down himself at the vicinity of the edge of the pit, the Guru,
the instructor, should purify the pit by means of the fourfold inspection and other rites.
Having performed the eight purificatory rites beginning with *ghananāda*, the best of teachers should then place the five *kalās* there in the five locations, starting from the center.
One should encircle the sacrificial pit with a thread and then worship it with the *kalās*.
Whether in a pit, or on a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*), or even on sand or a heap of husks;
The wise man should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit;
he should draw two lines upon it with two *kuśa* blades, one pointing eastward and the other pointing northward.
One should draw the central line with the mantra *brahmajajñānam*;
one should draw [the line] to the south with the mantra *nāke suparṇam*;
and one should draw the northern line with the mantra *āpyāyasva*.
One should draw a horizontal line across the middle with the mantra "yo rudra" (10).
One should draw a horizontal line on the western [side] with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," and one should draw a line on the eastern [side] with the mantra "indraṃ viśvā" (11).
Having sprinkled with water, one should discard the wooden splinter;
one should cast away two blades of darbha grass, tripled and shaped like a trident.
And the preceptor performs this vajrīkaraṇa with the Śiva-mantra,
[using] two blades of darbha grass joined together, one with its tip pointing east and the other with its tip pointing north.
One should cast this four-line placement with the heart mantra;
the seat, free of knots, consists of twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass.
The wise one should wrap a circle with a cord sixteen *aṅgulas* long;
having placed the tip toward the northeast (Īśāna) in the center of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), he should invoke Vāgīśvarī.
Having performed the invocation and worship, one should then offer incense and a lamp.
Listen now as the fruit of that [offering] is described, provided it is a *kūrca* with a knot.
When the knot has been burnt, impurity shall arise here;
for the sake of purifying the defect of that day and the Sun, the wise person should perform a bath there.
For it is proclaimed that in the absence of bathing, the ritual action becomes fruitless;
for this reason, one should prepare a tuft of hair (kūrca) that is devoid of knots.
Then, having untied the knot, one should place the *sudhi* in either an earthen vessel or a copper vessel and cast it into the fire-altar at the southeast, northeast, or southwest corner.
The preceptor should cast the *śakala* toward the southwest with the weapon-mantra.
Having purified it through the rites of inspection and so forth, he should worship the form of the Fire-god.
The wise practitioner should join this fire into the navel-fire and the bindu-fire by means of the sequence beginning with exhalation (recaka); thereafter follows the joining of the external fire.
Having performed the worship together with [the attendants], having protected [the deity] and veiled [the altar],
and having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the root mantra, one should do so with the mantra "devasya tvā."
Having taken the vessel with both hands and whirled it three times around the pit,
one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Śiva while keeping the pair of knees level with the nose.
The preceptor himself should place the fire, which consists of the essence of Vāgīśa and Bindu, into the womb of Vāgīśvarī by means of the Śiva-mantra. (2)
Having cast the fire from his own city while reciting the mantra "juṣṭo damūnā," the Guru,
having performed the recitation and offered the upper garment according to the prescribed rite, [proceeds].
Having offered water for purification and likewise water for sipping (ācamanīya),
one should place fuel-wood into the fire and kindle it with the Astra-mantra.
(4) Having worshipped the fire of the womb (garbhāgni), one should perform the protective rite of the *kautuka*.
The wise one should place the weapon-mantras on the girdle on the right side. (5) One should perform the rite for the spirits following the tonsure ceremony up until the initiation.
One should likewise perform the rites for returning home up until the marriage ceremony. (6)
Thereafter, having worshipped the two parents and offered the oblation, one desiring to perform the rite should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.
If the flames, smoke, and sounds are contrary to the [prescribed] castes, the wise one, having sprinkled water around the fire, should prescribe the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
(7) If these are the opposite, the expiation is ordained.
After dismissing the two parents, one should perform the *vyāhṛti* oblations and the sprinkling of water.

(8) Having offered the limb-oblations (*aṅgāhuti*) into the fire, one should respectfully divide the fire according to the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḷa*), as prescribed in the scriptures, for the purpose of the incense, lamp, and *caru*. (9)
The best of preceptors should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) in each respective pit (*kuṇḍa*).
For if the pit is devoid of consecration, the fire will become fruitless.
One should prepare the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the fire of the *caru*, while the remaining fire is used for incense and lamps.
The wise man, having taken the sacrificial oblation (*caru*), should place it near the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
(11) Here, the learned one should pray to Agni and thereafter perform meditation (*dhyāna*): "O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor, for you are the supreme purifier. (i.83b)
Therefore, having led [the deity] beyond [that], I establish and satisfy the Lord within the lotus of the heart.
Having established the God right there, one should perform the worship along with the retinue.
One should perform the contemplation of the faces while reciting the root mantra.
The wise practitioner should cause the splendor arising from the nose of Śiva, which is absorbed in the crest, to move.
Then, for the sake of the teachers, one should perform the joining of the channels at the location of the fire-pot.
One should perform the libation one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. (3–4)
Having offered ten parts of that [number] to Brahmā and Agni, one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
One should also perform the special libation (*viśeṣatarpaṇa*) exactly as before.
The Guru should offer oblations according to his capacity for the sake of neutralizing defects such as ill omens and the like.
For the purpose of purification, one should offer the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
(6) Afterwards, one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and carry out the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the kindling (*dīpana*).
Thus, in the system known as the *kuṇḍa* [tradition], this is declared to be the root oblation. (7)
The four-thousandfold oblation is traditionally known as the "fifty."
The measure of the oblation is one *karṣa* of cow’s ghee; one should then perform a single offering.
Two finger-joints of ghee on the forefinger is designated as a "drop" (*bindu*). (I.84b) (2)
Six *bindus* make one *karṣa*; two of those make a *kuḍupa*.
Two *karṣas* make a *muṣṭi*, and two of those make a *prasṛti*. Two of those are declared to be a *kuḍupa*, and twenty of those make a *dhāraṇa*.
Retention is said to yield a fruit, while [the rite] performed with *pra* yields twentyfold fruit.

That which ends with *sa* and ends with *la*, mixed together, with *sa* at the end of the mixture and joined with *sa* at its conclusion—within that, one should perform the oblation in the fire, without an oblation in the middle. (4–5)
At the end of the mantra, the deity attains satisfaction; in the middle, it becomes dear to the Daityas. One should take twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the flame of the ghee-filled ladle.
If [the fuel] is cut into pieces the size of a barley grain, the oblation becomes fruitless.
Ghee should be taken with the thumb facing downwards, reaching to the end of the joint at its base.
Or else, this [offering] is declared to be the "delightful thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha-lalita*), consisting of thirty-two *bindu*s. One *niṣka* consists of a full *ghṛtāṅguli*;
having offered one hundred *prastha*s of clarified butter, five *prastha*s yield one thousand [units].
Without performing ten hundred thousand [oblations], one should perform five hundred thousand; however, a hundred thousand oblations for the *punarāvarta* is called the supreme offering.
And having divided the highest into three parts— the middle and the lowest—
one should likewise divide the lowest into three parts, according to one's wealth and the time.
With milk and honey, curd should be offered as a full oblation;
one should likewise offer sesame and mustard seeds with only the power [of the mantra].
With twenty-five measures of rice increased by two,
and likewise with *priyaṅgu* and *gomaru*, it should be carried like a small measure of sesame;
when filled, it is called a *śukti*, and one should have it made according to that very standard of measurement.
One should offer cooked rice with a handful [of water] reaching the eye, and *kuluttha* beans with half a handful;
*niṣpāva* beans are said to be offered with nine [handfuls]. *Yava*, bamboo, and *kuluttha* are treated like [the preceding];
one should offer fragrant substances such as camphor and the like by the measure of a *māṣa*.
One should offer a *śāli* rice grain with a mere measure of power (*śakti*), twenty grains each of mung beans and black gram,
and a handful of parched grain (*pṛthuka*), coriander (*dhānyaka*), and roasted flour (*saktu*) for the oblation.
Having pierced the fruits with their own measure, the leaves with the number of arrows (five),
and the *phanasa* fruit with a thirty-first part, one should offer them into the fire.
Having pierced the bulbous root (*kanda*) with the measure of the fruit as prescribed, one should offer it into the fire.
A *guḍa* is said to be of that [same] measure, and a *mapūpa* according to its own standard.
One may offer milk-rice, *kṛsara*-rice, or *guḍa*-rice according to one's capacity;
the substance should be offered with the hand, and the prepared substance with a *sruva* ladle. (10–11)
Having placed the food in the vessel, one should offer it according to the prescribed measure.

One should prepare the *caru*—that which measures one *prastha*—for the rite of oblation (*homakarman*). That [measure] would be the lowest for the oblation; double that would be the middling. (I.85b, 2–3)
The best [vessel] is said to be threefold, not fashioned from an ordinary receptacle;
filled with a *kuḍupa* of [grain], one should cook it for the Piśācas.
(4) One should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with a *sruva* ladle using two *dīpa* measures of clarified butter. (5)
Its length should be one solar digit (ādityāṅgula), its circumference that of the little finger; it should be straight, well-polished, dry, and brings about auspiciousness. (I.85b, 5)
The length of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), equal to the width of the altar;
one should discard the middle finger’s circumference along with its tip.
It has been stated by Samitta that one should gather the enclosing sticks and fuel;
if the sacrificial pit has a single girdle, one should spread [the grass] around the girdles. (8)
In the second and third [fire-pits], there are three double-lines; however, in the middle pit, there are two double-lines.
It is said that the external strewing of grass is performed upon the pit or the sacrificial mound.
The seat (*viṣṭara*) is joined with *dhātukāśa* grass, knotted with its tips facing to the left;
the root and tip should be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the knot should be four finger-breadths.

The wise one should offer the oblation according to his means; whether residing in the *liṅga* or in the fire, he should worship with the sacrificial offering (*havis*) as is fitting for the Arhat. Since Śiva is indeed one, Sadāśiva is therefore present in both places.
Having reflected thus, one should diligently worship Śiva with *eluṅga* in the fire;
[this is] the external *bali*.
